# Thesis-Grade Codebase Report: whatif-freight-router

Date: May 6, 2026

Repository basis: local repository snapshot at the repository root, inspected and edited on May 6, 2026. Repo-relative paths are used in this report unless a generated artifact explicitly records an exporter-origin path as metadata.

Evidence policy: implementation truth, generated-result truth, test truth, and artifact truth are repo-local. External academic papers, standards, and product documentation are used for literature positioning, comparator framing, method provenance, and publication context; they do not override repository evidence or convert empirical results into theorem-backed claims.

## Abstract

WhatIf Freight Router investigates how freight-routing software can move from returning a plausible path to returning an auditable route decision. In operational freight routing, the useful answer is rarely just the minimum-distance or minimum-time route: the decision also depends on cost, emissions, tolls, terrain, departure time, traffic/weather pressure, route-source disagreement, evidence freshness, and the user's tolerance for trade-offs. The thesis problem is therefore a decision-quality problem under incomplete candidate search, uncertain evidence, and partially specified preferences. A better solution means a better decision contract: the system should expose why a recommendation is supported, which alternatives remain plausible, which assumptions were used, which evidence was fresh enough to trust, and when the available evidence justifies a set-valued answer or a typed abstention instead of a forced singleton route.

The core design contribution is **Evidence-Bounded Route-Decision Certification (EB-RDC)**, an implemented route-decision architecture that composes mature routing substrates with certification-facing decision logic. Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM), OpenRouteService (ORS), and local graph search provide candidate route evidence; Decision-Critical Candidate Screening (DCCS) identifies candidates whose refinement can materially affect the decision; Route-Evidence Frontier Certification (REFC) evaluates candidates across bounded, replayable evidence worlds; the preference-state layer preserves ambiguity instead of collapsing every user into one hidden weight vector; and the VOI-AD2R controller chooses whether to refine routes, refresh evidence, resample stochastic worlds, ask preference questions, stop, or abstain using an auditable value-per-cost surrogate. The terminal object is a decision package whose certification-facing outcome is one of `certified_singleton`, `certified_set`, or `typed_abstention`, with abstention reason families for search, evidence, preference, support, budget, and model-assumption insufficiency.

The software design is part of the research contribution rather than merely implementation detail. The system is built as a Python/FastAPI backend, a Next.js frontend, prepared OSRM/ORS routing services, strict UK-focused model/data assets, and artifact/provenance stores that preserve route candidates, certificates, sampled-world manifests, VOI traces, support summaries, cache-reuse evidence, and reviewer exports. Strict runtime checks, signature/provenance records, bounded evidence worlds, and endpoint-level terminal semantics turn the application into a design-science artifact: a working system whose architecture encodes the research claim. This aligns with design-science guidance that an information-systems contribution should connect a relevant problem, an artifact, design rationale, evaluation, and communicated knowledge [Hevner et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.2307/25148625), [Peffers et al. 2007](https://doi.org/10.2753/MIS0742-1222240302), [Gregor and Hevner 2013](https://doi.org/10.25300/MISQ/2013/37.2.01), [Wieringa 2014](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-43839-8).

The chapter organisation follows the dependency structure of the artifact. The introduction motivates the route-decision problem and states the contribution; the background and literature review establish why shortest-path routing, alternative-route generation, multicriteria decision analysis, robust/stochastic routing, value of information, selective prediction, and reproducible software evidence each solve only part of the problem; the mathematical chapters define candidates, frontiers, bounded evidence worlds, preference state, certificate thresholds, and terminal decisions; the algorithm chapter names EB-RDC and its DCCS, REFC, preference, VOI, and abstention subroutines; the requirements and experimental-design chapter links the intended claims to tests, artifacts, baselines, and validity threats; the architecture chapter shows how the software design realizes those requirements in backend, frontend, data, and provenance modules; and the evaluation chapter interprets checked results, ablations, limitations, and design implications. That ordering matters because each chapter makes the next one evaluable: literature defines the gap, mathematics defines the objects, algorithms define the procedure, software architecture makes it runnable, and evaluation checks whether the implemented artifact supports the scoped thesis claim.

The design implications are intentionally practical. Freight-routing recommendations become inspectable evidence objects rather than one-line route answers; uncertainty becomes a typed part of the API rather than a hidden caveat; preference ambiguity is preserved until there is enough information to resolve it; and failure states become operationally meaningful because they point to remedy families such as widening search, refreshing evidence, expanding support, increasing budget, or eliciting preferences. The work draws on value-of-information theory [Howard 1966](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074), decision-theoretic control of computation [Russell and Wefald 1991](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(91)90015-C), reject-option decision making [Chow 1970](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406), road-network routing [Dijkstra 1959](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390), [Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael 1968](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136), [Yen 1971](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.17.11.712), [Geisberger et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-68552-4_24), [Delling et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.2014.0579), and multicriteria/preference reasoning [Ehrgott 2005](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-27659-9), [Opricovic and Tzeng 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0377-2217(03)00020-1), [Lahdelma and Salminen 2001](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.49.3.444.11220), [Boutilier et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2006.02.003). The repository contribution is the route-specific, source-readable composition of these ideas into a bounded freight-route decision contract.

Evaluation is treated as artifacted evidence rather than anecdotal demonstration. The repository records unit and contract tests, endpoint parity checks, docs consistency checks, generated reviewer bundles, lane manifests, current checked metrics, theorem maps, claim matrices, and negative-result ledgers. The current checked reviewer package supports the paper's applied-evidence framing: headline adoption-style checks, sample-size evidence, hot-rerun/cache-reuse evidence, current fairness count, and suite-level publication-blocker fields are green on the checked slice, with `publishable_on_current_evidence=true`, `adoption_claim_supported=true`, and `publishability_blockers=[]` under the maintained evidence policy. The thesis claim remains deliberately evidence-bounded: certification claims are scoped to the generated candidate set, sampled evidence-world manifest, support assumptions, configured thresholds, preference state, budgets, and model validity recorded for each run. This makes the project strongest as an applied computer-science thesis and later applied-systems paper: it contributes a traceable software design and named algorithmic decision architecture for freight-route certification, with clear evidence of implementation depth, evaluation discipline, and the conditions under which its results should be read.

## Method Provenance And Originality Policy

Throughout this report, standard algorithm names denote cited ingredients. Dijkstra/A*, Yen-style K-shortest paths, Pareto filtering, VIKOR-style compromise ranking, epsilon constraints, CVaR, confidence sequences, value-of-information reasoning, metareasoning, and reject-option/selective-decision ideas should be cited to their source literatures whenever they are discussed. The project-owned contribution is the freight-route decision contract and artifacted integration: candidate generation is lifted into decision-critical screening, multicriteria route evidence is lifted into bounded-world certification, preference ambiguity is preserved as state, further computation is selected by a route-specific value-per-cost controller, and terminal outcomes are exposed as certified singleton, certified set, or typed abstention.

The safe originality sentence for the thesis is: **EB-RDC is an implemented algorithmic architecture for evidence-bounded freight-route decision certification; it composes and adapts mature routing, multicriteria, uncertainty, preference, VOI, and selective-decision methods into a source-readable route-decision contract with replayable evidence artifacts.** Appendix AX97 gives the detailed source-attribution audit and code snippets that show where standard algorithms are cited and where the repository adds route-specific constraints, thresholds, diagnostics, artifacts, and terminal semantics.

## Proof Status And Theorem Map

This report treats the theorem package, theorem-to-artifact map, and claim matrices as front-door evidence rather than appendix-only references, and the substance is summarized here so a reader is not forced to leave this file to understand the proof boundary. The maintained theorem package is a named `partial-proof` package, not a full theorem-backed closure of the whole system. Its purpose is to make the proof obligations explicit: every theorem-style, proposition, or lower-bound family must name its assumptions, code objects, tests, artifact fields, evaluator metrics, and report landing zone before it can be cited as more than empirical implementation evidence.

The proof-status surface can be read as follows.

| Family | Current maturity | Main claim being mapped | Code/test/artifact evidence style | Open proof boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Safe DCCS elimination | `partial-proof` | Candidate pruning is safe when envelope assumptions hold. | `backend/app/decision_critical.py`, `backend/app/candidate_bounds.py`, DCCS tests, `dccs_candidates.jsonl`, safe-prune metrics. | Full proof text and assumption packaging are still incomplete. |
| Anytime winner certification | `partial-proof` | Route-evidence frontier certification (REFC) winner certificates are meaningful under confidence-sequence and world-model assumptions. | `confidence_sequences.py`, `evidence_certification.py`, REFC tests, `winner_confidence_state.json`, certificate metrics. | Time-uniform proof closure remains incomplete. |
| Pairwise challenger separation | `partial-proof` | Active challengers and runner-up gaps are exposed rather than hidden. | `pairwise_gap_model.py`, REFC artifact contract tests, `pairwise_gap_state.json`, runner-up-gap metrics. | Dedicated challenger-gap proof text remains incomplete. |
| Flip-radius and decision-region stability | `partial-proof` | Stability is expressed as a minimum perturbation or flip budget. | `flip_radius.py`, `decision_region.py`, exact-synthetic tests, `flip_radius_summary.json`. | Full perturbation proof text remains incomplete. |
| Preference robustness and irrelevance | `partial-proof` | Necessary/possible-best reasoning and no-query conditions must be conservative. | `preference_state.py`, preference-surface tests, `preference_state.json`, query-count and success metrics. | Preference proof text and elicitation assumptions remain incomplete. |
| Certified set and singleton refusal | `partial-proof` | A set can be safely certified while a singleton remains unjustified. | `certified_set.py`, terminal-semantics tests, `certified_set_summary.json`, singleton-not-justified metrics. | Certified-set theorem closure remains incomplete. |
| Hidden challenger and search impossibility | `partial-proof` | Search cannot close certification while possible-winner mass remains live. | DCCS/VOI tests, `dccs_summary.json`, `voi_stop_certificate.json`, search-gap metrics. | Impossibility proof text and evaluator-scale closure remain incomplete. |
| Proxy-audit correction and audit necessity | `partial-proof` | Proxy evidence needs overlap, positivity, and audit-correction metadata. | `audit_correction.py`, support/fidelity tests, `world_support_summary.json`, proxy-only and weak-overlap metrics. | Validity and lower-bound proof text remain incomplete. |
| VOI controller justification | `partial-proof` | Search, evidence, and preference actions are selected by a deterministic value-per-cost surrogate whose calibration and realized lift remain open proof obligations. | `voi_controller.py`, replay-oracle tests, `voi_action_trace.json`, stop certificates, replay-regret metrics. | Near-optimality or calibrated-surrogate proof remains incomplete. |

The report appendices used by that mapping are `Appendix D` for public request and response models, `Appendix N` for runtime module narratives, `Appendix R` for test evidence, `Appendix X, subsection X2` for core route endpoints, `Appendix AE10` and `Appendix AE11` for support and elicitation limits, and `Appendix AH21` for the certification-effort lower-bound discussion. The detailed theorem map keeps the exact object-level ledger; this report keeps the thesis-readable explanation of what each proof family establishes, which assumptions it uses, and where future proof work remains open.

The theorem families are presented as source-linked extensions of established research lineages. Safe candidate elimination sits in the lineage of multicriteria shortest paths and dominance pruning; anytime winner certification is related to concentration bounds and confidence sequences [Howard et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1214/20-AOS1991); preference robustness follows incremental utility elicitation and minimax regret [Boutilier et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2006.02.003); proxy-audit correction depends on overlap, propensity, and leakage-safe validation assumptions; and certified refusal inherits from reject-option/selective-decision work [Chow 1970](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406). The repository contribution is a source-readable mapping from these families to route-decision code, tests, artifacts, and claim boundaries.

The claim matrices separate theorem-backed claims, empirical claims, heuristic-but-measured surfaces, and non-claim / descriptive-only framing. That separation matters because the same repository contains rigorous invariants, passing implementation tests, generated empirical results, negative results, and future validation boundaries. This report therefore treats a green test, a generated artifact, and a formal theorem statement as different kinds of evidence instead of blending them into one undifferentiated success claim.

The current evidence is deliberately scoped: this repository slice publishes a named partial-proof package of theorem-style propositions and lower-bound candidates for the current thesis families, while full end-to-end theorem-backed closure remains a future proof layer. Foregrounding [`docs/theorem_package.md`](theorem_package.md) and [`docs/theorem_map.md`](theorem_map.md) makes that proof status central and explicit.

## Redesign Tracker Summary

The redesign tracker is absorbed here because it is the compact status ledger for what is source-present, test-present, doc-present, checked green, still being validated, or only conditional. Its evidence legend matters: `source-present` means code exists; `test-present` means a regression or contract test exists; `doc-present` means prose exists; `checked-evidence-green` means the maintained generated or test evidence is currently green for that surface; `checked-evidence-scoped` means the surface exists but should not be overclaimed beyond its checked context; and `conditional-claim-only` means the report may describe the design but must not promote it into a completed empirical claim.

The strongest green redesign areas are artifact provenance/cache reuse and evaluation-lane/cohort/benchmark contracts. Preference evidence should be cited from the maintained full-suite focused-VOI proof family and seed companions, not from the older `current_checked` preference-burden sidecars. Artifact provenance/cache reuse is green because the hot-rerun gate is no longer the blocker: the current checked hot-rerun companion records `all_green=true` for the cold/hot pair. Evaluation lanes and cohort contracts are present because the suite now names roles such as broad cold proof, focused REFC proof, focused VOI proof, optional stopping, perturbation, proxy audit, public transfer, threshold sensitivity, and synthetic ground truth rather than leaving evaluation slices informal.

The conditional redesign areas are equally important. Core identity/runtime backbone, DCCS/search deficiency, multi-fidelity and support-aware evidence, REFC/selective certification/fragility, VOI/tri-source controller behavior, application programming interface (API)/frontend semantics, and documentation/claim discipline all have source and documentation structure, but they should not be overclaimed as deployment-certified. The current checked suite is publishable on the applied-evidence reading (`publishable_on_current_evidence=true`) and supports the paper-level adoption framing (`adoption_claim_supported=true`). That means the redesign tracker should be read as an implementation-and-evidence map: strong enough to support an applied thesis/paper framing, but not a blanket deployment, organisational adoption, or theorem-complete success statement.

This tracker is better than a vague roadmap because it prevents the thesis from confusing implementation breadth with evidence maturity. A feature can be implemented and documented while still needing broader validation. Conversely, a generated lane can satisfy sample-size requirements while still needing stronger calibration or deployment evidence. That separation is central to the project's claim discipline.

The local repo currently contains evidence-backed comparison machinery rather than one universal aggregate statement such as "the system beats OSRM by X% overall across all freight trips." The report therefore explains:

- how the baselines are computed
- what realism multipliers are applied
- why the smart system can outperform them in principle
- what local scripts and UI compare panels can measure

Universal win-rate wording should be introduced only when a checked local artifact directly supports that exact percentage.

## Plain-English System Overview

### Project Problem Statement

At the simplest level, the software helps a user choose freight routes between UK origin and destination points. It treats the shortest route as one candidate signal inside a broader freight-decision problem, because a freight operator usually cares about several competing goals at the same time:

- arriving quickly
- paying less money
- producing less CO2
- avoiding toll surprises
- handling weather and incident pressure
- understanding uncertainty, not just average estimated time of arrival (ETA)
- comparing scenario assumptions such as no sharing, partial sharing, and full sharing

This repository turns those competing goals into a multi-objective routing workflow.

That early problem statement should be read with freight-route-choice and value-of-time evidence in mind. Long-haul truck routing choices trade off time, distance, cost, and operational reliability [Knorring, He, and Kornhauser 2005](https://doi.org/10.1177/0361198105192300106), route-choice studies show that truck route characteristics are measurable decision factors [Sun et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.3141/2354-12), and freight value-of-time meta-analyses show that time savings are heterogeneous rather than one universal constant [Zamparini and Reggiani 2007](https://doi.org/10.1080/01441640701322834), [Binsuwadan et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11116-021-10207-2). The repository's multiobjective design is therefore not decoration: it reflects the fact that a freight route is a decision under operational trade-offs.

### Frontend User Capabilities

A user can:

- place an origin, destination, and optional intermediate stops on a UK map
- request either a single recommended route or a full Pareto set of trade-off routes
- compare routes under different scenario modes
- inspect segment-level breakdowns for distance, duration, cost, emissions, tolls, and incidents
- optimize departure time across a time window
- build duty chains across multiple stops
- run experiments and save scenario-comparison bundles
- inspect live-source diagnostics and strict readiness state
- view a baseline comparison against plain OSRM and ORS-style reference routing
- inspect route-certification summaries, active evidence families, and VOI stop reasons when the thesis pipeline is enabled
- inspect artifact manifests, provenance, signatures, and quality dashboards
- define custom vehicles in addition to built-in profiles

The time-window and duty-chain features are decision-support features, not a claim to solve the full vehicle routing problem with time windows (VRPTW) or UK driver-compliance regime. VRPTW research is its own large field [Braysy and Gendreau 2005a](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1030.0056), [Braysy and Gendreau 2005b](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1030.0057), and UK goods-vehicle drivers' hours remain an external compliance surface [GOV.UK drivers' hours: goods vehicles](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/drivers-hours-goods-vehicles). That boundary matters because the report should claim route-decision evidence, not a complete statutory planning system.

### UK-only scope

The code and assets are deliberately UK-centered:

- default OpenStreetMap Protocolbuffer Binary Format (PBF) source is the Geofabrik United Kingdom extract
- terrain handling uses a UK bounding box and fail-closed policy
- departure profiles, bank holidays, toll data, stochastic regimes, and calibration assets are UK-specific
- graph coverage report bounding box is approximately latitude 49.75 to 61.10 and longitude -8.75 to 2.25
- non-UK terrain behavior is explicitly handled as unsupported in strict mode

In plain language, the project has been narrowed to one geography so the models can be deeper and stricter instead of being globally shallow.

The UK scope also has an external justification. The Department for Transport maintains official road-freight statistical series and 2024 sector reporting [DfT road freight statistics collection](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/road-freight-domestic-and-international-statistics), [DfT road freight statistics 2024](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/road-freight-statistics-2024), and the Future of Freight plan frames freight as a national logistics and policy concern [DfT Future of Freight](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/future-of-freight-plan). The repo uses that UK context as its applied boundary, with transfer to other countries framed as a separate evidence and calibration exercise.

### Deployment shape

The full containerized local architecture in `docker-compose.yml` is a seven-service graph:

1. `osrm_download` downloads the configured region PBF.
2. `osrm` prepares cached OSRM data if needed, then serves routing on port 5000.
3. `osrm_ready` waits for OSRM readiness.
4. `ors` runs the self-hosted OpenRouteService heavy goods vehicle (HGV) reference engine on port 8082.
5. `ors_ready` waits for ORS readiness.
6. `backend` serves the FastAPI API on port 8000 with internal `OSRM_BASE_URL=http://osrm:5000` and `ORS_BASE_URL=http://ors:8082/ors`.
7. `frontend` serves the Next.js app on port 3000.

The root `docker-compose.yml` wires these together. The shell scripts under `osrm/scripts` manage PBF download caching and OSRM preprocessing reuse. The PowerShell developer script `.\\scripts\\dev.ps1` is a related but different topology: it starts OSRM, waits for OSRM, runs strict preflight, then starts local backend and frontend processes if their ports are free; ORS is supplied by the compose stack or by an already running local service, so strict preflight can still fail when ORS is unavailable.

### OSRM Role Alongside The Custom Route Graph

The system is hybrid and OSRM-compatible.

OSRM is used for:

- road-level geometry
- leg annotations
- baseline route generation
- via-path refinement once candidate corridors are known

The custom route graph is used for:

- fast feasibility checks
- candidate diversification
- corridor exploration
- generating multiple structurally different candidate paths before OSRM refinement

In plain language, the graph layer is the route idea generator and feasibility gate; OSRM is the road-geometry and baseline engine.

## Codebase Construction And Evolution Narrative

### Current Codebase Assembly History

The current repository was not built as one single algorithm dropped into a web app. The file structure shows a layered construction order:

1. stand up a dependable road-routing substrate with OSRM and a UK-only graph asset
2. add a strict FastAPI route-construction backend that converts geometry into rich freight options
3. build calibrated UK asset families for departure, scenario, stochastic, toll, fuel, carbon, and terrain logic
4. add a Next.js workbench that can expose those controls and diagnostics without hiding them
5. add artifact, signature, provenance, and experiment surfaces so runs become citable evidence
6. add the later DCCS, REFC, and VOI thesis pipeline on top of the existing route-production path rather than replacing the earlier system

That order matters. It explains why the repository contains both simpler reference helpers and later, richer thesis-facing modules. It also explains why many scripts exist: the codebase was created as a pipeline of build, calibration, publication, runtime, and evaluation steps.

### Raw evidence to runtime asset chain

The build path encoded by the repo is:

1. collect or fetch raw UK evidence into `backend/data/raw/uk`
2. compile those raw inputs into strict runtime assets under `backend/out/model_assets`
3. publish selected compiled assets back into tracked runtime targets under `backend/assets/uk`
4. gate backend startup through strict preflight before route-producing endpoints are considered ready

The scripts make this sequence explicit:

- raw collectors such as `collect_dft_raw_counts_uk.py`, `collect_fuel_history_raw_uk.py`, `collect_carbon_intensity_raw_uk.py`, `collect_stochastic_residuals_raw_uk.py`, and `collect_toll_truth_raw_uk.py` create inspectable evidence families instead of hiding collection inside runtime calls
- fetch/build shapers such as `fetch_scenario_live_uk.py`, `fetch_fuel_history_uk.py`, `fetch_carbon_intensity_uk.py`, `fetch_stochastic_residuals_uk.py`, and `fetch_toll_truth_uk.py` turn raw evidence into asset-ready forms
- asset builders such as `build_routing_graph_uk.py`, `build_departure_profiles_uk.py`, `build_scenario_profiles_uk.py`, `build_stochastic_calibration_uk.py`, `build_pricing_tables_uk.py`, and `build_terrain_tiles_uk.py` compile those sources into runtime artifacts
- `build_model_assets.py` acts as the umbrella orchestrator for the model-asset bundle
- `publish_live_artifacts_uk.py` is the promotion step that copies generated artifacts into the tracked strict-runtime files actually referenced by settings and preflight
- `preflight_live_runtime.py` is the operational gate that tests whether those assets are fresh and structurally valid enough to support fail-closed routing

The manifest evidence currently present locally confirms that this is not just a conceptual chain. `backend/out/model_assets/manifest.json` fixes the model bundle at `model-v2-uk`, `backend/out/model_assets/refresh_manifest.json` hashes the raw inputs that fed that build, and `backend/out/model_assets/live_publish_summary.json` records the handoff from generated outputs into tracked runtime assets.

### OD Corpus And Ambiguity Prior Creation

The thesis workflow is now a second pipeline layered on top of the route runtime.

`backend/scripts/build_od_corpus_uk.py` samples or assembles UK OD cases, bins them by distance and corridor shape, probes graph feasibility, and records candidate-generation side signals such as path count, objective spread, corridor-family count, and engine disagreement pressure. `backend/scripts/enrich_od_corpus_with_ambiguity.py` then turns those raw probes plus historical bootstrap evidence into normalized ambiguity priors, support ratios, source entropy measures, budget priors, and hard-case indicators.

That means the later thesis evaluator is not inventing ambiguity labels after the fact. The corpus itself is constructed with explicit upstream ambiguity evidence. This is a major part of how the codebase was created: not only were route models built, but a corpus-generation and corpus-enrichment workflow was added so evaluation cases would stress the right parts of the system.

Publication citation bridge: OD ambiguity should be described as geospatial evidence quality, not as a calibrated geocoding-error theorem. Address/geocoding studies show that positional error can materially affect downstream spatial analysis [Cayo and Talbot 2003](https://doi.org/10.1186/1476-072X-2-10), and GIScience uncertainty work explains why spatial data quality and uncertainty propagation need explicit treatment [Goodchild 2020](https://doi.org/10.5311/JOSIS.2020.20.664). The repo's `support_ratio`, `source_entropy`, and source-mix ledgers are therefore evidence-quality proxies for OD ambiguity: they record whether multiple local sources agree strongly enough to support an ambiguity prior, but they should not be described as calibrated metre-level geocoding-error estimates.

### Thesis Pipeline Extension Of The Original Router

The earlier route engine already had:

- graph-led candidate generation
- OSRM refinement
- cost, terrain, toll, fuel, carbon, and uncertainty modeling
- Pareto filtering and scalar selection
- manifests, provenance, and signatures

The later thesis-facing extension adds three extra decision layers:

- DCCS in `backend/app/decision_critical.py`, which triages raw candidates before expensive refinement
- REFC in `backend/app/evidence_certification.py`, which certifies strict-frontier winners across bounded sampled worlds and computes fragility/value-of-refresh summaries
- VOI-AD2R in `backend/app/voi_controller.py`, which chooses whether to refine more, refresh evidence, resample uncertainty, or stop

In the current code, DCCS is best understood as a candidate-level triage stage rather than a theorem statement: each record can carry lower/upper envelope bounds, envelope provenance, support status, dominance metadata, criticality score terms, and explicit safe-elimination provenance fields such as `safe_eliminated`, `necessary_dominated`, `dominated_by_route_id`, `dominance_margin`, and `safe_elimination_reason`.

This layered construction explains why the repository still contains simpler reference selectors, baseline endpoints, and classic Pareto logic. The thesis work was added on top of a functioning enriched router, not in place of it.

### Newer Cache And Reporting Layers

Once DCCS, REFC, and VOI were added, the repo gained new runtime reuse layers because repeated thesis evaluation makes intermediate reuse measurable and valuable. The newer cache modules split reuse by stage instead of keeping one monolithic route cache:

- `k_raw_cache.py` caches raw graph candidate sets
- `route_option_cache.py` caches expensive route-option construction, including a core/full split
- `route_state_cache.py` caches downstream state needed for replay or resumed decision stages
- `certification_cache.py` caches REFC results
- `voi_dccs_cache.py` caches VOI/DCCS cross-stage material
- `_process_cache.py` supplies a size-aware in-process cache primitive used by multiple higher-level stores

The reporting layers grew for the same reason. Once thesis evaluation became central, the repo needed not just `results.json` but also `dccs_candidates.jsonl`, `strict_frontier.jsonl`, `certificate_summary.json`, `route_fragility_map.json`, `value_of_refresh.json`, `voi_action_trace.json`, `voi_stop_certificate.json`, `thesis_summary.json`, `methods_appendix.md`, and `thesis_report.md`. The checked bundle names are local evidence of the current artifact contract; this report is not claiming that older `dccs_summary.json` bundles were regenerated under a newer schema.
In other words, the codebase evolved from "serve a route" to "serve a route and preserve enough evidence to defend why that route was chosen."

## Frontend Capability Chapter

### Plain-English view

The frontend is a single-page analyst workbench rather than a minimal route form. The user is not just submitting an origin and destination; they are exploring trade-offs, scenario variants, uncertainty, diagnostics, and reproducibility artifacts.

### Main frontend shell

The root page is `frontend/app/page.tsx`. It orchestrates:

- request building
- streaming Pareto mode
- single-route mode
- baseline overlays
- scenario comparisons
- departure optimization
- duty-chain planning
- experiments CRUD and comparison
- route certification and VOI stop summaries
- tutorial steps
- diagnostics and developer tools
- oracle-quality dashboard rendering

This makes the frontend effectively a control room for the backend's optimization pipeline.

### Map behavior

`frontend/app/components/MapView.tsx` is the central visual interaction surface. Important behaviors include:

- UK-bounded map navigation
- origin, destination, and stop markers
- alternative route overlays
- baseline route overlays
- ORS/reference baseline overlays
- segment and incident overlays
- route failure overlays
- tutorial highlighting
- time-lapse position display

In non-jargon terms, the map is not decorative. It is the main way a user sees how route choices physically diverge and how incidents or stops are attached to them.

The map overlay contract is also now explicit enough to include in the master report. The UI can independently toggle stop overlays, incident overlays, segment tooltips, preview connectors, the OSRM baseline, the OpenRouteService/reference baseline, and academic reference routes through state such as `showStopOverlay`, `showIncidentOverlay`, `showSegmentTooltips`, `showPreviewConnector`, `showBaselineRoute`, `showGoogleBaselineRoute`, and `showReferenceRoute`. Overlay inputs come from route `geometry`, per-route `segment_breakdown`, synthetic or live `incident_events`, baseline-route state, tutorial-map state, and those visibility toggles. Stop overlays are built from origin, destination, and duty stops, and duplicate coordinates are deduplicated so stacked markers do not make the route unreadable. Preview connectors exist before a route is computed, so a planned multi-leg route still has a visible path; their connector nodes are color-graded from start to end so directionality survives even before the backend returns full route geometry. Segment tooltips expose segment label, distance, duration/ETA, cost, CO2, and incident delay. The `buildSegmentBuckets` helper groups segment rows into map-hover buckets so the tooltip is informative without trying to render every row on the map at once. The segment breakdown panel keeps a 40-row preview by default before expansion, which is a deliberate readability and performance cap rather than a data-loss step. Incident overlays place deterministic `dwell`, `accident`, and `closure` events onto route geometry and show delay, start offset, segment index, and source. Failure overlays preserve `reason_code`, stage detail, and backend message, which means a map-level failure can still be interpreted as strict fail-closed behavior, not just as an empty map. Route badges and colors distinguish selected, OSRM baseline, ORS/reference, and academic-reference routes, while simplified sampling for preview and badge layers keeps map pan/zoom performance acceptable. Tooltips are intentionally lightweight and sticky enough to stay readable during interaction without becoming a large React-rendered table inside the map layer.

### Scenario editor and advanced controls

`ScenarioParameterEditor.tsx` exposes a large number of user-adjustable routing controls:

- scenario mode: `no_sharing`, `partial_sharing`, `full_sharing`
- route count / max alternatives
- objective weights for time, money, and CO2
- Pareto method: dominance or epsilon-constraint
- epsilon thresholds
- departure time
- cost toggles such as toll usage, carbon price, fuel multiplier
- terrain profile: flat, rolling, hilly
- stochastic configuration: enabled, seed, sigma, samples
- optimization mode: expected value or robust
- risk aversion
- emissions context: fuel type, Euro class, ambient temperature
- weather configuration
- incident simulation configuration

This is unusually rich for a route planner. It turns the frontend into an experimental interface suitable for dissertation demonstrations.

### Baseline comparison UI

The tracked frontend implementation includes a dedicated baseline-comparison view:

- `frontend/app/components/RouteBaselineComparison.tsx`
- `frontend/app/lib/baselineComparison.ts`
- `frontend/app/api/route/baseline/route.ts`
- `frontend/app/api/route/baseline/ors/route.ts`

The comparison layer computes:

- ETA delta
- cost delta
- CO2 delta
- distance delta
- "Epic score" based on balanced ETA, cost, and CO2 improvement
- qualitative tier labels: `Epic`, `Strong`, `Positive`, `Limited gain`

The newer reporting doc and component code show that the panel now also exposes:

- smart compute elapsed time
- baseline fetch elapsed time
- smart candidate count
- live-source coverage
- live calls observed

and that it can present three baseline styles:

- OSRM baseline
- OpenRouteService baseline, including the local-service path
- academic reference selection

This is a presentation layer over backend comparison outputs, not a separate optimization engine. The important thesis point is that the project is explicitly set up to defend its route choice against simpler baselines.

### Other frontend workflows

Other user-facing components include:

- `ParetoChart.tsx`: trade-off chart for non-dominated solutions
- `ScenarioComparison.tsx`: multi-scenario result comparison
- `DepartureOptimizerChart.tsx`: best departure-slot exploration
- `DutyChainPlanner.tsx`: multi-stop chain planning
- `CounterfactualPanel.tsx`: what-if adjustments such as fuel/carbon/departure shifts
- `SegmentBreakdown.tsx`: per-segment accounting
- `ScenarioTimeLapse.tsx`: route evolution over time/scenario playback
- `EtaTimelineChart.tsx`: ETA stage decomposition
- `ExperimentManager.tsx`: saved scenario experiment bundles
- `OracleQualityDashboard.tsx`: source quality and freshness summaries
- `TutorialOverlay.tsx`: guided walkthrough
- devtools panels for batch runs, custom vehicles, ops diagnostics, run inspection, and signature verification

The devtool surface is operationally concrete:

- `OpsDiagnosticsPanel` is backed by same-origin frontend proxy routes that expose backend `GET /health`, `GET /health/ready`, `GET /metrics`, `GET /cache/stats`, and `DELETE /cache` behavior to the browser, so the UI can show strict route readiness, graph status, strict-live readiness, cache/checkpoint state, and metrics without direct browser-to-backend calls or raw backend logs
- `CustomVehicleManager.tsx` keeps the create/edit payload as raw JSON, so advanced users can tune terrain parameters, aliases, and freight-class mappings directly
- `BatchRunner.tsx` supports both JSON OD-pair input and CSV-plus-options import paths instead of only one batch form
- the current built-in batch defaults exposed in docs target `rigid_hgv`, `no_sharing`, and `max_alternatives: 8`
- `RunInspector.tsx` is the main in-app reporting surface for thesis, DCCS, REFC, and VOI bundles rather than only a generic download panel; it uses the allowlisted manifest, provenance, signature, artifact, DCCS, REFC, VOI, OD-corpus, ORS-snapshot, and thesis-report endpoints enumerated in the in-app artifact retrieval scope in this chapter and the route-by-route endpoint appendix
- `SignatureVerifier` maps to `POST /verify/signature` and accepts raw text or JSON payload input, optionally with a secret, so exported report bundles and payload signatures can be checked from inside the app shell
- adjacent panels keep backend behavior inspectable: `ScenarioComparison` explains missing metrics, `OracleQualityDashboard` exports source-quality CSVs, `ExperimentManager` saves and replays run bundles, `RouteBaselineComparison` compares OSRM/ORS/reference routes, `DecisionStateSummary` exposes terminal and preference state, `PreferenceElicitationPanel` round-trips preference actions, `RouteCertificationPanel` exposes controller and evidence traces, and `ProofDashboardPanel` groups proof slices by variant, lane, route engine, and theorem/artifact family

The current accessibility and i18n surface is also part of the frontend evidence base rather than a cosmetic add-on. Locale support is implemented through `frontend/app/lib/i18n.ts` and `frontend/app/lib/format.ts` for `en` and `es`; locale changes affect labels and number/date formatting but do not change route scoring. Translation coverage includes panel title/subtitle copy, compute-mode labels, route hints, live progress/success/failure messages, and overlay labels for stops, incidents, and segment views. The UI uses `Intl.NumberFormat` and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with fallback formatting where the host runtime lacks a requested locale shape. Accessibility mechanics include a skip link to the controls panel, focus-visible styling, live regions for async compute/tutorial state, keyboard-friendly form controls, custom select listbox behavior with arrow/Home/End/Enter/Space/Escape support, collapsible cards with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, accessible tooltips, tutorial dialog semantics, map status/failure live-region messages, table captions, and hidden labels for screen-reader summaries. The component-level details matter: `Select.tsx` keeps active-option state synchronized with keyboard navigation; `CollapsibleCard.tsx` uses button disclosure semantics with `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, a region wrapper, and delayed mounting for closed sections; `FieldInfo.tsx` closes on outside click, blur, or Escape and resizes/repositions the tooltip to avoid viewport clipping; `TutorialOverlay.tsx` behaves like a dialog, can be dismissed by keyboard, shows internal progress/checklist state, and is gated to desktop workflows where the guided route UI is usable; `MapView.tsx` keeps marker text readable, exposes status/error overlays, labels map actions, and uses polite live-region status for map and route changes. Manual release verification should include `pnpm -C frontend build`, then checking the desktop tutorial overlay and both `en` and `es` locale toggles. That matters because a thesis decision tool should make evidence inspectable through keyboard and assistive technology paths, not only through visual map interaction.

The frontend is therefore a visual analytics and decision-support surface. The design follows the visual analytics principle that users need overview, filtering, and detail-on-demand [Shneiderman 1996](https://doi.org/10.1109/VL.1996.545307), and it fits nested visualization-design methodology because backend evidence, task semantics, visual encodings, and interaction choices are all linked [Munzner 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2009.111). Accessibility should be read against WCAG 2.2 as the external standard reference [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/). The code-level point is that the UI preserves the same evidence discipline as the backend: `Select.tsx` provides listbox semantics, `CollapsibleCard.tsx` provides disclosure semantics, `TutorialOverlay.tsx` provides dialog/live-region behavior, and `MapView.tsx` labels map controls and route-state changes.

### Reporting, tutorial, and operator-assistance surfaces

The frontend has grown well beyond "request a route and draw a line." Three additional frontend responsibilities are now part of this thesis evidence base.

First, tutorial mode is now a real workflow layer. The guided overlay has four operational states, `blocked`, `chooser`, `running`, and `completed`; it is desktop-gated; it stores progress locally; and it can resume an unfinished walkthrough. The tutorial step catalog can prefill canonical route, duty-chain, and experiment examples, which means the tutorial is tied to real repo workflows instead of being generic decoration.

Second, the frontend is now a reporting instrument. The run inspector and related panels surface:

- manifests and scenario manifests
- provenance and signatures
- route and thesis artifacts
- DCCS candidate ledgers
- strict frontier files
- certificate and fragility summaries
- value-of-refresh outputs
- VOI action traces and stop certificates
- thesis results, thesis summaries, methods appendices, and thesis reports

Third, the UI has become an operator-assistance layer rather than a simple presentation layer. `ScenarioComparison.tsx` now exposes missing-metric reason details, `SegmentBreakdown.tsx` can copy the visible table as CSV, `OracleQualityDashboard.tsx` exposes per-source freshness/schema/signature/latency summaries plus CSV export, and the compute diagnostics overlay captures stage timing, retry/fallback behavior, graph diagnostics, live-call traces, slowest calls, and an optional AI diagnostic bundle. These features matter for a thesis because they show the frontend was built to explain, audit, and reproduce computation.

### In-app artifact retrieval scope

The newer reporting docs make clear that the Next.js proxy layer intentionally allowlists the backend artifact/report surface rather than exposing arbitrary file paths. The currently documented in-app retrieval set includes:

- `manifest`, `scenario-manifest`, `provenance`, `signature`, `scenario-signature`, and `artifacts`
- standard run files such as `results.json`, `results.csv`, `metadata.json`, `routes.geojson`, and `results_summary.csv`
- thesis-pipeline files such as `dccs_candidates.jsonl`, `dccs_summary.json`, `refined_routes.jsonl`, `strict_frontier.jsonl`, `winner_summary.json`, `certificate_summary.json`, `route_fragility_map.json`, `competitor_fragility_breakdown.json`, `value_of_refresh.json`, `sampled_world_manifest.json`, `voi_action_trace.json`, `voi_action_scores.csv`, `voi_stop_certificate.json`, and `final_route_trace.json`
- evaluation/report files such as `report.pdf`, `od_corpus.csv`, `od_corpus_summary.json`, `ors_snapshot.json`, `thesis_results.csv`, `thesis_summary.csv`, `methods_appendix.md`, and `thesis_report.md`

That allowlist is an important architectural clue. It shows the frontend is coupled to a curated evidence contract, not to ad hoc backend file browsing.

Grouped by purpose, the allowlist covers identity and provenance files (`manifest`, `scenario-manifest`, signatures, and provenance), operational route outputs (`results`, `metadata`, `routes.geojson`, and result summaries), thesis pipeline internals (`dccs_*`, refined-route/frontier files, certificate, fragility, world-manifest, value-of-refresh, VOI trace, action-score, stop-certificate, and final-route-trace files), and evaluation/report outputs (`od_corpus`, `ors_snapshot`, thesis result/summary files, methods appendix, and thesis report). This grouping is important because it explains why the frontend proxy is narrow: it exposes exactly the artifacts needed to audit a decision while avoiding arbitrary filesystem disclosure.

### Frontend API proxy pattern

The Next.js app routes backend interaction through `frontend/app/api/...` handlers as a proxy layer. That layer:

- forwards requests to the FastAPI backend
- centralizes timeout handling
- classifies transport failures into reason codes
- forwards `x-route-request-id` headers for diagnostics
- relays NDJSON streams for streaming Pareto responses

The helper `frontend/app/lib/backendFetch.ts` defines:

- `computeAttemptTimeoutMs()` default 1,200,000 ms
- `computeRouteFallbackTimeoutMs()` default 900,000 ms
- transport reason codes such as `backend_headers_timeout`, `backend_body_timeout`, `backend_connection_reset`, and `backend_unreachable`

### Frontend type system

`frontend/app/lib/types.ts` mirrors backend models and is substantial. It defines:

- request and response shapes
- route option metrics
- stream event types
- strict reason-code unions
- quality dashboard types
- run artifact types
- vehicle profile types

This is important because the frontend is not loosely typed UI glue. It mirrors the backend contract closely enough to make streaming, diagnostics, and detailed panels reliable.

## Backend Request-Flow Chapter

### Plain-English summary

The backend is a staged route-computation pipeline. A request moves from "origin/destination" through readiness gates, data refresh logic, candidate generation, OSRM refinement, physical and economic modeling, Pareto filtering, scalar ranking, and artifact persistence before a route decision is returned.

### Backend routing pipeline in prose-table form

| Stage | What happens | Why it exists | Main failure gates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Request validation | Pydantic models validate coordinates, weights, toggles, and advanced configs | stop bad inputs early | validation errors |
| 2. Health/readiness context | strict graph and live-data readiness can be checked | protect strict runtime behavior | `routing_graph_warming_up`, `routing_graph_warmup_failed`, source unavailability |
| 3. Live refresh/prefetch | scenario, fuel, carbon, departure, stochastic, toll, and terrain prerequisites are refreshed depending on mode | make route compute use fresh data | `live_source_refresh_failed`, data-specific strict errors |
| 4. Graph OD feasibility | route graph checks whether origin/destination are connected and inside covered graph space | avoid expensive OSRM work for impossible or poor-coverage trips | disconnected OD, coverage gap, warmup problems |
| 5. Candidate path generation | route graph runs K-shortest / A*-assisted search and corridor rescue logic | produce structurally different candidate corridors | no path, timeout, state-budget exhaustion |
| 6. Candidate diversification | routes are deduplicated/prefiltered using signatures, corridor grouping, and family rules | prevent many tiny variants of the same route | reduced candidate set |
| 7. OSRM refinement | OSRM fetches actual via routes for graph candidates | obtain realistic geometry and per-leg annotations | OSRM fetch failure, timeouts |
| 8. Option build | each refined route is converted into a rich `RouteOption` with cost, emissions, uncertainty, terrain, toll, incidents, and summaries | turn geometry into decision-ready options | terrain/toll/fuel/carbon/scenario/stochastic failures |
| 9. Pareto processing | options are filtered by dominance or epsilon-constraint and can be backfilled | keep trade-offs rather than one naive optimum | `epsilon_infeasible`, empty candidate set |
| 10. Scalar selection | one representative route can be selected using academic or modified profiles | allow a single recommendation after multi-objective analysis | no surviving options |
| 11. Response and artifacts | result, diagnostics, manifests, signatures, provenance, and optional reports are persisted | reproducibility and auditability | artifact I/O failures |

### Important backend endpoints

Core user-facing compute endpoints are:

- `POST /route`
- `POST /pareto`
- `POST /pareto/stream`
- `POST /api/pareto/stream`
- `POST /route/baseline`
- `POST /route/baseline/ors`
- `POST /route/preference`
- `POST /departure/optimize`
- `POST /duty/chain`
- `POST /scenario/compare`
- `POST /batch/import/csv`
- `POST /batch/pareto`

Supporting endpoints include:

- readiness and health
- vehicle profile CRUD
- cache stats and cache clear
- hot-rerun cache restore through `POST /cache/hot-rerun/restore`
- metrics
- experiments CRUD
- oracle quality checks/dashboard
- run artifact and signature endpoints
- debug live-call traces

Appendix X expands this list into route-by-route backend methods, frontend proxy mappings, artifact/signature retrieval paths, run-inspector surfaces, diagnostics endpoints, and strict-error semantics. The summary here is enough to understand the pipeline; Appendix X exists to make endpoint parity checkable.

The current backend docs make the cache and diagnostics surface concrete. The active supporting endpoints notably include:

- `GET /metrics`
- `GET /cache/stats`
- `DELETE /cache`
- `POST /cache/hot-rerun/restore`
- `GET /debug/live-calls/{request_id}`

Those endpoints are part of how the repo proves cache reuse, strict-live readiness, and evaluation replay behavior.

The current API docs also make two observability surfaces explicit:

- `GET /metrics` reports totals such as `total_requests`, `total_errors`, and per-endpoint duration summaries
- `GET /cache/stats` distinguishes `route_cache`, `hot_rerun_route_cache_checkpoint`, `hot_rerun_certification_cache_checkpoint`, `hot_rerun_route_state_cache_checkpoint`, `hot_rerun_voi_dccs_cache_checkpoint`, `certification_cache`, `k_raw_cache`, `route_option_cache`, `route_state_cache`, and `voi_dccs_cache`
