- In thesis terms, context is what makes sharing-mode effects specific rather than generic.

### `corridor bucket`

- A corridor bucket is a geography-aware context class used in calibration.
- In plain English, it is the system's way of saying "this trip belongs to this broad regional movement type."
- Corridor buckets influence scenario, departure, and uncertainty behavior.
- In thesis terms, they are one of the main mechanisms that make the repo UK-specific.

### `departure profile`

- A departure profile is the time-sensitive multiplier model used to adjust route behavior by departure context.
- In plain English, it tells the system how timing changes expected route pressure.
- It is used directly by the departure optimizer and route builder.
- In thesis terms, it is the engine behind schedule-aware routing.

### `stochastic regime`

- A stochastic regime is a calibrated uncertainty pattern tied to context.
- In plain English, it tells the system what kind of variability to expect for this sort of trip.
- Different regimes can have different spreads, correlations, and factor behavior.
- In thesis terms, regimes make uncertainty context-aware rather than one-size-fits-all.

### `quantile`

- A quantile is a cutoff in the distribution of sampled outcomes.
- In plain English, q95 is the level below which about 95 percent of sampled results lie.
- The repo uses q50, q90, and q95 heavily.
- In thesis terms, quantiles are core uncertainty summary statistics.

### `CVaR`

- CVaR is the average behavior in the bad tail beyond a chosen quantile threshold.
- In plain English, it says how bad things are on average once you are already in the nasty tail.
- This is more conservative than using q95 alone.
- In thesis terms, CVaR is one of the strongest risk measures in the repo.

### `robust score`

- The robust score is the uncertainty-aware utility after tail-risk penalization.
- In plain English, it is the "safe compromise" score under uncertainty.
- A route can have a good mean utility and still a worse robust score if its tail is ugly.
- In thesis terms, robust score is what turns uncertainty summaries into decision-relevant ranking.

### `risk aversion`

- Risk aversion controls how strongly the robust objective penalizes bad tails.
- In plain English, it is the dial for how much the user or config fears nasty outcomes.
- This matters most when routes differ in volatility rather than average.
- In thesis terms, it is the preference bridge from stochastic summary to decision rule.

### `terrain coverage`

- Terrain coverage is the fraction of the route for which the backend has usable elevation evidence.
- In plain English, it is how much of the journey the terrain model can actually see.
- Under strict UK settings, insufficient coverage can block the route.
- In thesis terms, coverage is a validity condition for terrain-aware routing.

### `counterfactual`

- A counterfactual is a "what would change if this modeled factor were different?" view of the route.
- In plain English, it is the system's explanatory alternate-world comparison.
- Counterfactuals help separate mechanism from total score.
- In thesis terms, they improve route explainability.

### `baseline route`

- A baseline route is a simpler reference answer used for comparison against the smart pipeline.
- In plain English, it is the control case.
- The repo supports both OSRM and ORS-style baselines.
- In thesis terms, baselines are essential for comparative evaluation.

### `manifest`

- A manifest is a stored summary of a run, its settings, and related artifact context.
- In plain English, it is the official record for one analytical result.
- Manifests make route runs reproducible and inspectable.
- In thesis terms, they are central evidence objects.

### `provenance`

- Provenance is the record of where the run's important inputs came from.
- In plain English, it is the source-history of the result.
- Provenance is especially important for live-backed and published assets.
- In thesis terms, it supports claims about traceability and trust.

### `signature`

- A signature is the integrity check attached to a manifest or related payload.
- In plain English, it helps detect whether stored result material was altered.
- The repo uses HMAC-based signing.
- In thesis terms, this is an integrity feature rather than a full security architecture.

### `oracle quality`

- Oracle quality is the repository's term for upstream source-health monitoring.
- In plain English, it is the scorecard for how healthy the input feeds are.
- It tracks stale counts, failures, and latency separately from route quality.
- In thesis terms, it is a governance layer over external data.

### `live-call trace`

- The live-call trace is the per-request record of expected and observed upstream calls.
- In plain English, it is the backend's memory of what external data work happened.
- This makes live dependency visible to users and developers.
- In thesis terms, it is a major observability artifact.

### `batch Pareto`

- Batch Pareto means running Pareto route analysis over many OD pairs.
- In plain English, it is the study-scale version of trade-off routing.
- This is used for evaluation, not just one-off route recommendation.
- In thesis terms, it enables broader empirical evidence.

### `duty chain`

- A duty chain is a multi-stop route sequence treated as one operational plan.
- In plain English, it is a shift or run of work rather than one journey.
- The backend composes multiple legs to build it.
- In thesis terms, it extends the project into operational scheduling territory.

### `tutorial mode`

- Tutorial mode is the guided walkthrough embedded in the frontend.
- In plain English, it teaches a user how to use the tool without leaving the app.
- It covers real workflows rather than generic onboarding.
- In thesis terms, it supports the usability side of a complex research system.

### Appendix Significance

- A thesis report often has to serve readers with different technical backgrounds.
- This appendix helps the same document work for supervisors, examiners, developers, and operators.
- It keeps the report readable without dumbing the system down.
- That is important because the repository combines routing, optimization, live data, risk, and artifact governance in one place.

## Appendix AC: Baseline Improvement Semantics For OSRM And ORS

This appendix is deliberately careful.

The repo can compare smart routes against baseline routes.

It can also benchmark and inspect those comparisons in local workflows.

What it does not provide as a checked-in fact is one universal, externally validated percentage by which it beats every baseline in all freight situations.

That distinction should be explicit in a thesis.

### AC1. There Are Several Different Meanings Of "Better"

- A route can be better in time.
- It can be better in money.
- It can be better in emissions.
- It can be better in robust tail risk.
- It can be better in explainability.
- It can be better in auditability.
- The project often improves some of these dimensions simultaneously, but not always.
- In thesis terms, "better" must be tied to a named objective or evaluation context.

### AC2. Baselines In This Repo Are Not Purely Raw Provider Outputs

- The repo includes realism multipliers for baseline duration and distance.
- This matters because a fair comparison should not depend on the baseline being unrealistically optimistic.
- In plain English, the baseline is adjusted to be a more believable operational reference.
- This is important to state because some readers may assume the baseline is a raw provider response.
- In thesis terms, the repo is trying to compare against a plausible reference, not a straw man.
- The exact multipliers are local configuration choices and should be reported as such.

### AC3. Candidate Diversity Can Broaden Certification-Relevant Frontier Coverage

- Plain shortest-path systems often commit early to one dominant path family.
- The certification-facing system first searches for multiple plausible corridors using the custom graph.
- In plain English, it tries not to get trapped in the first obvious corridor.
- This matters because some trade-off routes are only visible if candidate generation is diversity-aware.
- In thesis terms, better candidate breadth can improve frontier quality before any cost model is applied.
- This is a capability difference relative to provider-only routing, not a blanket win-rate claim.

### AC4. Richer Operational Scoring Can Change The Supported Decision

- The smart route is not judged only by raw distance or nominal ETA.
- It incorporates terrain effects, vehicle physics, toll logic, fuel prices, emissions, carbon cost, and scenario pressure.
- In plain English, it uses a richer operational evidence basis than a basic shortest-path provider.
- That can change which route is truly better for freight.
- In thesis terms, realism layers can produce a more operationally meaningful winner than plain shortest path.
- This does not mean the geometry is always radically different.

### AC5. Risk-Aware Evaluation Can Change The Certification Basis

- Baselines are often deterministic.
- The certification-facing system can summarize uncertainty through q95, CVaR, and robust score.
- In plain English, it can reject a route that looks good on average but is too ugly in the tail.
- That is an important capability for operational planning.
- In thesis terms, risk-aware comparison is different from mean-value comparison.
- The report should keep those comparison types separate.

### AC6. Scenario-Aware Evaluation Extends The Decision Surface

- A baseline route usually ignores sharing-policy context.
- The certification-facing system can evaluate the same trip under no-sharing, partial-sharing, and full-sharing assumptions.
- In plain English, it can answer a richer question.
- That means "better" sometimes refers to better policy sensitivity rather than just lower ETA.
- In thesis terms, scenario awareness is a capability improvement even when raw path geometry looks similar.
- This is important in discussing the novelty of the project.

### AC7. Departure-Aware Evaluation Extends The Decision Surface Over Time

- If departure context matters, then a baseline computed for one moment may not reflect the best operational timing.
- The certification-facing system can optimize over departure windows using departure profiles.
- In plain English, it can improve the timing of the trip, not just the path.
- This is a different kind of gain from path-only optimization.
- In thesis terms, the system expands the decision space.
- That should be presented as a core advantage over static baseline routing.

### AC8. Decision Evidence Can Be Richer Than A Baseline Route Response

- Even when the final path is similar, the certification-facing system can still provide richer evidence because it explains why it chose the route.
- Segment breakdowns, counterfactuals, Pareto charts, and baseline deltas all contribute to this.
- In plain English, the user gets reasoning support rather than only a line on a map.
- This matters for dispatch trust and for dissertation evidence.
- In thesis terms, explainability is a legitimate certification and governance objective.
- It should not be ignored simply because it is not a raw travel metric.

### AC9. The Certification Stack Can Surface Richer Decision Evidence Than A Baseline Route Response

- Manifests, provenance, signatures, and oracle-quality diagnostics do not directly shorten travel time.
- But they do improve the quality of evidence around a route decision.
- In plain English, the system can prove more about how it got its answer.
- This is a stronger auditability and governance surface, not a claim of route-quality dominance.
- In thesis terms, the project's contribution is not only route scoring but also route accountability.
- That is especially important for research-grade software.

### AC10. Avoiding Universal Percentage Claims

- The repo contains comparison machinery and benchmark scripts.
- It does not include one checked-in, all-cases summary proving a universal average improvement over OSRM or ORS across all freight scenarios.
- In plain English, the system can compare itself carefully, but the report should not invent a global win-rate.
- This is an evidence limitation, not a system flaw.
- In thesis terms, local evidence supports per-run and benchmarked comparisons, not unlimited generalization.
- Saying this clearly increases credibility.

### AC11. Local Evidence Support Boundary

- Local code and docs support that baseline endpoints exist and are intentionally compared.
- Local config supports that realism multipliers are applied.
- Local benchmark tooling supports that the project is designed to measure performance and quality systematically.
- Local runtime artifacts support that the strict/live model assets were built successfully.
- In plain English, the repo contains real comparison infrastructure, not vague aspirational comments.
- In thesis terms, that is enough to support measured, scoped claims.
- It is not enough to support universal external dominance claims.

### AC12. Smart Route Losses Against Baselines

- Some trips are simple.
- Some corridors have one obvious dominant motorway path.
- Some context layers may not move the route enough to matter.
- Some weight settings may align closely with what a baseline already optimizes.
- In plain English, the certification-facing system is not guaranteed to look different or better on every trip.
- A strong thesis should admit this.
- It should explain when the extra model depth matters most.

### AC13. When The Certification-Facing System Is Most Likely To Matter

- The certification-facing pipeline is most useful when there are genuine corridor alternatives.
- It is also more useful when toll exposure, terrain, emissions, cost, or risk meaningfully differ across those corridors.
- Scenario-sensitive or time-sensitive trips also magnify the value of the richer model.
- In plain English, the certification-facing system matters most when the route problem is multidimensional.
- This is exactly when pure shortest path is least sufficient.
- In thesis terms, these are the conditions under which the project should be evaluated most seriously.
- That helps frame case-study selection.

### AC14. Separate ORS And OSRM Comparison Channels

- OSRM and ORS are not identical reference systems.
- Their profiles, routing behavior, and deployment assumptions differ.
- In plain English, comparing against two references is more informative than pretending all baselines are the same.
- The repo even distinguishes true ORS from ORS-like proxy fallback where needed.
- In thesis terms, this is a careful comparative design choice.
- It supports more honest evaluation language.

### AC15. Realism Multipliers As Legitimate Adjustments

- A naive reader may worry that baseline realism multipliers unfairly handicap the baseline.
- The better interpretation is that the project is trying to avoid comparing a richly modeled route with an overly idealized reference.
- In plain English, the goal is a fairer operational comparison, not a fake victory.
- These multipliers are explicit, configurable, and reportable.
- In thesis terms, transparency makes them defensible.
- Hidden realism adjustments would be much harder to justify.

### AC16. Per-Run Comparison Value

- Even without a universal checked-in win-rate, individual case comparisons are useful.
- They reveal when terrain, tolls, sharing modes, or risk-awareness produce materially different choices.
- In plain English, a good case study can still teach the reader what the smart router adds.
- The key is not to oversell one case as a universal truth.
- In thesis terms, carefully chosen per-run comparisons remain legitimate evidence.
- They are especially strong when paired with manifests and diagnostics.

### AC17. Benchmark Scripts In The Comparison Argument

- Benchmark scripts let the repo measure runtime and, in some cases, comparison-oriented behavior systematically.
- They are not the same as one-off UI screenshots.
- In plain English, they provide a more repeatable way to test the system.
- This matters for any claim about practicality or repeatability.
- In thesis terms, benchmark scripts are an evidence amplifier.
- They make comparative evaluation more defensible than anecdote alone.

### AC18. Safe Thesis Comparison Claim Language

- A safe claim is that the repository provides a richer, more context-aware, and more auditable routing system than a plain baseline route provider.
- Another safe claim is that local comparison machinery can show per-case advantages in route quality, realism, or explainability.
- A less safe claim would be that the system universally beats OSRM or ORS by a fixed percentage everywhere.
- In plain English, the thesis should be specific about what kind of improvement is being claimed.
- This is not a limitation of the project alone.
- It is a standard expectation of careful evaluation writing.
- The repo's own design encourages that caution.

### Appendix Significance

- The question "does it beat OSRM/ORS?" is a natural one.
- But it is too coarse unless the meaning of "beat" is unpacked.
- This appendix gives that unpacking.
- It shows why the smart system can be better, when that difference matters, and where the evidence stops.
- That makes the overall thesis argument much more defensible.
- It also protects the report from overclaiming.

### AD31. `dccs_refc` Default Pipeline Justification

The current default is explicit in `backend/app/settings.py`:

```python
route_pipeline_default_mode: str = Field(
    default="dccs_refc",
    alias="ROUTE_PIPELINE_DEFAULT_MODE",
)
```

The alternative would be to keep a legacy "return the best route from the routing engine" default. That would be simpler, but it would hide the two thesis contributions that matter most: selective search over challenger routes and evidence certification over uncertain inputs. `dccs_refc` is better for this project because it makes the normal path include both parts of the claimed contribution. DCCS decides which candidate refinements are worth spending route-computation budget on; REFC then asks whether the apparent winner remains defensible under bounded evidence-world perturbations. Legacy routing remains useful as a compatibility baseline, but it is not a complete thesis method.

### AD32. Main Pipeline Budget Defaults

The defaults are:

```python
route_pipeline_search_budget: int = Field(default=6, ge=1, le=128)
route_pipeline_evidence_budget: int = Field(default=3, ge=0, le=64)
route_pipeline_cert_world_count: int = Field(default=64, ge=10, le=500)
```

These are tuned as a practical reviewer-facing budget, not as arbitrary constants. A search budget of 6 is large enough to let the graph challenger mechanism escape the first few obvious alternatives, but still small enough that the thesis can discuss selective computation rather than exhaustive enumeration. An evidence budget of 3 forces the controller to prioritize the most decision-relevant evidence families instead of refreshing everything. A world count of 64 gives REFC enough stress-world resolution to expose winner fragility without making each request behave like an offline Monte Carlo study. Many systems either use one fixed route result or a very large brute-force scenario sweep; this design is more appropriate for the dissertation objective because the budgets make the cost/benefit tradeoff visible and measurable.

### AD33. Certificate Threshold `0.70` Justification

The current threshold is:

```python
route_pipeline_certificate_threshold: float = Field(default=0.70, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
```

The certificate is an empirical winner-frequency threshold over bounded stress worlds, not a mathematical proof that a route is universally optimal. A threshold of 0.95 would look stronger, but it would over-convert ordinary data noise into abstention and would make the system reluctant to recommend routes even when one route is clearly more supported than the others. A threshold of 0.70 is better here because it is strict enough to reject fragile winners while still allowing the freight router to return a useful recommendation when the evidence majority is stable. The thesis should state this as an operational certification threshold, not as a universal optimality guarantee.

### AD34. VOI Stop Tolerance `tau_stop=0.03` Justification

The stop tolerance is:

```python
route_pipeline_tau_stop: float = Field(default=0.03, ge=0.0)
```

This parameter defines when the expected marginal value of continuing is too small to justify another action. The alternative would be a fixed number of actions or a hard "always use all budgets" rule. The fixed-budget approach is easier to explain but worse for this project because it wastes effort when the winner is already stable and underspecifies why the system stopped. A 0.03 tolerance makes the stopping decision part of the auditable controller: continue only if the estimated value of another search, evidence, or preference action clears a small positive margin.

### AD35. Search Completeness And Action Bonus Tuning

The relevant defaults are:

```python
route_pipeline_search_completeness_threshold: float = Field(default=0.84)
route_pipeline_search_completeness_action_bonus: float = Field(default=0.22)
route_pipeline_world_increment: int = Field(default=32)
```

Search completeness is deliberately not set to 1.0 because the graph space is large and route alternatives are not enumerable in a clean finite way. The 0.84 threshold says that search can be treated as sufficiently mature before every possible corridor has been explored, while the 0.22 bonus raises the value of additional search actions when the controller sees a meaningful completeness gap. The world increment of 32 lets the system expand certification resolution in chunks rather than paying for a large stress-world expansion immediately. Other projects often hide this behind a fixed "k alternatives" parameter; this design is more appropriate for thesis purposes because the controller can explain whether the weak point is search incompleteness or evidence ambiguity.

### AD36. DCCS Overlap Threshold And Bootstrap Count

The DCCS diversity defaults are:

```python
route_dccs_overlap_threshold: float = Field(default=0.82, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
route_dccs_bootstrap_count: int = Field(default=3, ge=1, le=32)
```

The overlap threshold prevents the challenger set from being filled with near-duplicates of the same road path. A very low threshold would reject routes that share unavoidable road segments in sparse corridors; a very high threshold would allow trivial variants. `0.82` is a compromise that keeps corridor diversity without pretending that UK freight routes can always be completely disjoint. The bootstrap count of 3 gives DCCS enough initial contrast to estimate challenger value before it starts spending selective refinement budget. The thesis point is that DCCS is not just "take k shortest paths"; it actively manages candidate diversity and refinement cost.

### AD37. DCCS Flip-Probability Weight Tuning

The current flip-probability defaults are:

```python
route_dccs_pflip_bias: float = Field(default=-0.15)
route_dccs_pflip_gap_weight: float = Field(default=2.1)
route_dccs_pflip_mechanism_weight: float = Field(default=1.2)
route_dccs_pflip_overlap_weight: float = Field(default=1.4)
route_dccs_pflip_detour_weight: float = Field(default=0.9)
```

The largest weight is on objective gap because a challenger that is close to the current winner is more likely to overturn it. Mechanism disagreement and overlap are next because a challenger from a different generation mechanism or corridor supplies more information than a same-shape duplicate. Detour receives a smaller but still positive weight because detours can reveal hidden cost/emissions improvements, but large detours are not automatically good. The negative bias prevents the model from marking every challenger as likely to flip. A generic route planner normally ranks alternatives by travel time or a static utility score; this project is more suitable for the thesis objective because the selection feature is "expected decision impact under incomplete search", not just route quality.

### AD38. Fixed Refine-Cost Model Rationale

`backend/app/decision_critical.py` makes the design explicit:

```python
# Deterministic refine-cost coefficients are fixed in-repo so the predictor
# stays auditable and does not refit at runtime.
_REFINE_COST_PIPELINE_ALIASES = {"dccs": "dccs", "dccs_refc": "dccs_refc", "voi": "voi"}
```

Runtime refitting would make the model harder to reproduce and would let later artifacts quietly change the decision policy. Fixed coefficients are better for this thesis because every cost estimate can be traced back to source-controlled values. The model still distinguishes pipelines, graph features, source labels, and fallback stages; it just avoids training during request handling. That matters because the controller is supposed to be auditable, not an opaque online learner.

### AD39. Legacy Refine-Cost Scale For Unlabelled Graph Candidates

The code records the reason directly:

```python
_REFINE_COST_UNLABELED_STAGELESS_LEGACY_SCALE: dict[str, float] = {
    "dccs": 0.08,
    "dccs_refc": 0.04,
    "voi": 0.066,
}
```

The surrounding comment says broad-suite artifacts showed the unscaled legacy model overpredicting graph-only candidates by an order of magnitude. The better thesis interpretation is not "the model was made to pass a metric"; it is "legacy cost features were calibrated for a different evidence shape, so unlabelled graph candidates need an explicit conservative correction." The alternative would be to drop those candidates from calibration, which would make the metrics look cleaner but would hide an important class of route-generation behavior. Keeping a visible shrink factor is better because it is honest, reproducible, and inspectable.

### AD40. DCCS Anti-Collapse Quotas

The quota labels are:

```python
_ANTI_COLLAPSE_FAMILY_QUOTA = "high_significance_corridor_family"
_ANTI_COLLAPSE_DISAGREEMENT_QUOTA = "disagreement_driven_challenger"
_ANTI_COLLAPSE_RESCUE_QUOTA = "representative_capital_rescue"
```

Without quotas, a selective algorithm can become self-confirming: it refines the candidates that already look good and starves the unusual candidates that might expose hidden failure. The anti-collapse design is better than a simple top-k ranker because it reserves room for high-significance corridor families, engine-disagreement challengers, and representative rescue candidates. In thesis language, this is a guard against premature narrowing of the candidate frontier.

### AD41. Objective Vocabulary: `time`, `money`, And `co2`

The DCCS and REFC modules share a compact objective basis:

```python
OBJECTIVE_NAMES: tuple[str, str, str] = ("time", "money", "co2")
```

The alternative would be to add many user-facing dimensions such as safety, comfort, reliability, toll complexity, depot convenience, and driver preference. That would be broader, but it would weaken the empirical story because not all those objectives are supported by equally strong data. Time, money, and CO2 are better here because they map directly to route metrics, cost models, emissions models, Pareto selection, REFC perturbations, and thesis evaluation metrics. Other criteria can still appear as evidence or constraints, but the main objective space stays interpretable.

### AD42. REFC Evidence Family Boundary

The evidence family catalog is:

```python
EVIDENCE_FAMILIES = (
    "scenario", "toll", "terrain", "fuel", "carbon", "weather", "stochastic",
)
```

These families correspond to independent reasons a freight-route recommendation can change: traffic/incidents, direct toll cost, grade/energy burden, fuel price/consumption, carbon pricing or emissions factors, weather effects, and residual stochastic travel/cost variation. A narrower system would certify only route travel time; a broader system might include every possible logistics factor. This catalog is better because it covers the major decision-sensitive inputs that the code actually models and can audit.

### AD43. Evidence States Instead Of A Single Confidence Score

The state catalog is:

```python
EVIDENCE_STATES = (
    "nominal", "mildly_stale", "severely_stale",
    "low_confidence", "proxy", "refreshed",
)
```

A single confidence number is easy to display but loses the cause of uncertainty. Staleness, proxy substitution, low confidence, and refreshed data have different implications. This project is more inspectable because state labels are interpretable in a viva: "the route changed because toll evidence was proxy" is more defensible than "confidence was 0.62." It also lets REFC stress worlds combine specific evidence weaknesses rather than applying a generic noise multiplier.

### AD44. Negative Refreshed-Evidence Effects

The state-effect table includes:

```python
DEFAULT_STATE_EFFECTS = {
    "proxy": (0.185, 0.152, 0.132),
    "refreshed": (-0.038, -0.030, -0.024),
}
```

Positive values widen uncertainty or stress the objective; refreshed evidence slightly reduces perturbation. This is better than treating refreshed evidence as merely "nominal" because a current live source should actively reduce ambiguity compared with stale or proxy evidence. The negative values are small, so refreshed data does not magically prove correctness; it only earns a modest reduction in stress-world burden.

### AD45. Objective-Specific Evidence Sensitivities

The source-backed table is:

```python
DEFAULT_FAMILY_SENSITIVITY = {
    "toll": (0.05, 1.00, 0.12),
    "terrain": (0.52, 0.22, 0.78),
    "weather": (0.72, 0.18, 0.18),
}
```

The tuple order is time, money, CO2. Toll evidence mostly affects money; terrain affects time and CO2; weather mostly affects time. The alternative would be one generic uncertainty multiplier, but that would be wrong for freight routing because the mechanism of evidence failure matters. Objective-specific sensitivity is better because it makes the stress worlds physically and economically interpretable.

### AD46. Ambiguity-Scaled REFC World Caps

The current adaptive caps are:

```python
route_refc_low_ambiguity_world_cap: int = Field(default=24)
route_refc_medium_ambiguity_world_cap: int = Field(default=48)
route_refc_high_ambiguity_world_floor: int = Field(default=72)
```

The code also preserves the older alias `ROUTE_REFC_CERTIFIED_SET_CAP`, but the comment clarifies that this caps low-ambiguity world sampling rather than certified-set cardinality. This is important thesis hygiene. Other systems often use a fixed Monte Carlo size regardless of case difficulty. The adaptive design is better because easy cases do not pay for high stress-world resolution, while ambiguous cases get more worlds before the system certifies or abstains.

### AD47. Deterministic Myopic VOI Controller

The module states the design:

```python
# VOI-AD2R uses a deterministic myopic value-per-cost controller.
# The design is inspired by decision-theoretic control of computation
# and one-step value-of-information policies rather than by learned RL.
```

RL would be fashionable, but it would require a training environment, a reward model, and enough representative freight-routing episodes to avoid overfitting. This project instead needs a controller whose decisions can be replayed and justified. The myopic value-per-cost controller is better here because it can explain every action as "this search/evidence/preference action currently has the best expected decision value per cost." That matches the auditability goal.

### AD48. VOI Action-Family Separation

The action-family routing is:

```python
def _action_family_for_kind(kind: str) -> str:
    if kind in {"refine_top1_dccs", "refine_topk_dccs"}:
        return "search"
    if kind in {"refresh_top1_vor", "increase_stochastic_samples"}:
        return "evidence"
    if kind in _PREFERENCE_ACTION_KINDS:
        return "preference"
    if kind == "stop":
        return "terminal"
```

This is better than one undifferentiated action list because each family consumes different budgets and answers a different uncertainty question. Search asks whether an unrefined challenger can win. Evidence asks whether the current winner survives better data. Preference asks whether the user's value model is underdetermined. Stop says further computation is not worth the cost. The separation is central to the thesis because the system does not merely compute more; it chooses what kind of uncertainty to reduce.

### AD49. Typed Preference Actions

The preference action mapping is:

```python
_PREFERENCE_ACTION_MODALITY_BY_KIND = {
    "preference_pairwise_route_query": "pairwise_route_query",
    "preference_tradeoff_threshold_query": "tradeoff_threshold_query",
    "preference_ratio_query": "ratio_query",
    "preference_veto_query": "veto_query",
    "preference_time_guard_query": "time_guard_query",
}
```

Free-text questions would be easy to generate but hard to validate, replay, and score. Typed questions are better because they connect directly to preference-state updates: pairwise route choice, threshold, ratio, veto, and time guard each has a different mathematical meaning. The thesis should describe this as structured preference elicitation, not chatbot questioning.

### AD50. VOI Support-Richness Calculation

The support-richness score uses a weighted blend:

```python
return _clamp01(
    (0.24 * prior_strength)
    + (0.22 * support_strength)
    + (0.18 * support_ratio)
    + (0.14 * source_entropy)
    + (0.08 * source_count)
    + (0.06 * source_mix)
    + (0.04 * corridor_count)
    + (0.04 * candidate_paths)
)
```

The larger weights are on prior/support strength because a support-rich ambiguity window should first be backed by enough historical or contextual evidence. Entropy and source count matter because a single source is weaker than a mixed source base. Corridor count and candidate paths are small terms because they are useful context but should not dominate the evidence signal. This is better than a binary "has support" flag because the controller can distinguish thin support from broad, diverse support.

### AD51. VOI Ambiguity-Pressure Calculation

The current formula is:

```python
return _clamp01(
    (0.30 * pending_flip)
    + (0.22 * pending_mass)
    + (0.18 * near_tie)
    + (0.14 * completeness_gap)
    + (0.10 * max(0.0, 1.0 - frontier_recall))
    + (0.06 * certificate_margin_pressure)
)
```

Pending flip probability receives the largest weight because the most urgent ambiguity is that an unrefined challenger can become best. Pending mass and near ties follow because they indicate that the current frontier is not settled. Completeness and frontier recall measure search coverage, while certificate margin pressure catches weak certificates. The alternative would be to use only certificate score; this project is more diagnostically useful because it decomposes why the certificate is weak.

### AD52. Strict Runtime Fast-Startup Disablement

`settings.py` deliberately overrides the fast-startup default:

```python
self.route_graph_fast_startup_enabled = False
self.route_graph_skip_initial_search_long_corridor = False
```

Fast startup is useful for developer responsiveness, but it can make reviewer-facing proof runs report readiness before the graph route pipeline is actually warm. The strict runtime chooses reproducibility over startup speed. That is better for a thesis because a benchmark or validation run should not depend on whether a graph cache happened to be warm.

### AD53. Long-Corridor Initial Search Requirement

The code comment gives the reason:

```python
# Reviewer-facing strict proof runs cannot skip long-corridor graph
# search up front, otherwise DCCS collapses to bounded fallback with
# zero graph-generated challengers on the broad-cold evidence lane.
self.route_graph_skip_initial_search_long_corridor = False
```

The alternative is to bypass expensive graph search on long corridors and rely on fallback routes. That is tempting for speed, but it undermines the DCCS claim because challenger discovery collapses. The stricter choice is better for this thesis because it ensures the selective-search mechanism is actually exercised.

### AD54. A* Heuristic Max Speed `220` kph

The route graph heuristic bound is:

```python
route_graph_a_star_heuristic_enabled: bool = Field(default=True)
route_graph_heuristic_max_speed_kph: float = Field(default=220.0, ge=30.0, le=500.0)
```

The heuristic uses a very high plausible upper speed so it remains optimistic rather than overestimating remaining travel cost. A low max-speed bound would make A* faster in some cases but could bias pruning or ranking by making the heuristic too aggressive. `220` kph is better here because it is safely above legal freight speeds, making the heuristic conservative for correctness while still useful for search ordering.

### AD55. Route Graph `k_paths=24` And `max_hops=220`

The core graph-search settings are:

```python
route_graph_k_paths: int = Field(default=24, ge=1, le=128)
route_graph_max_hops: int = Field(default=220, ge=8, le=2000)
```

This is not "find 24 final recommendations." It is a candidate-generation breadth setting. The route selector and DCCS later decide which candidates are worth refining or returning. A smaller value risks missing hidden challengers; a much larger value would turn the system into brute-force enumeration. `24` and `220` are better for this project because they supply enough graph diversity for DCCS without pretending the graph search is exhaustive.

### AD56. Adaptive Hop Settings From Distance And Edge Length

The adaptive-hop parameters are:

```python
route_graph_hops_per_km: float = Field(default=18.0)
route_graph_edge_length_estimate_m: float = Field(default=75.0)
route_graph_hops_safety_factor: float = Field(default=1.8)
route_graph_max_hops_cap: int = Field(default=15_000)
```

Route graphs vary in density. A fixed hop limit that works for a rural corridor can fail in a dense urban network. Adaptive hops are better because they scale the search envelope with corridor length and expected edge density, while the 15,000 cap prevents runaway expansion. This is a practical engineering choice that supports the thesis claim of controlled computation.

### AD57. Graph Search State-Budget Rescue

The state-budget rescue defaults include:

```python
route_graph_state_space_rescue_enabled: bool = Field(default=True)
route_graph_state_budget_per_hop: int = Field(default=1600)
route_graph_state_budget_retry_multiplier: float = Field(default=2.5)
route_graph_state_budget_retry_cap: int = Field(default=8_000_000)
```

The alternative is to fail immediately when a search exceeds the first state budget. That makes tests clean but is brittle on real corridors. Rescue is better because it escalates compute only when the first budget is insufficient. It preserves the "selective" principle: the system spends more only after there is evidence that the current limit is too tight.

### AD58. Separate Long-Corridor Treatment

The long-corridor settings are:

```python
route_graph_long_corridor_threshold_km: float = Field(default=150.0)
route_graph_long_corridor_max_paths: int = Field(default=4)
```

Long corridors have a larger combinatorial search space and a higher chance of repeated route variants. Treating them separately is better than using one global setting because a 20 km urban trip and a 250 km freight corridor do not have the same search shape. The `max_paths=4` long-corridor bound keeps graph generation from flooding DCCS with many slight variants of the same strategic route.

### AD59. ORS And OSRM Baseline Multiplier Differences

The settings carry engine-specific correction factors:

```python
route_graph_osrm_baseline_duration_multiplier: float = Field(default=1.16)
route_graph_osrm_baseline_distance_multiplier: float = Field(default=1.13)
route_graph_ors_baseline_duration_multiplier: float = Field(default=1.24)
route_graph_ors_baseline_distance_multiplier: float = Field(default=1.18)
```

Different routing engines and graph builds can return systematically different baselines. One generic multiplier would hide that engine identity matters. Engine-specific multipliers are better because comparisons remain honest: OSRM and ORS are not assumed to be interchangeable black boxes. The thesis should explain these as calibration guards for route-generation surfaces, not as arbitrary route penalties.

### AD60. ORS Runtime Manifest Design

`backend/app/routing_ors.py` verifies graph identity:

```python
identity_status = "graph_identity_verified"
if not graph_dir.is_dir():
    identity_status = "graph_missing"
elif not build_info_path.is_file():
    identity_status = "graph_build_info_missing"
elif not bool(config_state.get("exists")):
    identity_status = "config_missing"
elif not bool(pbf_state.get("exists")):
    identity_status = "source_pbf_missing"
```

The manifest also records config state, source PBF state, graph file counts, graph listing digest, and a `manifest_hash`. This is better than a black-box ORS call because a route result is only reproducible if the graph, profile, source data, and config are known. The thesis should use this as evidence of audit discipline: the project records the routing engine's data identity, not just its HTTP response.

### AD61. Detailed Route-Option Cache Key

The cache key includes route identity, policy settings, and user-facing decision inputs:

```python
"inputs": {
    "vehicle_type": str(vehicle_type),
    "scenario_mode": str(getattr(scenario_mode, "value", scenario_mode)),
    "terrain_profile": str(getattr(terrain_profile, "value", terrain_profile)),
    "stochastic": _normalize_key_component(stochastic),
    "utility_weights": [round(float(value), 6) for value in utility_weights],
    "risk_aversion": round(float(risk_aversion), 6),
}
```

The alternative would be caching only by route geometry. That would be faster but wrong because the same geometry can produce different cost, emissions, risk, terrain, and utility outputs under different settings. The detailed key is better because it prevents stale policy results from masquerading as fresh route builds.

### AD62. Geometry Signature Sampling And Coordinate Rounding

The geometry signature is:

```python
step = max(1, len(valid) // 30)
sample = valid[::step][:40]
parts = [f"{lon:.4f},{lat:.4f}" for lon, lat in sample]
return hashlib.sha1("|".join(parts).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
```

Hashing every point would make the key sensitive to tiny geometry encoding differences and large polylines. Sampling up to 40 rounded points is better because it captures route shape while avoiding noise from dense geometry detail. The thesis should describe this as a pragmatic route-shape fingerprint, not a legally exact geometry hash.

### AD63. Segment Annotation Signature Truncation

The segment signature records rounded distance and duration samples:

```python
"distance": [round(float(value), 3) for value in distances[:512]],
"duration": [round(float(value), 3) for value in durations[:512]],
```

Segment annotations can be very long. Keeping the first 512 values is enough to represent the detailed route-build surface for cache invalidation without making cache keys huge. This is better than ignoring annotations because cost and terrain calculations depend on segment structure, and it is better than full serialization because huge keys harm runtime performance.

### AD64. Process Cache Deep-Copy Semantics

The global cache store returns and stores deep copies:

```python
return copy.deepcopy(entry.payload)
payload = copy.deepcopy(value)
```

Without deep copies, one caller could mutate a cached payload and contaminate later requests. A shallow or raw cache would be faster, but it would make route evidence hard to trust. Deep copying is better for this project because correctness and reproducibility are more important than squeezing a few milliseconds out of mutable in-process objects.

### AD65. Process Cache TTL, Entry, Byte, And Oversize Accounting

The cache constructor stores all four controls:

```python
self._ttl_s = max(1, int(ttl_s))
self._max_entries = max(1, int(max_entries))
self._max_estimated_bytes = max(0, int(max_estimated_bytes))
self._oversize_rejections = 0
```

A blind memoization dictionary can grow without bound and can serve old evidence after the underlying assumptions have changed. TTL protects time validity, entry count protects cardinality, byte limits protect memory, and oversize rejection prevents one huge route artifact from evicting useful normal entries. This is better for a production-like thesis system because the cache is an engineered component, not an incidental speed trick.

### AD66. Scenario Context Feature Set

The context key is:

```python
return (
    f"{self.corridor_geohash5.strip().lower() or 'uk000'}|"
    f"h{max(0, min(23, int(self.hour_slot_local))):02d}|"
    f"{self.day_kind.strip().lower() or 'weekday'}|"
    f"{self.road_mix_bucket.strip().lower() or 'mixed'}|"
    f"{self.vehicle_class.strip().lower() or 'rigid_hgv'}|"
    f"{self.weather_regime.strip().lower() or 'clear'}"
)
```

This key is better than using origin/destination text alone because freight-route behavior depends on corridor, time, calendar type, road class mix, vehicle class, and weather. It is also better than a highly granular per-road key because sparse data would make many contexts uncalibrated. The chosen context is a compact middle ground: specific enough for scenario relevance, broad enough for data reuse.

### AD67. Scenario Policy Live-Coverage And Pressure Fields

The policy model includes live-source provenance:

```python
live_source_set: dict[str, str] = Field(default_factory=dict)
live_coverage: dict[str, float] = Field(default_factory=dict)
live_traffic_pressure: float = 1.0
live_incident_pressure: float = 1.0
live_weather_pressure: float = 1.0
```

This is better than storing only final multipliers because the thesis can explain why a multiplier changed. If weather pressure is high but traffic coverage is weak, that is different from a complete live scenario update. The model preserves both the transformed result and the evidence surface behind it.

### AD68. Clamped Scenario-Pressure Adjustment

The adjustment function is:

```python
adjusted = base * (1.0 + ((pressure - 1.0) * gain * sensitivity))
return _clamp(adjusted, low, high)
```

The alternative is to multiply raw live pressures straight into route cost. That is dangerous because live feeds can spike, be stale, or be only partially covered. The clamped formula is better because it lets pressure affect the route while bounding extreme behavior. It supports a thesis argument that live data is incorporated cautiously rather than trusted blindly.

### AD69. Strict Runtime Scenario Source Policy

The strict settings are policy-sensitive:

```python
self.live_scenario_allow_partial_sources_strict = policy != "strict_external"
self.live_scenario_min_source_count_strict = 3 if policy != "strict_external" else 4
self.live_scenario_min_coverage_overall_strict = 0.75 if policy != "strict_external" else 1.0
```

`strict_external` means the system is expected to validate against external live URLs, so it requires all sources and full coverage. `repo_local_fresh` allows freshly rebuilt local artifacts, so it permits three of four sources and 75 percent coverage. This is better than one rigid strict mode because the thesis can distinguish "external live proof" from "fresh local reproducibility proof" without weakening the meaning of either.

### AD70. Stable Seeds For Stochastic Uncertainty

The seed is deterministic:

```python
material = f"{route_signature}|{departure_slot}|{user_seed}"
return int(hashlib.sha1(material.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16], 16)
```

Random uncertainty without stable seeding is hard to debug and hard to cite in a thesis. Stable seeds are better because the same route, departure slot, and user seed replay the same stochastic world bundle. The project still models uncertainty, but it does so in a way that supports reproducible experiments.

### AD71. Fifteen-Minute Departure Buckets

The departure slot code is:

```python
# 15-minute deterministic slot for stable replay behavior.
minute_bucket = (local.minute // 15) * 15
return local.strftime(f"%Y-%m-%dT%H:{minute_bucket:02d}%z")
```

Minute-level uniqueness would fragment stochastic contexts and make repeated experiments hard to compare. Hour-level buckets would be too coarse for traffic-sensitive freight routing. Fifteen minutes is better because it preserves time-of-day sensitivity while keeping replay contexts stable and reusable.

### AD72. Rich Uncertainty Summaries

The summary exposes percentiles, CVaR, robust score, and clipping diagnostics:

```python
q95_duration_s: float
cvar95_duration_s: float
utility_q95: float
utility_cvar95: float
robust_score: float
sample_count_clip_ratio: float
sigma_clip_ratio: float
```

Mean and standard deviation are not enough for risk-sensitive freight decisions because tail delays and tail costs matter. CVaR and q95 are better for the thesis because they let the project discuss worst-tail behavior rather than only average behavior. Clip ratios are also important because they reveal when requested uncertainty parameters were bounded by the system.

### AD73. Hyndman-Fan Type-7 Quantiles

The code documents the convention:

```python
# Use the Hyndman-Fan type-7 sample quantile convention.
pos = q_clamped * (len(ordered) - 1)
```

There are many valid sample quantile definitions. The project chooses and documents one instead of leaving percentile behavior implicit. That is better for thesis reproducibility because a reader can match the calculation exactly when checking reported q90 or q95 values.

### AD74. CVaR Tail-Quantile Integration

The CVaR function documents its basis:

```python
# Empirical CVaR / expected shortfall integrates the tail quantile
# function on [alpha, 1].
```

A simpler implementation might average only samples above the empirical quantile. Integrating the tail quantile is better because it behaves more smoothly for small to medium sample sizes and is easier to link to expected shortfall theory. The thesis should still call it empirical CVaR, not a closed-form distributional CVaR.

### AD75. Default `cvar_excess` Risk Family With `alpha=0.95`

The current defaults are:

```python
risk_cvar_alpha: float = Field(default=0.95, ge=0.5, le=0.999)
risk_family: str = Field(default="cvar_excess")
```

`0.95` focuses on the upper tail without collapsing to the single worst sample. `cvar_excess` penalizes tail risk above the mean rather than replacing the objective with tail value alone. This is better for freight routing because it balances normal operating performance with resilience against bad outcomes.

### AD76. Thesis-Specific Risk Variant Labelling

The implementation is explicit:

```python
# This is a thesis-specific entropic-style tail penalty, not the
# canonical entropic risk measure on the full loss distribution.
```

This prevents overclaiming. Other projects might name a metric after a textbook concept without preserving the exact definition. This report is stronger academically because it marks where a risk variant is an engineered penalty inspired by a concept rather than the canonical mathematical object.

### AD77. Vehicle-Specific Terrain Physics

The terrain model distinguishes vehicle classes:

```python
if key == "artic_hgv":
    return VehicleTerrainParams(
        mass_kg=38_000.0,
        c_rr=0.0075,
        drag_area_m2=8.2,
        drivetrain_efficiency=0.86,
        regen_efficiency=0.12,
    )
```

A route that is good for a van is not necessarily good for an articulated HGV. Vehicle-specific terrain parameters are better because mass, rolling resistance, drag area, drivetrain efficiency, and regenerative recovery materially affect grade penalties and emissions. The thesis should highlight this as a freight-specific improvement over passenger-car route scoring.

### AD78. Terrain Profile Weight Defaults

The profile weight function is:

```python
if terrain_profile == "flat":
    return 0.2
if terrain_profile == "rolling":
    return 0.7
return 1.0
```

The weights let the same physical grade calculation respond differently to user or scenario terrain intent. Flat does not ignore terrain completely; it applies a small effect. Rolling applies most of the effect. Hilly applies the full effect. This is better than three unrelated formulas because the profiles remain comparable while still changing sensitivity.

### AD79. Terrain Segment Multiplier Floors And Clamps

The segment duration multiplier is bounded:

```python
floor_by_profile = {"flat": 1.0, "rolling": 1.02, "hilly": 1.05}
return _clamp(
    max(floor_by_profile.get(terrain_profile, 1.0), weighted / max(0.70, params.drivetrain_efficiency)),
    0.85,
    1.65,
)
```

Without bounds, noisy grade samples could create unrealistic speedups or penalties. The floors ensure rolling and hilly profiles actually impose a minimum burden, while the clamps stop extreme multipliers. This is better than unconstrained physics in this context because the model is used in routing decisions, not a high-resolution vehicle dynamics simulator.

### AD80. UK-Bounded Fail-Closed DEM

The relevant settings are:

```python
terrain_dem_fail_closed_uk: bool = Field(default=True)
terrain_dem_coverage_min_uk: float = Field(default=0.96)
terrain_uk_only_support: bool = Field(default=True)
terrain_uk_bbox: str = Field(default="49.75,61.10,-8.75,2.25")
```

The alternative is to allow synthetic or partial terrain everywhere. That would make demos easier but would weaken evidence quality. UK-bounded fail-closed behavior is better because the project knows its geographic scope and refuses to pretend unsupported terrain data is reliable. This should be framed as a limitation and a strength: narrow scope, stronger guarantees inside scope.

### AD81. Terrain Sampling Defaults

The settings are:

```python
terrain_sample_spacing_m: float = Field(default=180.0)
terrain_long_route_sample_spacing_m: float = Field(default=320.0)
terrain_max_samples_per_route: int = Field(default=1500)
```

Dense terrain sampling improves local grade detail but can become expensive on long freight corridors. The long-route spacing increases to 320 m to keep runtime under control, while the 1500 sample cap prevents runaway route builds. This is better than a single fixed sample count because it adapts to route length without ignoring terrain.

### AD82. Raw Duration, Money, And Emissions In Pareto Selection

The selector's default objective key is:

```python
lambda route: (
    float(route.metrics.duration_s),
    float(route.metrics.monetary_cost),
    float(route.metrics.emissions_kg),
)
```

Using raw objectives is better than using a hidden weighted utility for Pareto filtering because Pareto dominance is supposed to be preference-light. A weighted utility can remove routes that are genuinely non-dominated under another user's preferences. The project keeps utility and risk scoring elsewhere, which makes the Pareto layer easier to defend.

### AD83. Strict Pareto Frontier Expansion

The selector accepts:

```python
strict_frontier: bool = False
```

Strict frontier mode is useful when the thesis wants to analyze the mathematical frontier without truncation effects. A UI normally needs a smaller list, but an evaluation run may need the complete non-dominated set. Supporting both is better because the same codebase can serve product ergonomics and dissertation evidence without conflating them.

### AD84. Crowding/Diversity For Alternatives

The DCCS comment cites multi-objective diversity ideas:

```python
# objective-space coverage and diversity terms borrow from standard
# multi-objective search ideas such as normalized nearest-neighbour spacing
# and crowding/diversification.
```

If the app returns only the top utility routes, alternatives often cluster around the same corridor. Crowding/diversity is better because a human decision-maker needs meaningfully different options, not just tiny variants. The thesis can explain this as preserving decision coverage.

### AD85. Knee Score As Heuristic

The knee score is based on distance to an ideal point:

```python
score = math.sqrt(sum((_norm(values[idx], mins[idx], maxs[idx]) ** 2) for idx in range(dim_count)))
```

This is useful, but it is not a formal proof that a route is the unique knee of the Pareto frontier. Calling it a heuristic is better because it avoids overclaiming. The route closest to normalized ideal objectives is often a good compromise candidate, but the thesis should present it as an interpretable selection aid.

### AD86. Modified Selection Weight Components

The defaults are:

```python
route_selection_modified_regret_weight: float = Field(default=0.35)
route_selection_modified_balance_weight: float = Field(default=0.10)
route_selection_modified_distance_weight: float = Field(default=0.22)
route_selection_modified_eta_distance_weight: float = Field(default=0.18)
route_selection_modified_entropy_weight: float = Field(default=0.08)
route_selection_modified_knee_weight: float = Field(default=0.12)
```

Regret is the largest configured non-default modified-selector coefficient, but the current default `modified_vikor_distance` branch does not apply it. In the default branch, distance and ETA-distance are the largest added route-domain terms, with balance, knee, entropy, and backend time-preservation penalty shaping the final score. This is better than one opaque utility score because the thesis can explain what each term contributes and where each term is actually used.

### AD87. Tchebycheff `rho=0.001` And VIKOR `v=0.5`

The settings are:

```python
route_selection_tchebycheff_rho: float = Field(default=0.001)
route_selection_vikor_v: float = Field(default=0.5)
```

The small Tchebycheff rho acts as an augmentation term without overpowering the max-deviation objective. VIKOR `v=0.5` balances group utility and individual regret rather than privileging one side. These defaults are better for thesis comparison because they are neutral, transparent starting points, not tuned to make one route family win.

### AD88. Standard Dominance With Balanced Gain And Diversity Metrics

The metric script defines the objective fields:

```python
OBJECTIVE_FIELDS = ("duration_s", "monetary_cost", "emissions_kg")
```

Dominance alone says whether one route is better in all objectives, but many freight tradeoffs are non-dominated. Balanced gain and diversity make the evaluation richer: balanced gain asks whether improvements are spread across objectives, while diversity asks whether the frontier gives the user meaningfully different choices. This is better than reporting one win rate because route recommendation is multi-objective.

### AD89. Avoiding Universal Win-Rate Claims

The system has multiple modes, budgets, evidence states, and objective weights. A single universal win rate would collapse all that context into a misleading number. The better claim is conditional: under specified data, budgets, and evaluation metrics, DCCS/REFC/VOI improves certain evidence or decision-quality measures. This is more academically defensible than "our system is X percent better" without context.

### AD90. Focused Test Failures As Dated Evidence

A May 5, 2026 focused-slice snapshot recorded:

```text
ERROR backend/tests/test_refc.py
ImportError: cannot import name 'ABSTENTION_REASON_CODES' from 'app.abstention'
1 error during collection
```

That snapshot is no longer the current focused-backend truth. As of the May 6, 2026 local source audit, `backend/app/abstention.py` exports `ABSTENTION_REASON_CODES` as the tuple of typed abstention reason literals, and the import succeeds with seven codes. The exact focused command:

```powershell
uv run --project backend pytest -q backend/tests/test_dccs.py backend/tests/test_refc.py backend/tests/test_voi_controller.py backend/tests/test_preference_runtime_api.py
```

now reaches test assertions rather than stopping at collection in the dated local snapshot. The narrower compatibility subset recorded in Appendix AQ.12 remains useful as a targeted green compatibility signal, but the maintained publishability/adoption reading should come from the full-suite verdict bundle rather than from this older focused command. The old ImportError is valuable only as dated process history; the current report should not use it to imply a missing abstention symbol or a maintained issue.

### AD91. GitHub CI Versus Local Focused Slice

CI may run a narrower workflow, a different environment, or a different test selection. The repo notes that CI is backend-only, and local focused slices can expose tests that are not part of the current CI gate. This is not a contradiction; it means "CI green" and "all local focused tests pass" are different claims. The thesis should state exactly which command produced each result.

### AD92. `python scripts/check_docs.py` As Thesis Gate

The docs checker validates the six default output labels emitted by `scripts/check_docs.py`: `Markdown link validity`, `Docs index/orphan/related-doc coverage`, `Referenced local path existence`, `Endpoint parity against backend/app/main.py`, `Theorem-map / claim-matrix semantic consistency`, and `Notebook reference ban`. That matters because this report is meant to consolidate the codebase understanding, not become an isolated essay. A manual report without consistency checks can drift silently. The checker is better because it turns documentation integrity into a repeatable build-like check.

### AD93. Generated Results As Evidence Artifacts

Generated route outputs, evaluation summaries, manifests, and reviewer table/figure source files are not just byproducts; they are the empirical evidence behind the thesis narrative. The report should name the artifact, command, date, and interpretation whenever possible. This is better than paraphrasing results because future readers can distinguish source code, generated data, and author interpretation.

### AD94. Scripts As Primary Evidence Mechanism

The repository policy is notebook-free and script-first: routine development, evaluation, and reporting should use `backend/scripts/`, `scripts/`, tests, and generated `backend/out/` or `out/` artifacts as maintained evidence surfaces. Exploratory interactive analysis is not the source of thesis truth unless its data, scripts, and generated outputs are traceable through those maintained surfaces.

### AD95. Abstention As Feature

An abstention is the system refusing to overclaim when evidence, search, or preference information is insufficient. That is better than always returning a route because freight decisions can have real cost, emissions, and operational consequences. The superseded May 5 ImportError around `ABSTENTION_REASON_CODES` should not be used to say abstention is broken because the current code exports that symbol. The thesis should instead discuss abstention through the current typed API: `typed_abstention_recommended`, search insufficiency, evidence insufficiency, preference ambiguity, out-of-support world models, exhausted budgets, and model-assumption limits are different terminal reasons with different remedies.

### AD96. Preference-State Monotonicity

The preference update layer rejects impossible updates such as compatible volume increasing after a query. In thesis terms, preference elicitation should narrow the feasible preference set or leave it unchanged, not invent new ambiguity after receiving information. This is better than an unconstrained questionnaire engine because every user answer must respect mathematical state invariants.

### AD97. Frontend Preservation Of Backend Reason Codes And Artifact Links

The frontend is not just a display layer; it is part of the audit trail. If the backend says a route was certified, abstained, or selected because of a specific reason code, the UI must preserve that explanation rather than replacing it with vague text. Artifact links matter for the same reason: a user or examiner should be able to move from a recommendation to the evidence that produced it.

### AD98. Careful UK Asset And Data Scope

The code has UK-specific terrain bounds, data assets, and road/corridor assumptions. Generalizing without equivalent data would make the system look broader but weaker. The project is better as a thesis when it states the UK scope honestly and then delivers stronger evidence inside that scope. Future work can expand geography, but the current claims should remain UK-grounded.

### AD99. Comparison To Simpler Route Planners

The fair comparison is not "this app finds a shorter route than Google Maps." The stronger comparison is: simple planners return a route under a hidden or fixed objective; this system returns, with evidence, whether a route remains defensible under incomplete search, uncertain evidence, and ambiguous preferences. The project is better for the thesis problem because it optimizes accountable decision quality, not just raw navigation convenience.

### AD100. Final Viva-Level Architecture Answer

The architecture is better for this project because every major decision has an audit surface: DCCS explains why a challenger was worth refining, REFC explains whether the winner survives bounded evidence perturbations, VOI explains which uncertainty-reduction action was worth its cost, strict runtime explains whether data sources are acceptable, and the report/docs checker explains whether the written evidence still matches the code. A simpler architecture would be easier to demo, but it would not support the dissertation claim that freight-route recommendation can be made selectively computed, evidence-certified, preference-aware, and reproducible.

## Appendix AE: Limitations, Risks, And Future-Work Directions

This appendix makes the report more academically balanced.

The repository is strong, but it is not unlimited.

A good thesis should state what remains hard, uncertain, or incomplete.

### AE1. Geographic Scope Remains Bounded

- The project is tuned for the UK and should be described that way.
- Extending it to another country would need new graph preparation, departure behavior, scenario context, toll assets, and likely new live-source policies.
- In plain English, the system does not become global merely by changing the map extract.
- In thesis terms, geographic transfer is future work, not a present claim.

### AE2. Calibration Can Age

- Scenario profiles, departure profiles, and stochastic regimes are only as current as the data and publication pipeline behind them.
- Certification-facing guarantees are therefore conditional on calibrated world models and support-aware evaluation staying in date.
- Drift tooling helps, but it does not magically eliminate temporal change.
- In plain English, calibrated realism still needs maintenance.
- In thesis terms, recalibration cadence is an important future-work consideration.

### AE3. Live Data Can Fail For Reasons Outside The Repo

- Even good code cannot control upstream outages, schema shifts, or rate limits.
- The repo handles this better than many systems by failing clearly and tracing calls.
- In plain English, live-data dependence remains an external risk.
- In thesis terms, upstream source volatility is a standing systems risk.

### AE4. Strictness Improves Trust But Reduces Availability

- Fail-closed behavior is methodologically strong.
- It also means some routes will fail instead of returning best-effort answers.
- The runtime can therefore favor certification quality and auditability over raw throughput.
- In plain English, the system chooses honesty over always answering.
- In thesis terms, this is a defendable tradeoff, but still a tradeoff.

### AE5. Richer Models Mean More Configuration

- The repo has many environment variables and calibration surfaces.
- That flexibility is useful but increases deployment and tuning complexity.
- In plain English, the system is powerful partly because it has many knobs.
- In thesis terms, configuration management is a real operational challenge.

### AE6. The Frontend Carries Significant Complexity

- The large page orchestration file is practical, but it is also heavy.
- Future work could decompose state and workflows into smaller modules while preserving clarity.
- In plain English, the UI is effective but not minimal.
- In thesis terms, frontend maintainability is a reasonable future-improvement area.

### AE7. Global Superiority Over Baselines Is Not Proven In-Repo

- The project supports careful local comparison.
- It does not include one final universal number proving superiority across all freight use cases.
- In plain English, evidence is strong for scoped comparison, not unlimited generalization.
- In thesis terms, wider benchmark corpora remain future work.

### AE8. Physical Modeling Is Purposeful But Approximate

- Terrain and energy logic use physically informed engineering approximations.
- They are not full vehicle-dynamics simulations.
- In plain English, the model is realistic enough to matter, but not infinitely detailed.
- In thesis terms, higher-fidelity physics would be future work if justified by data and runtime budgets.

### AE9. Scenario Modes Still Depend On Modeling Assumptions

- Even with data support, no-sharing, partial-sharing, and full-sharing are scenario constructs rather than ground truth labels for every trip.
- Their value lies in disciplined comparison, not in pretending to observe all coordination effects perfectly.
- In plain English, the scenario layer is useful but interpretive.
- In thesis terms, scenario semantics should be discussed carefully and honestly.

### AE10. Uncertainty Quality Depends On Regime Coverage

- The stochastic model is richer where contexts map well to calibrated regimes.
- Sparse or weakly matched contexts can reduce confidence even when the system still computes.
- Weak support or proxy-audit overlap can require widened bounds, extra auditing, certified-set downgrade, or typed abstention instead of singleton certification.
- In plain English, risk estimates are best where the calibration knows the context well.
- In thesis terms, regime coverage is a natural future-work area.

### AE11. Operator Usability Still Needs Study

- Preference-sensitive certification assumes operators can answer some queries, but real workflows may not always permit enough elicitation.
- The frontend is feature-rich, but the repo does not itself contain a formal user study.
- Tutorial mode, accessibility work, and help text are positive signs, but usability evidence could go further.
- In plain English, the interface looks serious, but user-research evidence could be deeper.
- In thesis terms, formal usability evaluation is an obvious extension.

### AE12. Cost Modeling Could Incorporate More Business Rules

- The current model already includes fuel, tolls, carbon cost, and physical effects.
- Real fleets may also care about labor rules, depot constraints, charging infrastructure, contractual penalties, and more.
- In plain English, there is room to widen the economics further.
- In thesis terms, richer operational business constraints are future-work candidates.

### AE13. Multi-Trip Network Effects Are Still Limited

- The duty-chain and batch features are important, but the repo is not a full fleet-network optimizer.
- It evaluates many trips and chains, but not a full dispatch network equilibrium.
- In plain English, it reaches toward operations planning without solving every fleet-allocation problem.
- In thesis terms, network-wide optimization remains future work.

### AE14. More External Benchmarking Would Strengthen The Story

- The repo's internal benchmarking and comparison scaffolding are strong.
- External benchmark corpora or third-party evaluations would strengthen generalization further.
- In plain English, more outside testing would be valuable.
- In thesis terms, independent evaluation is a high-value next step.

### AE15. Despite These Limits, The Current Scope Is Strong

- The project already combines enough algorithmic, physical, contextual, and operational depth to sustain a substantial thesis.
- The limitations are real but bounded and discussable.
- In plain English, the system is meaningfully ambitious without pretending to be complete.
- In thesis terms, that is exactly the kind of scope a strong dissertation can defend.

## Appendix AF: Repository Quality Scoring

This appendix explains the quality-scoring machinery more explicitly.

The phrase "quality gate" can sound vague if it is not unpacked.

In this repository, quality is not one single number.

It is a set of subsystem scores, threshold checks, dropped-route gates, diversity gates, and benchmark expectations.

### AF1. Quality Is Scored Per Subsystem

- The backend quality script does not collapse everything into one unstructured pass/fail.
- It scores multiple subsystems independently.
- Local script evidence shows named score families including risk aversion, dominance, scenario profile, departure time, stochastic sampling, terrain profile, toll classification, fuel price, carbon price, and toll cost.
- In plain English, the repo asks "is each important modeling layer behaving well enough?" rather than only "did the overall script run?"
- In thesis terms, this is a much stronger evaluation design than a single smoke test.

### AF2. The Threshold Philosophy Is Explicit

- The quality script defines threshold targets for those subsystems.
- Local code shows a threshold value of 95 for each named subsystem in the quality-threshold map.
- In plain English, the default standard is intentionally high.
- This matters because the project is not satisfied by barely functional outputs.
- In thesis terms, the score threshold is part of the system's acceptance contract.

### AF3. Quality Also Includes Availability Gates

- Subsystem scores are not the only gate.
- The script also tracks dropped routes and compares them against a configured cap.
- Local docs state the strict default target is zero dropped routes.
- In plain English, a model that scores well only by silently discarding too many cases is not considered acceptable.
- In thesis terms, availability is part of quality.

### AF4. Diversity Gates Matter Too

- The quality script also checks fixture diversity and corridor diversity.
- That is significant because route-quality evidence is weaker when all tests come from too few patterns.
- In plain English, the repo wants to ensure quality is being judged over a meaningfully varied route set.
- This connects directly to the graph-theory note that frontier quality depends on candidate-space coverage.
- In thesis terms, input diversity is treated as part of evaluation legitimacy.

### AF5. Risk-Aversion Scoring

- The risk-aversion score checks whether robust decision behavior responds correctly to different uncertainty profiles.
- This matters because robust routing is one of the advanced claims in the project.
- In plain English, the repo wants to know whether routes with worse bad tails are penalized as expected.
- This is not just a mathematical curiosity.
- In thesis terms, it validates that the robust layer behaves like a real decision mechanism.

### AF6. Dominance Scoring

- The dominance score checks the Pareto layer.
- It matters because the project's multi-objective identity depends on dominance filtering being correct.
- In plain English, it tests whether obviously dominated routes are handled properly.
- This also supports later frontier curation and selector behavior.
- In thesis terms, it validates the core multi-objective logic.

### AF7. Scenario-Profile Scoring

- The scenario-profile score is one of the most important subsystem scores.
- Local docs state that it expects strict monotonicity across scenario modes and completeness of `scenario_summary` fields.
- The script also checks holdout fit behavior and observed-versus-projected context share.
- In plain English, the repo wants scenario effects to be ordered sensibly, data-backed, and complete in output.
- In thesis terms, this is a formal check on the policy-like scenario subsystem.

### AF8. Monotonicity Across Modes

- Local docs explicitly state the expected mode ordering `no_sharing >= partial_sharing >= full_sharing`.
- This matters because the scenario modes are meant to represent increasing coordination benefit.
- In plain English, the system checks that the "more sharing" modes do not accidentally look worse in the wrong direction for core multipliers.
- That is an example of semantic validation, not only syntactic validation.
- In thesis terms, it is an important argument for calibrated interpretability.

### AF9. Holdout Metrics Matter In Scenario Quality

- The scenario builder and quality scorer refer to holdout behavior, separability, coverage, and row-share thresholds.
- Local script evidence shows strict checks around separability, MAPE, holdout coverage, observed-mode row share, projection-dominant context share, and identity collapse.
- In plain English, the repo tries to ensure the scenario layer has genuine predictive or structural value on held-out cases.
- This matters because scenario modeling is easy to overstate.
- In thesis terms, holdout scoring is a key defense against overfitting claims.

### AF10. Departure-Time Scoring

- The departure-time score checks the time-sensitive route layer.
- This matters because departure optimization should be grounded in a coherent departure profile, not an empty repeated loop.
- In plain English, the repo wants departure-aware routing to actually behave differently where it should.
- This supports the thesis claim that schedule matters in the model.
- In thesis terms, it validates the temporal-calibration subsystem.

### AF11. Stochastic-Sampling Scoring

- The stochastic-sampling score checks the uncertainty machinery.
- Local docs mention posterior regime probabilities, quantile mapping, and factor mappings for traffic, incident, weather, price, and eco.
- In plain English, the repo asks whether its uncertainty engine has the right kinds of calibrated moving parts and whether those parts behave sensibly.
- This matters because stochastic routing is easy to fake with arbitrary randomness.
- In thesis terms, it supports the seriousness of the risk layer.

### AF12. Posterior Regime Check Semantics

- Posterior regime checks ensure there is a context-aware mapping from trip situation to uncertainty regime.
- In plain English, the system wants to know that not every route shares the same uncertainty personality.
- This matters because motorway-heavy weekday-peak freight should not necessarily look like all other trips.
- The posterior machinery is one of the deeper statistical features in the repo.
- In thesis terms, it is a context-rich uncertainty validation target.

### AF13. Clipping And Coverage Diagnostics Matter

- The stochastic implementation includes clipping diagnostics and bounded factors.
- This matters because uncertainty models can become numerically unstable or unrealistic if tails are not governed.
- In plain English, the repo checks whether its uncertainty system stays within sane behavior ranges.
- This is one of the reasons the robust layer is more than a decorative checkbox.
- In thesis terms, bounded stochastic diagnostics are part of quality assurance.

### AF14. Terrain-Profile Scoring
