#### AM.30.36 Allowlisted Frontend Artifact Proxy

The frontend proxy only allows known run subpaths and known artifact names:

```ts
if (subpath[0] !== 'artifacts') return false;
if (subpath.length !== 2) return false;
return ARTIFACT_ALLOWED.has(subpath[1]);
```

Source: `frontend/app/api/runs/[runId]/[...subpath]/route.ts`.

This is better than a free-form filesystem proxy because reviewer-facing artifact access should not become arbitrary file access. The allowlist also makes frontend/backend artifact drift visible when docs are checked.

#### AM.30.37 Backend Proxy Routes Instead Of Direct Browser Calls

Frontend requests use an internal backend URL and controlled timeout/transport classification:

```ts
process.env.BACKEND_INTERNAL_URL ??
process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL ??
'http://localhost:8000'
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/backendFetch.ts`.

This is better than direct browser calls to arbitrary backend URLs because deployment, local development, and transport errors are centralized. The UI can show whether the backend timed out, reset, or was unreachable instead of flattening everything into a generic fetch failure.

#### AM.30.38 Dedicated `/route/preference` Proxy Route

The preference proxy forwards request bodies to the backend and returns backend status without caching:

```ts
resp = await fetchBackend('/route/preference', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body,
  timeoutMs: computeRouteFallbackTimeoutMs(),
});
```

Source: `frontend/app/api/route/preference/route.ts`.

This is better than mutating preference state only in the browser because preference updates affect certification semantics. Keeping the backend as the authority means the query history, compatible-set shrinkage, and abstention reasons remain part of the artifact-producing pipeline.

#### AM.30.39 Scripts And Tests As The Primary Method

The docs checker itself is executable:

```python
if not any(selected.values()):
    selected = {k: True for k in selected}
```

Source: `scripts/check_docs.py`.

This is better than notebooks-only because the repository can enforce links, local paths, endpoint parity, theorem-map consistency, and notebook-reference policy in a repeatable command. Notebooks are useful for exploration, but the thesis evidence must be scriptable and CI-checkable.

#### AM.30.40 Dated Compatibility Issue And Current Status

The current report records the stale `ABSTENTION_REASON_CODES` collection failure only as dated history. The related code now exposes the aggregate constant, typed reason values, and helper constructors:

```python
TypedAbstentionReason = Literal[
    "uncertified_due_to_search",
    "uncertified_due_to_evidence",
    "uncertified_due_to_preference",
    ...
]
```

Source: `backend/app/abstention.py`.

This is better than making the report look greener than the codebase. A thesis can include dated compatibility history, but it must not misrepresent that history as the maintained verdict. The important distinction is that docs consistency is a documentation gate, AQ.12 records a targeted `91 passed` compatibility subset, and the exact focused DCCS/REFC/VOI/preference command is a targeted compatibility check rather than the maintained full-suite publication verdict.

#### AM.30.41 Fast And Strict-Live Backend CI Lanes

The workflow separates deterministic regression checks from strict runtime checks. Appendix AM.29 quotes the two lane environments: fast lane uses `STRICT_RUNTIME_TEST_BYPASS=1`, strict-live lane uses `STRICT_RUNTIME_TEST_BYPASS=0` and disables signed fallback for scenario and fuel.

This is better than one generic CI job because fail-closed runtime behavior can conflict with fast deterministic tests. Splitting lanes means a green result has a precise meaning, and a failing strict-live lane points to source-policy or runtime-data behavior rather than ordinary unit-test logic.

#### AM.30.42 Coordination, File Claims, And Python Leases During Report Writing

The repository treats documentation assembly as a concurrent engineering workflow. A child agent must claim the work item and the specific report section before editing; heavy Python checks should run through lease tooling when long-running.

This is better than informal parallel editing because the thesis report is itself an evidence artifact. Section claims prevent two agents from rewriting the same appendix; heartbeat and cleanup state show whether the six-agent process was live or stale; leases make expensive checks visible to other sessions.

## Appendix AN: README And Documentation Absorption Rationale

Appendix AN consolidates the remaining README and documentation details that matter to the thesis report. It is not a file-by-file documentation summary. The aim is to explain why this repository uses layered operational docs, executable checks, artifact manifests, negative-result pages, notebook restrictions, and agent coordination instead of treating the root README as the only source of truth.

The short version is that the codebase is too evidence-heavy for a single README. A README can orient a reader, but it cannot safely carry endpoint parity, strict-live readiness, artifact provenance, reviewer bundle status, publishability blockers, notebook policy, and multi-agent write coordination at the same time. This repo therefore uses the README files as front doors, and the maintained docs/scripts as the enforceable evidence system behind those doors.

### AN.1 Root README As Front Door, Not Whole Thesis


```powershell
.\scripts\dev.ps1
```

Source: `README.md`.

That command is deliberately paired with explicit readiness and service URLs:

```text
Frontend: http://localhost:3000
Backend docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
Backend readiness: http://localhost:8000/health/ready
OSRM: http://localhost:5000
```

Source: `README.md`.

Why this is better than a README-only project description: the repository has runtime truth. A reviewer should not infer readiness from prose. They should check the local service state, strict route readiness, strict-live data readiness, OpenAPI surface, and generated artifacts. The root README is therefore best used as the orientation layer that points to executable checks and deeper documentation.

The README also records the current terminal semantics in the same vocabulary used by the backend and UI:

```text
certified singleton, certified set, or typed abstention
```

Source: `README.md`.

That is better than describing the app as a generic route planner because the thesis contribution is not merely a displayed path. The decision package, abstention classes, action-family split, strict data policy, and artifact bundle are part of the claimed system.

### AN.2 Conservative Backend And Frontend READMEs

The backend README says the FastAPI service is the current freight-router runtime, that the primary path is the redesigned certification engine, and that live `/route` uses the public `DecisionPackage` contract. It also keeps package-local wording conservative:

```text
This is a factual map of the current codebase, not a publishability claim.
```

Source: `backend/README.md`.

The frontend README mirrors that discipline. It describes the Next.js UI as a consumer of `DecisionPackage`, a route-centric shell with proof/governance surfaces, and a live preference elicitation surface that round-trips answers through `/route/preference`.

Source: `frontend/README.md`.

Why this split is better than one monolithic README: backend truth and frontend truth have different failure modes. The backend owns validation, reason codes, certification, artifact emission, and strict runtime policy. The frontend owns request construction, operator visibility, proxying, diagnostics, and reviewer navigation. Keeping separate READMEs prevents the common mistake of treating UI affordances as proof that backend certification is complete, or treating backend artifacts as proof that the browser exposes every artifact path.

This is also better than putting all current-state details only in the thesis report. The report can cite the current codebase shape, but day-to-day developers need short package-local guards that stop future work from reintroducing legacy assumptions such as `/route` being a flat route response or the UI being a mock-only proof panel.

### AN.3 Runbook Separation Between Startup And Proof

The runbook is intentionally short and operator-facing. It documents what to run, how to check readiness, where artifacts live, and how to stop the stack:

```powershell
.\scripts\dev.ps1
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/health/ready" -Method Get
docker compose down
```

Source: `docs/runbook.md`.

The key detail is that startup is strict. The runbook states that `dev.ps1` starts OSRM and runs strict live preflight before backend startup, but does not start ORS for the operator. Therefore strict preflight can fail even when OSRM is healthy.

Source: `docs/runbook.md`.

Why this is better than a friendlier "start everything and ignore missing services" script: missing ORS, stale live feeds, graph warmup failure, and terrain/source failures change the meaning of route results. A route computed under degraded or proxy data is not the same thesis evidence as a route computed under strict live readiness. Failing early is more useful than hiding a missing dependency behind a fallback because the failure itself preserves the support boundary.

The longer operations guide expands the same point with the current environment matrix:

```text
LIVE_RUNTIME_DATA_ENABLED=true
STRICT_LIVE_DATA_REQUIRED=true
LIVE_SCENARIO_ALLOW_PARTIAL_SOURCES_STRICT=false
LIVE_SCENARIO_MIN_SOURCE_COUNT_STRICT=4
LIVE_SCENARIO_MIN_COVERAGE_OVERALL_STRICT=1.0
ROUTE_GRAPH_WARMUP_FAILFAST=1
TERRAIN_DEM_FAIL_CLOSED_UK=true
```

Source: `docs/run-and-operations.md`.

It also records that runtime-effective scenario strictness is source-policy sensitive: strict external mode requires full external coverage, while the checked `repo_local_fresh` policy can use signed fresh repo-local evidence with a lower effective source gate.

Source: `docs/run-and-operations.md`.

Why this nuance matters: without it, the thesis would conflate "strict external live proof" with "fresh signed repo-local proof." The repository's documentation is stronger because it names the difference instead of collapsing both into a generic "strict mode."

### AN.4 Executable PowerShell API Examples

The API cookbook gives reproducible local CLI examples, starting with a JSON payload and then exercising `/route`, `/pareto`, `/pareto/stream`, scenario compare, batch, duty-chain, departure, baselines, run artifacts, signature verification, readiness, cache, and oracle quality endpoints.

```powershell
$base = @{
  origin = @{ lat = 52.4862; lon = -1.8904 }
  destination = @{ lat = 51.5072; lon = -0.1276 }
  vehicle_type = "rigid_hgv"
  scenario_mode = "no_sharing"
  weights = @{ time = 1; money = 1; co2 = 1 }
  max_alternatives = 24
  pareto_method = "dominance"
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10
```

Source: `docs/api-cookbook.md`.

The cookbook then makes the core transport distinction explicit:

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/route" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" -Body $base
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/route/baseline?realism=true" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" -Body $base
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/route/baseline/ors?realism=true" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" -Body $base
```

Source: `docs/api-cookbook.md`.

Why this is better than prose endpoint lists: the commands preserve request shape. A reviewer can see whether a route result came from the certification-facing `/route` path or from a baseline path intended for comparison, ablation, replay, historical comparison, or waypoint traffic. That distinction prevents baseline outputs from being mistaken for certified decision packages.

The cookbook also documents run-artifact retrieval:

```powershell
$runId = "<run_id>"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/runs/$runId/manifest"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/runs/$runId/scenario-manifest"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/runs/$runId/signature"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/runs/$runId/scenario-signature"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/runs/$runId/artifacts"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:8000/runs/$runId/artifacts/results.json"
```

Source: `docs/api-cookbook.md`.

This is better than a screenshot-only demo because a run id connects request, manifest, scenario manifest, signature, provenance, artifacts, and frontend proxy behavior. The thesis can then cite machine-readable evidence rather than asking readers to trust a displayed panel.

### AN.5 Executable Docs Checking

The docs checker treats maintained documentation as a testable surface. It defines the maintained markdown set as root README, backend README, frontend README, root claim matrix, and docs markdown files:

```python
def list_maintained_markdown() -> list[Path]:
    files = [ROOT_README, *EXTRA_MAINTAINED_MARKDOWN, *list_docs()]
```

Source: `scripts/check_docs.py`.

It also includes endpoint extraction patterns for FastAPI decorators and documented endpoint mentions:

```python
APP_ROUTE_RE = re.compile(r'@app\.(get|post|put|delete|patch)\("([^"]+)"')
DOC_ENDPOINT_RE = re.compile(r"`(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH)\s+(/[^`]*)`")
```

Source: `scripts/check_docs.py`.

The relevant command is:

```powershell
python scripts/check_docs.py
```

Source: `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`.

Why this is better than relying on reviewers to spot stale links: docs drift is a real source of false claims. This checker can validate maintained markdown, links, local path references, theorem-table consistency, endpoint documentation parity, and notebook-reference policy. It turns documentation from static prose into a regression surface.

This does not mean every documentation fact is machine-verified. `docs/backend-api-tools.md` explicitly limits endpoint parity: it validates FastAPI decorators against documented backend endpoint entries, not frontend Next.js proxy coverage, response-model fields, artifact allowlists, endpoint mentions in every prose page, or thesis prose.

Source: `docs/backend-api-tools.md`.

That limitation is important. It is better to state "backend endpoint documentation parity is checked, frontend proxy parity still needs source inspection" than to claim a single docs check proves the whole documentation graph.

### AN.6 Endpoint Parity And Artifact Allowlists As Separate Controls

The backend route surface and the frontend proxy surface are not identical by design. The tutorial/reporting docs describe the run inspector proxy as a strict allowlist for report and artifact paths. The UI uses browser paths such as `/api/runs/{runId}/...`, but the backend can serve a broader artifact route.

Source: `docs/tutorial-and-reporting.md`.

The API cookbook states the distinction plainly: backend generic artifact retrieval validates the run id and artifact name, resolves inside the run folder, and serves known file types; the frontend retrieval path is narrower and returns `404` for unsupported browser proxy paths before contacting the backend.

Source: `docs/api-cookbook.md`.

Why this is better than exposing arbitrary backend files through the browser: artifact access is a reviewer feature, not a filesystem tunnel. The allowlist means the UI can preview expected thesis artifacts while preventing accidental exposure of unrelated backend paths. It also makes drift visible. If the backend emits a new thesis artifact, the UI proxy and docs must be updated before the browser can treat it as a supported reviewer surface.

This design is also better than documenting frontend proxy coverage as if it were backend truth. The backend remains the authority for route semantics and artifact emission; the frontend is a curated transport and inspection layer.

### AN.7 Quality Gates Distinguish Local Evidence From Publishability

The quality-gates page gives the operational gate ladder:

```powershell
uv run python scripts/build_model_assets.py
uv run python scripts/preflight_live_runtime.py
uv run python scripts/score_model_quality.py
uv run python scripts/benchmark_model_v2.py --iterations 8 --p95-gate-ms 2000
```

Source: `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`.

It also records CI lane semantics:

```text
fast-lane: STRICT_RUNTIME_TEST_BYPASS=1
strict-live-lane: STRICT_RUNTIME_TEST_BYPASS=0
```

Source: `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`.

Why this is better than one generic "tests pass" claim: deterministic unit/regression behavior and strict-live fail-closed behavior answer different questions. A fast lane can protect day-to-day logic without needing all live sources. A strict-live lane can verify reason-code parity, strict data-path behavior, and fail-closed subsystem behavior. Collapsing them would make a green check ambiguous.

The page also states that the latest full-suite assessment is publishable on the applied-evidence policy and adoption-supported on the measured benchmark framing:

```text
```

Source: `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`.

That is better than hiding limitations behind local successes. The repository can have successful strict preflight, checked bundles, green hot-rerun companion surfaces, and deployment-scope caveats at the same time. The thesis is stronger when those layers remain separate: applied evidence can be positive while deployment certification remains future work.

### AN.8 Artifact-First Reproducibility

The reproducibility capsule documents a one-command demo:

```powershell

```

Source: `docs/reproducibility-capsule.md`.

It also gives the manual reproducibility path:

Why this is better than "rerun the app and compare screenshots": reproducibility requires fixed payloads, seeds, strict flags, asset signatures, comparator policy, route-graph subset policy, and provenance. The capsule docs therefore point to `backend/out/model_assets/manifest.json`, `backend/out/model_assets/refresh_manifest.json`, `backend/out/model_assets/live_publish_summary.json`, `backend/out/model_assets/preflight_live_runtime.json`, thesis campaign outputs, and the reviewer package index.

The same page warns that local strict-readiness anchors do not close publishability/adoption rows by themselves. The current checked publishability/adoption verdict comes from the full-suite assessment bundle, not merely from the preflight artifacts.

Source: `docs/reproducibility-capsule.md`.

This distinction is better than treating reproducibility as a single binary. A preflight can be reproducible, a focused bundle can be reproducible, a reviewer package can be inspectable, and the overall publishability verdict can still be negative.

### AN.9 Negative Results As First-Class Documentation

The root negative-results page says the repository does not justify universal superiority over OSRM or ORS, unconditional validity outside supported UK-style scope, complete reviewer-package materialization, or full publishability on current evidence.

Source: `negative_results.md`.

The detailed negative-results page gives the wording policy:

```text
Avoid language such as:
universal
always
provably optimal
complete
all conditions
unconditional
G11 is green
P14 is green
seed-robust
publishable
```

Source: `docs/negative_results.md`.

Why this is better than a positive-only documentation set: a thesis repository should help the writer avoid overclaiming. Negative-result pages are not admissions of irrelevance; they are guardrails that preserve the difference between implemented mechanisms, local evidence, claim closure, and theorem-backed proof. They also make reviewer expectations easier to manage: a failed strict readiness check, an unsupported region, or a blocked verdict is not a surprise if the documentation already says those are possible and meaningful.

For this codebase, negative-result documentation is especially important because route planners invite broad superiority claims. The safer thesis claim is narrower: the repository provides a governed, artifact-backed UK freight-routing decision system with explicit support boundaries and failure modes. It does not prove universal dominance over OSRM, ORS, or every operational geography.

### AN.10 Notebook-Free Repository Policy

The notebook policy is explicit:

```text
Do not introduce notebook files for routine development, evaluation, or reporting.
Prefer checked-in scripts under backend/scripts/ or repo-level helpers under scripts/.
Treat generated artifacts under backend/out/ as outputs of scripts, not hand-maintained analysis notebooks.
```

Source: `notebooks/NOTEBOOKS_POLICY.md`.

It names script replacements for notebook-like work, including:

```text
backend/scripts/run_thesis_lane.py
backend/scripts/run_thesis_evaluation.py
backend/scripts/run_hot_rerun_benchmark.py
backend/scripts/compose_thesis_suite_report.py
backend/scripts/check_eta_concept_drift.py
scripts/check_docs.py
```

Source: `notebooks/NOTEBOOKS_POLICY.md`.

Why this is better than notebook-first research for this project: the thesis evidence must be rerunnable, path-addressable, CI-checkable, and artifact-backed. Notebooks are useful for exploration, but they can hide execution order, implicit state, stale cells, and manual transformations. Script-first evaluation keeps command lines, seeds, outputs, manifests, and provenance visible.

This does not mean notebooks are intrinsically bad. It means they are not the right primary evidence chain for a repo whose strongest claims depend on strict runtime gates, generated artifacts, signed manifests, endpoint contracts, and docs checks.

### AN.11 Reviewer Quickstart And Sample-Manifest Docs Are Not Redundant

The reviewer quickstart gives conservative inspection and regeneration paths for the checked publication slice. It names the current checked bundle and the full-suite companion, then gives commands to inspect verdicts, lane metadata, and CSV summaries:

```powershell
$suiteBundle = ".\out\headline_exports\current_checked\full_suite_curated_latest_20260411"
Get-Content ".\out\headline_exports\current_checked\full_suite_curated_latest_20260411\publishability_verdict.json" -Raw |
  ConvertFrom-Json |
  Select-Object publishable_on_current_evidence, adoption_claim_supported, hot_rerun_all_green, publishability_blockers
```

Source: `docs/reviewer_quickstart.md`.

The sample-manifest page then explains how ordinary run bundles and thesis/VOI bundles are shaped. It records core files such as `results.json`, `results.csv`, `metadata.json`, `index.json`, `index.md`, and thesis files such as `dccs_summary.json`, `certificate_summary.json`, `world_support_summary.json`, `value_of_refresh.json`, `voi_action_trace.json`, `thesis_summary.json`, `thesis_metrics.json`, `methods_appendix.md`, and `evaluation_manifest.json`.

Source: `docs/sample-manifest.md`.

Why both are needed: the quickstart tells a reviewer what checked slice to inspect; the sample-manifest doc tells them what a run bundle means once they are inside it. A single README paragraph could list artifact names, but it would not explain run ids, signatures, provenance, route bundle indexes, thesis-like bundle forward-compatibility, or the difference between source CSV/JSON artifacts and rendered PDF/SVG publication surfaces.

This is better than shipping only a final paper artifact because the repository remains auditable. A reviewer can walk backward from a table or figure source to the bundle, from the bundle to manifests and provenance, and from those files to the commands and runtime gates that produced them.



```text
start-child
heartbeat-child
update-child
note-child
end-child
replace-child
ensure-six-subagents
```


The coordination protocol states that the canonical store is SQLite under the Git common dir:

```text
<git-common-dir>/codex-coordination/
coordination.sqlite3
```


It also states the parent-controller invariant: exactly 6 live child subagents for every active parent session, evaluated from registered child rows, not from role labels, config files, or slot projections alone.


Why this is better than informal collaboration: the thesis report is a large shared evidence artifact. Without file claims, section claims, heartbeats, child notes, and cleanup, parallel agents can overwrite each other or leave stale state that looks like active work. The coordination layer makes authorship and liveness inspectable. A coordinated report-editing packet is expected to have a registered parent or child session, a claimed work item, and an exclusive file or section claim before writing, which mirrors the repository's broader evidence discipline.

This is not a claim that agent coordination proves the freight-routing algorithm. It proves a narrower process property: concurrent report edits are governed rather than ad hoc. That matters because a thesis-codebase report assembled by many workers needs the same kind of provenance discipline that the runtime applies to route artifacts.

### AN.13 Controls Beyond Lighter README-Only Docs

A lighter alternative would be to keep only:

- one root README
- a few curl examples
- a screenshots folder
- notebooks for analysis
- a loose list of known failures

That would be easier to maintain in the short term, but weaker for this repository's thesis goals.

The current approach is better because:

- Startup commands are tied to strict preflight and readiness checks rather than a vague "run the app."
- API examples preserve request payloads and separate certification, baseline, batch, and artifact routes.
- Docs checks make maintained markdown, links, endpoint docs, theorem tables, and notebook policy partly executable.
- Negative-result pages keep unsupported claims visible instead of relying on memory.
- Reproducibility docs preserve seeds, asset signatures, strict flags, comparator policy, and artifact paths.
- Reviewer quickstart and sample-manifest docs make checked bundles inspectable without inventing new evidence.
- Notebook policy keeps the primary evidence chain scriptable and CI-compatible.

The tradeoff is documentation volume. The reason that tradeoff is acceptable is that this is not a small demo app. It is an evidence-producing freight-routing decision system with strict live data, generated artifacts, theorem/claim ledgers, model assets, reviewer bundles, frontend proxy constraints, and active publishability diagnostics and claim-boundary notes. A single README cannot carry that safely.

The practical thesis reading is therefore:

- Use `README.md`, `backend/README.md`, and `frontend/README.md` for orientation.
- Use `docs/runbook.md` and `docs/run-and-operations.md` for runtime and strict-live behavior.
- Use `docs/api-cookbook.md` for reproducible endpoint interaction.
- Use `scripts/check_docs.py` for maintained-doc drift checks.
- Use `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`, `docs/reproducibility-capsule.md`, and `docs/reviewer_quickstart.md` for evidence status.
- Use `negative_results.md` and `docs/negative_results.md` to avoid overclaiming.
- Use `notebooks/NOTEBOOKS_POLICY.md` to keep analysis script-first.

That layered design is the documentation equivalent of the runtime design: explicit contracts, visible failure modes, artifact-backed claims, and conservative wording are preferred over a smoother but less auditable story.

## Appendix AO - Backend Algorithm Evidence And Examiner-Facing Rationale

This appendix maps the backend algorithms and calculation paths that a thesis examiner is likely to probe. Snippets are exact unless marked as a shortened excerpt.

### AO.1 Route graph search uses bounded adaptive breadth, not a single shortest path

Shortened excerpt:

```python
base_hops = max(8, int(settings.route_graph_max_hops))
if not bool(settings.route_graph_adaptive_hops_enabled):
    return base_hops
cap_hops = max(base_hops, int(settings.route_graph_max_hops_cap))
straight_line_km = straight_line_m / 1000.0
scaled_hops = int(math.ceil(straight_line_km * max(0.1, float(settings.route_graph_hops_per_km)) * max(1.0, float(settings.route_graph_hops_detour_factor))))
return max(base_hops, min(cap_hops, max(scaled_hops, hop_floor)))
```

Source: `backend/app/routing_graph.py`.

Why this matters: the route graph search budget scales with OD distance and a detour factor while remaining capped. That is better than a single shortest path because DCCS/REFC need challenger routes, not merely the fastest candidate. It is also better than unbounded graph expansion because the hop cap makes runtime and memory behavior inspectable in the report.

### AO.2 Route graph warmup is observable and diagnosable

Shortened excerpt:

```python
return {
    "state": state,
    "ready_mode": ready_mode,
    "phase": phase,
    "timeout_s": int(max(60, int(settings.route_graph_warmup_timeout_s))),
    "timed_out": timed_out,
    "last_error": last_error,
    "nodes_seen": nodes_seen,
    "nodes_kept": nodes_kept,
    "edges_seen": edges_seen,
    "edges_kept": edges_kept,
    "component_count": component_count,
    "largest_component_ratio": largest_component_ratio,
    "thread_alive": thread_alive,
    "cache_loaded": bool(load_route_graph.cache_info().currsize > 0),
}
```

Source: `backend/app/routing_graph.py`.

Why this matters: warmup state is a first-class diagnostic artifact, including component health and cache status. This is better than silent fallback because a reviewer can distinguish "graph not loaded", "graph fragmented", "warmup timed out", and "cache ready" without inferring state from route results.

### AO.3 Strict live request gating is fail-closed but still performance-aware

Shortened excerpt:

```python
"""
Use cached loader paths for per-request strict prefetch to avoid re-running
expensive remote fanouts on every compute call.

Strict fail-closed behavior is still enforced by:
1) source-level exceptions (stale/unavailable data still raises),
2) prefetch row success/failure accounting,
3) expected-source gate reconciliation after prefetch.
"""
if bool(getattr(settings, "live_route_compute_force_uncached", True)):
    return _call_uncached(fn, *args, **kwargs)
return fn(*args, **kwargs)
```

Source: `backend/app/main.py`.

Why this matters: strict runtime mode is not a UI-only promise. Backend source failures still raise, source rows record success or failure, and the expected-source gate reconciles the route request. This is better than silent fallback because stale or missing live inputs become typed request failures rather than hidden substitutions in the certificate pipeline.

### AO.4 DCCS candidate envelopes support safe elimination

Shortened excerpt:

```python
slack = 0.03 + (0.12 * (1.0 - support_mass))
lower_objective = tuple(max(0.0, value * (1.0 - slack)) for value in objective)
upper_objective = tuple(value * (1.0 + slack) for value in objective)
support_status = "supported" if support_mass >= 0.50 else ("weak_support" if support_mass > 0.0 else "unknown")
...
if dominates_candidate:
    known_dominance = "dominated_by_frontier"
    safe_eliminated = True
    necessary_dominated = True
    safe_elimination_reason = "objective_dominated_by_frontier_envelope"
```

Source: `backend/app/candidate_bounds.py`.

Why this matters: the code records lower/upper objective envelopes, support mass, support status, dominance provenance, and explicit safe-elimination reasons. This is better than black-box route acceptance because a skipped candidate can be explained as dominated by a frontier envelope rather than merely absent from the final answer.

### AO.5 DCCS ranks decision-critical candidates instead of just nearest variants

Shortened excerpt:

```python
candidate_envelope = build_candidate_envelope(candidate, frontier=frontier_items)
candidate_criticality = build_candidate_criticality(
    candidate,
    objective_gap=objective_gap,
    mechanism_gap=mechanism_gap,
    predicted_refine_cost=predicted_cost,
    flip_probability=flip_probability,
    candidate_envelope=candidate_envelope,
    near_duplicate=near_duplicate,
)
...
return max(candidates, key=lambda record: (
    record.final_score,
    record.flip_probability,
    record.objective_gap,
    -record.predicted_refine_cost,
    record.candidate_id,
))
```

Source: `backend/app/decision_critical.py` and `backend/app/voi_controller.py`.

Why this matters: candidate selection combines possible objective improvement, route-mechanism difference, flip probability, envelope support, and predicted refine cost. This is better than taking the nearest alternatives from a K-shortest list because the selected work is tied to decision value and certificate risk, not path similarity alone.

### AO.6 REFC uses bounded evidence worlds and replayable certificates

Exact snippet:

```python
# REFC uses bounded stress-world analysis rather than an unconstrained noise
# model. The construction is closer to global sensitivity analysis and explicit
# stress testing than to learned simulation; see Saltelli et al., "Global
# Sensitivity Analysis: The Primer", https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470725184 .
# The route certificate itself is an empirical winner-frequency estimate over
# those worlds, following the sample-average-approximation perspective used in
# stochastic programming; see Shapiro, Dentcheva, Ruszczynski, "Lectures on
# Stochastic Programming", https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718751 .
```

Source: `backend/app/evidence_certification.py`.

Why this matters: REFC is deliberately bounded and replayable. This is better than unbounded Monte Carlo because evidence families, states, stress factors, and world ids are controlled artifacts. The examiner can ask which worlds were sampled and why; the answer is in the manifest, not in an implicit random process.

### AO.7 REFC targeted world construction avoids uniform stress flooding

Shortened excerpt:

```python
active_states = pack_states[: max(1, min(active_state_cap, len(pack_states)))]
...
if case_kind == "supported_ambiguity":
    repeat_signal = max(state_gap, 0.45 * route_exposure_signal)
    repeat_multiplier = max(0.18, min(0.72, 0.18 + (0.70 * repeat_signal)))
...
world_id = _stable_hash([
    f"{case_kind}_pack",
    str(seed),
    str(idx),
    str(repetition),
    str(round(stress_factor, 6)),
    json.dumps(state_map, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")),
])
```

Source: `backend/app/evidence_certification.py`.

Why this matters: stress worlds are targeted by pairwise gap, route exposure, support richness, and bounded active-state caps, then assigned stable ids. This is better than flooding every family/state combination because it keeps certification computationally bounded while preserving the worlds most likely to flip the decision.

### AO.8 VOI action scoring is explicit and auditable

Shortened excerpt:

```python
return {
    "iteration": int(iteration),
    "action_id": action.action_id,
    "kind": action.kind,
    "target": action.target,
    "cost_search": int(action.cost_search),
    "cost_evidence": int(action.cost_evidence),
    "predicted_delta_certificate": _as_voi_metric(action.predicted_delta_certificate),
    "predicted_delta_margin": _as_voi_metric(action.predicted_delta_margin),
    "predicted_delta_frontier": _as_voi_metric(action.predicted_delta_frontier),
    "predicted_delta_radius_or_flip_budget": predicted_delta_radius_or_flip_budget(action),
    "predicted_preference_shrinkage": predicted_preference_shrinkage(action),
    "predicted_certified_set_contraction": predicted_certified_set_contraction(action),
    "q_score": _as_voi_metric(action.q_score),
    "selected_route_id": selected_route_id,
    "selected_certificate": _as_voi_metric(selected_certificate),
}
```

Source: `backend/app/voi_controller.py`.

Why this matters: each VOI action leaves a score row with predicted certificate gain, margin gain, frontier gain, radius-or-flip-budget gain, preference shrinkage, certified-set contraction, costs, target, selected route id, selected certificate, and final score. This is better than a hidden controller or learned RL policy because the action choice is reproducible and inspectable from exported artifacts.

### AO.9 Physics, risk, and cost calculations are formula-backed rather than cosmetic

Shortened excerpts:

```python
rolling_force = params.mass_kg * G_MPS2 * params.c_rr
aero_force = 0.5 * AIR_DENSITY_KG_M3 * params.drag_area_m2 * (v_ms ** 2)
grade_force = params.mass_kg * G_MPS2 * grade
raw_force = rolling_force + aero_force + max(grade_force, -0.85 * baseline_force)
```

Source: `backend/app/terrain_physics.py`.

```python
tail_integral += 0.5 * (q_start + q_end) * (end - start)
denom = max(1e-12, 1.0 - alpha_clamped)
result = tail_integral / denom
threshold = quantile(ordered, alpha_clamped)
return max(result, threshold)
```

Source: `backend/app/risk_model.py`.

Why this matters: terrain changes duration and emissions through vehicle mass, rolling resistance, drag area, grade, drivetrain efficiency, and regeneration; risk uses empirical quantile/CVaR logic. This is better than UI-only validation or arbitrary multipliers because the formulas are in backend code and therefore affect ranking, certification, and artifacts consistently.

### AO.10 Route endpoints enforce backend authority

Exact snippet:

```python
@app.post("/route", response_model=DecisionPackage)
async def compute_route(
    req: RouteRequest,
    response: Response,
    osrm: OSRMDep,
    ors: ORSDep,
    _: UserAccessDep,
) -> DecisionPackage:
```

Source: `backend/app/main.py`.

Why this matters: the route endpoint binds request validation, live OSRM/ORS dependencies, authenticated access, backend option construction, DCCS/REFC/VOI execution, and response serialization in one server-side contract. This is better than browser-side route acceptance because the backend owns the evidence trail and cannot be bypassed by a client display decision.

### AO.11 Abstention is typed and conservative

Shortened excerpt:

```python
TypedAbstentionReason = Literal[
    "uncertified_due_to_search",
    "uncertified_due_to_evidence",
    "uncertified_due_to_preference",
    "uncertified_due_to_out_of_support_world_model",
    "uncertified_due_to_budget",
    "uncertified_due_to_model_assumption",
]
...
if budget_text or _contains_any(stop_text, ("budget", "exhausted", "quota")):
    return "uncertified_due_to_budget"
if support_flag is False or _contains_any(support_text, ("out_of_support", "unsupported", "outside_support", "out of support")):
    return "uncertified_due_to_out_of_support_world_model"
```

Source: `backend/app/abstention.py`.

Why this matters: an uncertified terminal result is not collapsed into a generic failure. The code preserves whether the unresolved uncertainty came from search, evidence, preference, support, budget, or model assumptions. This is better than forcing a winner because it keeps thesis claims honest when certification conditions are not met.

### AO.12 Provenance is persisted as a run artifact

Exact snippet:

```python
def provenance_event(run_id: str, event: str, **context: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "run_id": run_id,
        "event": event,
        "timestamp": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(),
        **context,
    }

def write_provenance(run_id: str, events: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> Path:
    payload = {
        "run_id": run_id,
        "created_at": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(),
        "event_count": len(events),
        "events": events,
    }
```

Source: `backend/app/provenance_store.py`.

Why this matters: provenance is stored as structured JSON with run id, event names, timestamps, and context. This is better than logs-only provenance because artifacts can be linked from the report and checked later without requiring access to the original terminal session.

## Appendix AP: Frontend, Operations, Proxy, And API Behavior Rationale

This appendix maps the frontend and operations surfaces that matter for thesis claims. The frontend is not just a map widget over a backend. It is the operator-facing boundary where route requests are assembled, long-running computation is bounded, backend failures are translated into actionable diagnostics, proof artifacts are inspected, and live-runtime startup assumptions become visible. That makes the UI and proxy layer part of the reproducibility argument.

### AP.1 Control Surface To Backend Payloads

The main page keeps operator choices in typed React state and then builds backend payloads through shared request builders rather than ad hoc object literals. The request builders preserve the common route fields and merge only the advanced patch fields that are explicitly present:

```ts
export function buildRouteRequest(input: ODRoutingInput): RouteRequest {
  return {
    origin: input.origin,
    destination: input.destination,
    waypoints: input.waypoints,
    vehicle_type: input.vehicle_type,
    scenario_mode: input.scenario_mode,
    max_alternatives: input.max_alternatives,
    weights: input.weights,
    ...input.advanced,
  };
}
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/requestBuilders.ts`.

Why it matters for the thesis: a route answer is not a button click; it is a structured experimental condition. Origin, destination, waypoints, vehicle type, scenario mode, weights, candidate budget, Pareto method, departure time, cost toggles, terrain profile, stochastic settings, emissions context, weather, incident simulation, and risk settings all affect what the backend is asked to prove. Keeping the construction in typed helper functions is better than UI-only assumptions because the thesis can trace a visible control to a concrete request field instead of relying on prose that says "the UI set the route up correctly."

This is also better than magic defaults. Defaults still exist, but they are made visible at the payload boundary. If a result changes when `max_alternatives`, `scenario_mode`, or `weights` changes, the code path makes that difference inspectable.

### AP.2 Frontend Fetch Helpers And Typed Failure Messages

The browser-side API helper centralizes JSON, text, and NDJSON behavior. Error bodies are parsed for `detail.message`, `detail.reason_code`, `detail.cause`, warning summaries, and validation arrays before an exception is shown:

```ts
if (detailMessage) {
  const core = reasonCode ? `${detailMessage} (${reasonCode})` : detailMessage;
  return cause ? `${core} cause=${cause}` : core;
}
if (reasonCode) return cause ? `${reasonCode} cause=${cause}` : reasonCode;
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/api.ts`.

Why it matters for the thesis: fail-closed routing is only useful if the operator can see why the run failed. A generic `fetch failed` message would hide whether the issue was graph warmup, strict-live source freshness, an unreachable backend, a timed-out stream, or a typed abstention. The UI helper keeps backend reason codes visible to the frontend trace and therefore preserves the difference between model uncertainty, data unavailability, and transport failure.

### AP.3 Next.js Proxy Routes Over Direct Browser-To-Backend Calls

The frontend proxy layer forwards same-origin `/api/...` calls to the backend using an internal backend base URL:

```ts
export function backendBaseUrl(): string {
  return (
    process.env.BACKEND_INTERNAL_URL ??
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL ??
    'http://localhost:8000'
  );
}
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/backendFetch.ts`.

This is better than direct browser-to-backend calls for three reasons.

First, deployment topology is isolated from the browser. The browser can call `/api/route`; the server-side proxy can resolve the backend through `BACKEND_INTERNAL_URL` in Docker, local PowerShell, or a hosted environment.

Second, transport errors are classified once. The proxy distinguishes header timeout, body timeout, connection reset, and backend unreachable:

```ts
type TransportReasonCode =
  | 'backend_headers_timeout'
  | 'backend_body_timeout'
  | 'backend_connection_reset'
  | 'backend_unreachable';
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/backendFetch.ts`.

Third, cancellation and no-store semantics are enforced at the proxy boundary. The route proxy passes the incoming request signal to the backend fetch and disables caching:

```ts
resp = await fetchBackend('/route', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body,
  requestSignal: req.signal,
  timeoutMs: computeRouteFallbackTimeoutMs(),
});
```

Source: `frontend/app/api/route/route.ts`.

For a thesis, this is better than direct browser calls because it makes the frontend an auditable transport adapter rather than an uncontrolled second API client. The backend remains the source of truth for route semantics; the proxy owns only transport, timeout, caching, and safe exposure behavior.

### AP.4 Timeout And Fallback Behavior

Long route computations are expected in this repository because strict graph search, live-source checks, stochastic profiles, terrain, certification, and artifact emission can all be expensive. The frontend backend-fetch helper gives long attempts explicit clocks:

```ts
const DEFAULT_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS = 1_200_000;
const DEFAULT_ROUTE_FALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 900_000;
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/backendFetch.ts`.

The helper aborts with a reason-coded timeout rather than waiting indefinitely:

```ts
const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => {
  try {
    ctrl.abort(new Error(`backend_fetch_timeout:${timeoutMs}`));
  } catch {
    ctrl.abort();
  }
}, timeoutMs);
```

Source: `frontend/app/lib/backendFetch.ts`.

Why it matters for the thesis: bounded attempts are a methodological choice. An unbounded browser request can look like a hung algorithm, a broken backend, or a network issue. A bounded attempt can be reported as a controlled timeout with a reason code and recovery path. This is better than magic waiting because failures become part of the evidence trail.

The operations docs surface the same knobs as runtime settings:

```text
COMPUTE_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS=1200000
COMPUTE_ROUTE_FALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS=900000
NEXT_PUBLIC_COMPUTE_DEGRADE_STEPS=12,6,3
```

Source: `docs/run-and-operations.md`.

That is better than hardcoding a single candidate budget because fallback behavior is part of the experimental protocol. A thesis reader can distinguish "the algorithm found no certified answer" from "the interactive UI reduced the candidate budget to keep a run bounded."

### AP.5 Streaming Proxy Behavior

The Pareto stream proxy forwards the backend NDJSON stream and emits a fatal NDJSON event if the proxy is interrupted while reading:

```ts
const fatal = JSON.stringify({
  type: 'fatal',
  message: 'Streaming proxy interrupted while reading backend response.',
  reason_code: classified.reasonCode,
  warnings: [classified.cause || classified.detail],
});
safeEnqueue(encoder.encode(`${fatal}\n`));
```

Source: `frontend/app/api/pareto/stream/route.ts`.

Why it matters for the thesis: streaming is an operational affordance, not a different algorithm. It allows progress and diagnostics during long computations, but it must not silently corrupt the result if the stream breaks. Returning a typed fatal event is better than letting the browser infer failure from a closed stream because the compute trace can record where transport failed and whether fallback should run.

### AP.6 Endpoint Parity And Proxy Coverage

The backend exposes the main API contract through FastAPI decorators, including health, readiness, metrics, cache, Pareto, route, baseline, preference, batch, experiment, vehicle, signature, and run-artifact endpoints. The frontend has a corresponding set of Next.js proxy routes under `frontend/app/api`, including:

```text
frontend/app/api/health/ready/route.ts
frontend/app/api/pareto/stream/route.ts
frontend/app/api/route/route.ts
frontend/app/api/route/preference/route.ts
frontend/app/api/runs/[runId]/[...subpath]/route.ts
frontend/app/api/verify/signature/route.ts
```

Source: `frontend/app/api`.

The docs checker has an endpoint-parity mode, but it compares FastAPI decorators with documented backend endpoint entries. The backend API docs explicitly note the current limit:

```text
It does not validate frontend Next.js proxy coverage, response-model field details,
artifact allowlists, endpoint mentions in docs/api-cookbook.md, or thesis prose.
```

Source: `docs/backend-api-tools.md`.

Why it matters for the thesis: endpoint parity has layers. Backend-to-docs parity can be checked by `scripts/check_docs.py --check-endpoints`, but frontend proxy parity still needs inspection. That is better than claiming a single "API check" proves every UI path, because the thesis can state exactly which contract is machine-checked and which is reviewed by code evidence.

### AP.7 Artifact Download And Preview Constraints

Run artifact access is deliberately allowlisted in the frontend proxy:

```ts
function isAllowedSubpath(subpath: string[]): boolean {
  if (subpath.length === 0) return false;
  if (subpath.length === 1) return CORE_ALLOWED.has(subpath[0]);
  if (subpath[0] !== 'artifacts') return false;
  if (subpath.length !== 2) return false;
  return ARTIFACT_ALLOWED.has(subpath[1]);
}
```

Source: `frontend/app/api/runs/[runId]/[...subpath]/route.ts`.

The allowlist includes core run documents such as `manifest`, `scenario-manifest`, `provenance`, `signature`, and `scenario-signature`, plus known artifact files such as `results.json`, `results.csv`, `routes.geojson`, `certificate_summary.json`, `value_of_refresh.json`, `voi_action_trace.json`, `thesis_results.csv`, `methods_appendix.md`, and `thesis_report.md`.

Why it matters for the thesis: artifact inspection is evidence access, not arbitrary file serving. This is better than a free-form proxy because a reviewer can inspect the artifacts the system says are part of a run without giving the browser a general backend filesystem tunnel. The constraint also reveals drift: if the backend starts emitting a new thesis artifact, the UI proxy must be updated before it can preview or download it.

The run inspector then turns those artifacts into an operator-facing audit surface. It groups decision-package, certified-set, support, witness, controller, theorem-hook, and artifact-presence information instead of treating the run id as a blob download.

### AP.8 Operations Diagnostics In The UI

The frontend exposes health, metrics, and cache state through a small operations panel:

```tsx
<OpsDiagnosticsPanel
  health={opsHealth}
  metrics={opsMetrics}
  cacheStats={opsCacheStats}
  loading={opsLoading}
  clearing={opsClearing}
  error={opsError}
  onRefresh={() => {
    void refreshOpsDiagnostics();
  }}
  onClearCache={() => {
    void clearOpsCache();
  }}
/>
```

Source: `frontend/app/page.tsx`.

The panel itself renders health, cache stats, and metrics snapshots as JSON:

```tsx
<pre className="devPre">{pretty(health ?? { status: 'unknown' })}</pre>
<pre className="devPre">{pretty(cacheStats ?? {})}</pre>
<pre className="devPre">{pretty(metrics ?? {})}</pre>
```

Source: `frontend/app/components/devtools/OpsDiagnosticsPanel.tsx`.

Why it matters for the thesis: route quality claims depend on runtime state. Cache hits, graph readiness, strict-live availability, and backend errors affect observed behavior. Showing those values in the UI is better than assuming a clean environment because the operator can connect a route answer to the current runtime condition.

### AP.9 Docs Serving And OpenAPI Access

The local docs server is intentionally simple:

```powershell
$docsDir = Join-Path $repoRoot "docs"
& $pythonExe -m http.server $Port --directory $docsDir
```

Source: `scripts/serve_docs.ps1`.

The live stack script prints the main local access points:

```powershell
Write-Host "Startup complete:"
Write-Host "  Frontend: http://localhost:3000"
Write-Host "  Backend:  http://localhost:8000/docs"
Write-Host "  OSRM:     http://localhost:5000"
```

Source: `scripts/dev.ps1`.

Why it matters for the thesis: the report, OpenAPI UI, and frontend runtime are different evidence surfaces. Serving docs from `docs/` is better than burying the report inside an IDE because a reviewer can navigate the markdown as a static artifact. Exposing FastAPI OpenAPI at `/docs` is better than hand-maintained endpoint screenshots because it reflects the running backend contract.

### AP.10 Live Runtime Startup And Preflight

The full development script does more than start Next.js. It ensures Docker is available, starts OSRM, waits for OSRM readiness, runs strict live-data preflight, then launches backend and frontend terminals. Excerpt:

```powershell
Write-Host "Starting OSRM (Docker)..."
docker compose up -d osrm | Out-Null
...
uv run python scripts/preflight_live_runtime.py --output $summaryPath
...
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
...
pnpm dev
```

Source: `scripts/dev.ps1`.

The runbook records an important operational gap:

```text
dev.ps1 starts OSRM, but it does not start ORS for you.
If ORS is not already running, strict preflight can still fail even when OSRM is healthy.
```

Source: `docs/runbook.md`.

Why it matters for the thesis: live runtime startup is part of validity. A route result can depend on graph availability, strict live source readiness, OSRM, ORS, cache state, and model assets. Running strict preflight before backend startup is better than discovering these failures halfway through a route computation. Documenting the ORS gap is better than implying one script proves the entire external stack is healthy.

### AP.11 Batch, Run Inspection, And Signature Tools

The frontend includes operator tools for batch Pareto requests, CSV import, run artifact inspection, and signature verification. The batch runner keeps the request payload visible:

```tsx
const DEFAULT_BATCH_JSON = JSON.stringify(
  {
    pairs: [
      {
        origin: { lat: 51.5074, lon: -0.1278 },
        destination: { lat: 53.4808, lon: -2.2426 },
      },
    ],
    vehicle_type: 'rigid_hgv',
    scenario_mode: 'no_sharing',
    max_alternatives: 8,
  },
  null,
  2,
);
```

Source: `frontend/app/components/devtools/BatchRunner.tsx`.

Why it matters for the thesis: batch evaluation is not only a backend script concern. The UI exposes the same request vocabulary used by route and Pareto endpoints, which helps an examiner see how a single OD route scales into a corpus-style request. This is better than a hidden batch button because the payload is inspectable before execution.

The run inspector is similarly explicit: it loads core docs, lists artifacts, previews selected artifact text, and downloads allowed documents through the run proxy. This is better than treating artifacts as afterthoughts because the thesis evidence is primarily in persisted manifests, provenance, signatures, and result files.

### AP.12 Practical Behavior Gaps To State Accurately

The frontend and operations layer is strong enough to support thesis demonstrations, but it has boundaries that should be stated precisely.

- Frontend proxy coverage is broad but not automatically parity-checked against every backend decorator.
- The artifact proxy is intentionally allowlisted, so newly emitted backend artifacts are not automatically downloadable through the UI.
- `scripts/dev.ps1` starts OSRM and the app stack, but strict preflight can still fail if ORS or strict live payloads are unavailable.
- Docs serving and OpenAPI access are runtime conveniences; they do not replace `python scripts/check_docs.py`.
- UI controls construct typed payloads, but the backend remains the authority for validation, reason codes, certification, and artifact emission.

These limits make the thesis stronger, not weaker. They separate what the repository proves mechanically from what it exposes operationally. That is better than untyped UI-only assumptions because a reader can audit the boundary: controls build requests, proxy routes transport them safely, backend endpoints decide and persist evidence, and docs/check scripts define what has actually been verified.

The compatibility changes are intentionally narrow. They do not change the thesis semantics of certification, preference elicitation, or VOI control. They restore compatibility constructors and payload adapters that tests and report-facing artifacts now expect.

| Code surface | Current compatibility behavior | Thesis-useful interpretation |

| `backend/app/abstention.py` | `AbstentionRecord.from_preference_state(state)` scans `state.stop_hints` for `typed_abstention_recommended`, copies hint metadata into `detail`, and exposes `trigger_metric`, `observed_value`, `recommended_action`, and `severity` through stable record fields/properties. | Preference-state abstention is now a typed artifact, not only an informal hint. The expected no-certified-route case yields reason `typed_abstention_recommended`, trigger metric `certified_route_count`, observed value `0.0`, recommended action `expand_worlds`, and severity `high`. |
| `backend/app/main.py` | `_global_certification_cache_payload(...)` accepts omitted `frontier_signatures` by treating it as an empty mapping, while supplied mappings are still preserved and compacted into the cache signature payload. | Cache-key construction is backward-compatible with callers that predate frontier-signature threading, without erasing the stronger signature evidence when it exists. |
| `backend/app/pairwise_gap_model.py` | `PairwiseGapState.from_score_maps(...)` and `PairwiseGapState.from_certificate_gap(...)` rebuild pairwise gap records from older score-map and certificate-gap payload shapes. | Gap evidence can be reconstructed from both direct score comparisons and certificate-derived gap summaries, preserving the nearest-challenger explanation path. |
| `backend/app/flip_radius.py` | `FlipRadiusState.from_pairwise_gap(...)` derives flip-radius evidence from pairwise gap state. | The report can explain how a nearest-challenger gap becomes an evidence-perturbation radius rather than a disconnected scalar. |
| `backend/app/decision_region.py` | `DecisionRegionState.from_states(...)` joins pairwise gap, flip radius, certified-set, and preference state objects into a decision-region explanation. | Decision-region evidence is explicitly assembled from typed sub-states, which makes "why did the controller stop or abstain?" auditable. |
| `backend/app/certified_set.py` | `CertifiedSetState.from_confidence_states(...)` rebuilds a certified-set summary from confidence-state style inputs. | Set-level certification can be represented even when the winner is not a singleton, preserving the distinction between certified singleton and certified set outcomes. |
| `backend/app/certification_models.py` | `CertificationState.from_refc_outputs(...)` preserves `unique_world_count` and `effective_world_count` as distinct manifest facts. | The thesis can distinguish distinct sampled-world support from effective/adaptive world effort; those are not interchangeable in optional-stopping and reuse discussions. |

```python
class AbstentionRecord(BaseModel):

    @classmethod
    def from_preference_state(cls, state: Any) -> "AbstentionRecord":

            metadata = getattr(hint, "metadata", {}) or {}
            detail = dict(metadata) if hasattr(metadata, "items") else {"metadata": metadata}
            ...
            return cls(
                reason_code="typed_abstention_recommended",
                message=getattr(hint, "message", None) or _ABSTENTION_MESSAGES["typed_abstention_recommended"],
                detail=detail,
                support_flag=getattr(summary, "support_flag", None),
            )
```
