| The thesis novelty is shortest-path search. | The thesis contribution is the integration of route evidence, multiobjective modelling, uncertainty support, VOI, preference updates, abstention, and provenance into an auditable decision system. | Appendix AS, theorem docs (the theorem package and theorem-to-artifact map, which state assumptions, code/test/artifact anchors, and current proof gaps), DCCS/REFC/VOI implementation sections, artifact inventories. |

The final dissertation should keep returning to this table. It prevents overclaiming while preserving ambition. The work is not smaller because it refuses to claim better maps or better fleet optimization. It is stronger because it claims exactly what the repository is built to show: a route decision can be made, certified, questioned, or refused with an evidence trail that is visible to the reader.

### AS15. Paper-By-Paper Literature Synthesis And Contribution Positioning

This section turns the literature base into a contribution map. The goal is not to imply that each paper is incomplete in its own field. Many of these works are foundational precisely because they solve a sharply defined problem well. The thesis contribution here is different: it assembles path search, alternative generation, multiobjective modelling, uncertainty, bounded computation, preference state, selective abstention, and reproducibility into one auditable freight-route decision artifact. The repository therefore goes beyond individual sources by changing the object of study from "compute a route" to "justify, certify, or refuse a route recommendation under explicit evidence."

The following paper-by-paper synthesis should be read as an applied-systems literature review. Each entry identifies the problem solved by the source, the gap left open for a thesis about evidence-aware freight decisions, how the repository uses the source, and the narrow way the repository goes beyond it. The "goes beyond" column is deliberately bounded. It means "beyond for the thesis objective," not beyond in mathematical depth, global production coverage, commercial routing quality, or operational logistics maturity.

| Paper/source | Field | What it solves | What it leaves open for this thesis | How this repo uses it | Why this repo goes beyond it for the thesis objective |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dijkstra (1959), "A note on two problems in connexion with graphs"](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390) | Single-objective shortest paths and graph algorithms. | Gives the canonical label-setting basis for shortest paths with nonnegative costs. | Does not address freight-specific modelling, route alternatives, uncertain worlds, decision certification, preference conflict, or abstention. | Treats shortest-path computation as a baseline primitive that route engines and internal decision layers can rely on. | Adds an evidence contract around the route decision: candidate support, certification state, artifacts, and refusal semantics. |
| [Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael (1968), A* formal basis](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136) | Heuristic search and target-directed path finding. | Shows how admissible heuristic information can guide search efficiently while preserving optimality under the stated assumptions. | Does not determine which freight route should be recommended when costs are multiattribute, uncertain, or evidence-limited. | Positions target-directed routing as an efficiency tool inside the broader routing ecosystem. | Separates fast path computation from the later question of whether the computed alternative is certifiable. |
| [Yen (1971), k shortest loopless paths](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.17.11.712) | Alternative path enumeration. | Produces loopless path alternatives beyond the single shortest path. | Does not decide whether the alternative set is diverse enough, evidentially supported enough, or decision-safe under uncertainty. | Inspires the candidate-diversification logic and the need to reason over more than one path. | Treats alternatives as decision witnesses whose unresolved mass and evidence support affect certification. |
| [Eppstein (1998), k shortest paths](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539795290477) | Efficient k-shortest-path algorithms. | Provides efficient structure for enumerating many short paths after preprocessing. | Does not attach freight economics, sampled worlds, preference-state updates, or typed abstentions to the path list. | Supports the thesis premise that route alternatives are computationally legitimate, not ad hoc UI decoration. | Turns a candidate list into part of a proof object, with route frontier evidence and non-certification outcomes. |
| [Geisberger et al. (2012), contraction hierarchies](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1110.0401) | Scalable road-network routing. | Shows how preprocessing can accelerate shortest-path queries on large road networks. | Does not expose a thesis-grade decision certificate, preference audit trail, or uncertainty-world witness. | Frames why production route engines can answer routing queries quickly and why this repo can treat engines as evidence sources. | Uses fast route evidence as an input to auditable certification rather than making query speed the sole research claim. |
| [Delling et al. (2015), customizable route planning](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.2014.0579) | Metric customization and scalable route planning. | Separates network preprocessing from metric customization so route planning can adapt to changing cost functions. | Does not by itself certify decisions under conflicting objectives, evidence gaps, or preference uncertainty. | Supports the repository's distinction between graph/path machinery and scenario-sensitive cost or policy layers. | Adds local replayable artifacts that explain which customized evidence mattered and why the decision did or did not certify. |
| [Luxen and Vetter (2011), OSRM and real-time OSM routing](https://doi.org/10.1145/2093973.2094062) | Open-source road routing systems. | Demonstrates practical high-performance routing on OpenStreetMap-derived road networks. | Does not aim to expose route-decision proof objects, theorem maps, claim matrices, or abstention policy. | Uses OSRM-style routing as a comparator and evidence-source model for route generation. | Places a transparent decision layer above route-engine output, making the recommendation auditable rather than only routable. |
| [Martins (1984), multicriteria shortest path](https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-2217(84)90077-8) | Multiobjective and label-setting path optimization. | Establishes techniques for handling multiple path criteria and nondominated labels. | Does not solve the full decision problem when a user must choose among tradeoffs with incomplete preferences and uncertain evidence. | Grounds the route-scoring need to track time, money, emissions, risk, and other dimensions rather than collapse them prematurely. | Adds preference-state and certification layers that explain whether a multiattribute route choice is justified for the stated decision context. |
| [Hassin (1992), restricted shortest path approximation](https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.17.1.36) | Resource-constrained shortest paths and approximation. | Studies paths that optimize one measure while respecting another resource constraint. | Does not provide route-decision provenance, evidence freshness, VOI actions, or refusal semantics. | Frames freight decisions as constrained tradeoffs rather than unconstrained shortest-path lookups. | Connects constrained feasibility with explainable certification, so a rejected or uncertified route can be reported as an evidence outcome. |
| [Salzman et al. (2023), multi-objective shortest path survey](https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2023/757) | Survey of multiobjective shortest-path methods. | Organizes algorithmic approaches for paths with multiple objectives. | Surveys the algorithmic field but does not instantiate this repository's freight evidence, abstention, provenance, and thesis-report contract. | Gives the related-work bridge between path algorithms and the repository's multiobjective route decision design. | Converts the surveyed idea of multiple objectives into a reproducible applied system with visible claims and limitations. |
| [Yu and Yang (1998), robust shortest path](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0305-0548(97)00085-3) | Robust routing under uncertainty. | Studies path choice when arc costs are uncertain or scenario-dependent. | Does not expose the full artifact chain for why a route is certified, uncertified, or refused in a freight decision workflow. | Supports the use of uncertainty worlds and robustness checks in route evaluation. | Adds sampled-world manifests, support-conditioned summaries, and decision outcomes that can be inspected by a thesis reader. |
| [Dokka and Goerigk (2017), uncertainty sets for robust shortest paths](https://doi.org/10.4230/OASIcs.ATMOS.2017.16) | Robust optimization and uncertainty-set modelling. | Examines how uncertainty-set choices affect robust shortest-path behavior. | Does not prescribe the local software artifact model, decision certificate, or user-facing abstention categories needed here. | Informs the project's care around world manifests, uncertainty support, and what robust claims depend on. | Makes uncertainty modelling part of a documented certification state rather than an implicit modelling assumption. |
| [Filippi, Maggioni, and Speranza (2025), robust/distributionally robust shortest path survey](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cor.2025.107096) | Robust and distributionally robust shortest-path research. | Synthesizes robust and distributionally robust formulations for uncertain shortest paths. | Does not itself deliver an applied freight-route evidence platform with replayable artifacts and abstention. | Helps position this repository in the robust-routing literature without claiming a new robust optimization theorem. | Implements a practical evidence-aware route-decision wrapper that records the uncertainty basis for certification. |
| [Howard (1966), information value theory](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074) | Value of information and decision analysis. | Provides a formal basis for deciding whether information is worth acquiring before acting. | Does not define a freight-routing pipeline, route-candidate frontier, or typed route-decision artifact. | Grounds the VOI layer that asks whether more search, evidence, or preference information is worth the cost. | Embeds VOI as an operational controller that can stop, query, or abstain with visible reasons. |
| [Russell and Wefald (1991), bounded rationality and control of computation](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(91)90015-C) | Metareasoning and bounded rational decision making. | Shows that computation itself has cost and must be controlled rationally. | Does not specify freight-route evidence bundles, route-engine comparators, or certification documents. | Justifies treating additional route search and evidence collection as decisions, not free background work. | Connects bounded computation to route certificates and typed abstentions, so stopping behavior becomes inspectable. |
| [Keeney and Raiffa, Decisions with Multiple Objectives](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139174084) | Multiattribute utility and decision analysis. | Provides a rigorous framework for evaluating decisions with multiple objectives and tradeoffs. | Does not solve route evidence generation, algorithmic candidate discovery, or reproducible software certification. | Provides the decision-analysis vocabulary for preference tradeoffs across cost, time, emissions, risk, and reliability. | Implements preference state as part of a route-decision artifact that can reveal conflicts and insufficient preference information. |
| [Boutilier et al. (2006), utility elicitation and minimax regret](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2006.02.003) | Preference elicitation and regret-based decision making. | Studies how to choose actions and ask questions when utility information is incomplete. | Does not implement freight route certification or provenance over physical/economic route models. | Supports preference queries, compatible preference sets, and regret-aware reasoning in the route-decision pipeline. | Makes preference insufficiency a first-class abstention or VOI condition rather than a hidden weight-selection issue. |
| [Chow (1970), reject option](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406) | Classification with rejection. | Formalizes the value of refusing to classify when error risk is too high. | Does not address route planning, multiobjective path evaluation, or evidence provenance. | Provides the conceptual legitimacy for typed abstention in route recommendations. | Translates rejection into route-specific refusal reasons tied to search, evidence, support, budget, or preference gaps. |
| [Geifman and El-Yaniv (2017), selective classification](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/7073-selective-classification-for-deep-neural-networks) and [SelectiveNet (2019)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/geifman19a.html) | Selective prediction and abstaining machine learning systems. | Develops modern selective-prediction methods that trade coverage for reliability. | Does not define logistics route certificates, route-engine evidence sources, or thesis artifact replay. | Strengthens the argument that abstention can be designed, measured, and explained rather than treated as failure. | Applies selective-decision thinking to route recommendation with domain-specific abstention classes and proof artifacts. |
| [Wilkinson et al. (2016), FAIR principles](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18) | Research data stewardship and reproducibility principles. | Defines findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data principles. | Does not provide an application-specific freight-routing certification architecture. | Guides artifact manifests, provenance expectations, and the need for inspectable data/evidence records. | Treats FAIR-style artifact discipline as part of the decision claim, not merely as a repository hygiene matter. |
| [Wilson et al. (2014), best practices for scientific computing](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001745) | Scientific software engineering and reproducible computation. | Codifies practices for making scientific code more reliable, testable, and maintainable. | Does not tell a freight-routing system what to certify or when to abstain. | Grounds the repository's tests, docs checks, runbooks, local artifacts, and claim discipline. | Uses software-engineering practice to make the thesis argument auditable through code, tests, and reports. |

#### AS15.1 Foundational Shortest-Path Papers As Baseline, Not Thesis Novelty

The shortest-path literature establishes the computational base on which route engines stand. Dijkstra's algorithm is the clean starting point: given a graph with nonnegative edge weights, it gives a principled way to find the lowest-cost path. A* adds heuristic focus, showing that search can be guided toward a target without losing correctness when the heuristic conditions hold. Yen and Eppstein then show that alternatives can be enumerated systematically rather than invented after the fact.

For this repository, those results are necessary but intentionally not the novelty claim. The repository should not present itself as a new shortest-path algorithm. Its contribution begins after path computation has produced candidates. The hard question is whether any candidate should be recommended once the system considers freight cost, time, emissions, uncertainty, route-source agreement, user preferences, evidence support, and unresolved candidate mass.

That distinction matters for the thesis. A shortest-path algorithm can be correct and still be insufficient for a freight decision. It can optimize the wrong scalar, ignore an objective the user cares about, rely on stale or partial evidence, or select a path that is not robust across sampled worlds. The repository's decision model is built to expose those gaps rather than hiding them behind a single route polyline.

The candidate-diversification layer is the direct bridge from k-shortest-path thinking to the thesis contribution. It treats alternatives as a decision resource. A route that is not selected may still matter because it bounds regret, exposes a conflicting objective, reveals missing support, or shows why the chosen route is not uniquely certifiable. This is why the report should discuss the candidate frontier rather than only the final route.

#### AS15.2 Scalable Routing Papers As Infrastructure Context

Contraction hierarchies, customizable route planning, and OSRM-style routing explain why large road-network routing is practical. These works are essential to the system context. They show that routing at useful scale can be engineered through preprocessing, graph contraction, target-directed search, metric customization, and highly optimized service layers.

The repository uses that context in a bounded way. It does not claim to replace these engines or outperform them on query latency. Instead, it treats route engines as evidence-producing components. Their outputs become inputs to a decision layer that asks a different question: what can be certified about this route recommendation, under which assumptions, and with which artifact trail?

This framing also clarifies why OSRM and open-source route engines are such useful comparators. They are strong at the route computation problem and transparent enough to be included in a research workflow. But their public APIs generally return route geometry, distance, duration, alternatives, annotations, and similar routing outputs. They do not by default return theorem maps, route-decision certificates, claim matrices, or typed abstention reasons.

The thesis should therefore use scalable routing literature as an enabling foundation. It supports the claim that route computation is mature enough to serve as infrastructure. The repository's contribution is the evidence-aware layer that sits above that infrastructure.

#### AS15.3 Multiobjective Path Literature And Freight Tradeoffs

Freight route decisions rarely have a single honest objective. A route may be fast but expensive, cheap but risky, short but emissions-heavy, or attractive in nominal conditions but fragile under disruption. Martins, Hassin, Salzman and coauthors, and the broader multiobjective literature make this problem explicit. They show that path optimality can become a set-valued and preference-sensitive concept rather than a single scalar answer.

The repository uses this insight in the route scoring and decision layers. Time, cost, emissions, reliability, and other route attributes are not merely displayed after a route is chosen. They are part of the decision evidence. This allows the system to explain why a route is recommended under one preference state, why several routes remain compatible under another, and why the system may need a preference query before selecting a route.

The thesis goes beyond the algorithmic multiobjective setting by turning the tradeoff problem into an auditable interaction among candidates, preferences, and certification. A nondominated set is not yet a recommendation. A weighted score is not yet a defensible decision if the weights were guessed or if the evidence is weak. The repository adds a preference-state record and refusal path for cases where the tradeoff cannot be responsibly resolved.

This is a strong applied contribution because it makes multiobjective ambiguity visible. Instead of hiding a route choice inside a tuned weight vector, the system can state that a decision is underdetermined by current preferences or that multiple routes remain effectively tied. That behavior aligns with a thesis about explainable decision support rather than route-output convenience.

#### AS15.4 Robust And Distributionally Robust Shortest-Path Literature

Yu and Yang, Dokka and Goerigk, and Filippi, Maggioni, and Speranza all point toward the same thesis issue: route costs are not fixed facts. They depend on uncertainty about traffic, incidents, weather, fuel or energy assumptions, model error, and data availability. Robust and distributionally robust shortest-path work studies how path decisions change when uncertainty is represented explicitly.

The repository uses this family of work through uncertainty worlds and support-conditioned summaries. A route can be evaluated not only on its nominal score but also on how it behaves across the manifest of worlds the system is willing to consider. The distinction between unique world count and effective world count is important because a certification claim should be tied to actual support, not just the existence of many nominal scenarios.

The thesis contribution is not a new robust shortest-path theorem. It is an applied certification mechanism that records how uncertainty was used. The route decision can say which evidence worlds supported it, which ones failed it, and whether the result is robust enough to certify. That artifact-level transparency is what a thesis examiner can inspect.

The limitations remain important. The repository's uncertainty worlds are only as good as their construction, assumptions, and data sources. It should not claim to model every operational disruption. Its stronger claim is that uncertainty assumptions are surfaced in the decision record instead of buried in a black-box score.

#### AS15.5 Value Of Information And Bounded Computation

Howard's value-of-information theory and Russell and Wefald's bounded-rationality work justify a central design choice: the system should reason about whether more computation or more evidence is worth obtaining. In freight routing, more search can discover better alternatives, more evidence can refine uncertain costs, and more preference information can resolve tradeoffs. But none of those actions is free.

The repository's VOI layer is the applied answer to that problem. It can represent actions such as expanding the candidate frontier, acquiring evidence, querying preferences, or stopping. This reframes the route-decision process as a controlled computation rather than a fixed pipeline that always spends the same effort regardless of uncertainty.

This matters for certification and abstention. If additional evidence has low expected value, the system may certify or stop with a bounded explanation. If additional evidence has high expected value but cannot be obtained within budget, the system may abstain for a budget or evidence reason. If preference information is the limiting factor, it can ask a preference question rather than pretending the route choice is settled.

The thesis goes beyond the abstract theory by wiring metareasoning into a reproducible freight-route artifact. A reader can inspect not only the final route but also why the system spent or declined to spend effort on additional search, evidence, or preference resolution.

#### AS15.6 Preference Elicitation And Multiattribute Decision Theory

Keeney and Raiffa establish the conceptual basis for decisions with multiple objectives. Boutilier and coauthors show how utility elicitation and minimax regret can guide decisions when preferences are incomplete. These works are directly relevant because a freight route recommendation depends on tradeoffs that cannot always be assumed in advance.

The repository uses this literature by treating preference information as state. Preferences can constrain the compatible route set, expose contradictions, or trigger VOI actions. They are not merely hidden configuration values. This supports the thesis claim that a route recommendation should be explainable in relation to the user's decision priorities.

The design goes beyond a static multiattribute scoring model because it recognizes preference insufficiency as a legitimate system state. If the available preference information cannot distinguish two routes, the system can return a certified set, ask a preference question, or abstain. That is more faithful to decision theory than forcing a single answer from arbitrary weights.

This framing also protects the thesis against overclaiming. The repository does not infer all human preferences, optimize an entire logistics organization, or guarantee that the chosen utility representation is universally correct. It demonstrates an auditable mechanism for representing, updating, and reporting preference-conditioned route decisions.

#### AS15.7 Reject Option, Selective Classification, And Typed Abstention

Chow's reject option and the selective-classification work by Geifman and El-Yaniv provide the conceptual language for abstention. A system can be more reliable by refusing to decide when conditions are outside its competence or evidence is insufficient. This idea is especially important for a route-decision system that might otherwise appear to fail whenever it withholds a route.

The repository translates this principle into typed route abstentions. It can distinguish search insufficiency, evidence insufficiency, support weakness, preference ambiguity, budget limits, and model-assumption failures. These categories are not cosmetic. They tell the reader what would need to change before the system could responsibly recommend a route.

The thesis contribution is the domain-specific abstention contract. Selective classification usually studies prediction coverage and risk. This repository applies the same discipline to freight-route recommendations, where the decision object includes path candidates, costs, uncertainty worlds, preference state, and provenance. The abstention is therefore tied to a route-decision proof state rather than a confidence score alone.

This is a defensible narrow contribution claim rather than a blanket product-superiority claim. The project is not more useful because it always produces an operational route. It is more suitable for the research objective because it can show why it should not decide.

#### AS15.8 FAIR And Scientific Computing As Evidence Infrastructure

Wilkinson and coauthors' FAIR principles and Wilson and coauthors' scientific-computing best practices shape the repository's evidence discipline. A route-decision thesis cannot rely only on prose assertions. It needs data and artifact provenance, runnable checks, traceable claims, and enough local structure for another reader to inspect the result.

The repository uses this literature through docs checks, theorem maps, claim matrices, negative results, runbooks, manifests, and testable outputs. These are not ancillary. They are part of the contribution because the thesis is about auditable decision evidence. If the evidence cannot be found, checked, or replayed locally, the system's claim to certification is weaker.

The design goes beyond ordinary documentation by aligning artifacts with route-decision claims. A route recommendation, a non-certification result, and an abstention should all have traceable evidence. This includes what candidates were considered, what worlds were used, what preferences were active, what VOI actions were selected, and what limitations were recorded.

The limitation is also clear. A repository can improve reproducibility without achieving perfect reproducibility. External route services, map-data vintages, and live evidence sources can change. The thesis should therefore distinguish local replayability and artifact inspection from universal historical replay of every external dependency.

#### AS15.9 Cross-Literature Synthesis

The contribution can be summarized as a layered argument:

| Literature layer | Core lesson | Repository translation | Thesis contribution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single-objective shortest path | Efficient path optimality is well understood under clear assumptions. | Use route engines and path algorithms as evidence sources and baselines. | Do not claim novelty in basic shortest-path computation. |
| Alternative paths | A serious route decision needs more than one candidate. | Maintain candidate frontiers and unresolved search evidence. | Treat alternatives as witnesses in certification, not only UI options. |
| Scalable routing | Production route queries are feasible at road-network scale. | Let specialized engines generate route evidence. | Focus research novelty on decision certification above engines. |
| Multiobjective paths | Route quality is vector-valued and preference-sensitive. | Model time, cost, emissions, risk, and reliability as decision evidence. | Make tradeoffs visible and preference-conditioned. |
| Robust routing | Uncertainty changes which route is defensible. | Evaluate across sampled worlds and evidence support. | Certify conditionally and record when support is insufficient. |
| Value of information | More information is useful only when worth its cost. | Score search, evidence, and preference actions. | Make stopping, querying, and abstaining rational and inspectable. |
| Preference elicitation | Preferences may be incomplete and must be queried or bounded. | Maintain preference state and compatible route sets. | Avoid hidden arbitrary weights when the decision is underdetermined. |
| Selective decision making | Refusal can improve reliability. | Return typed abstentions and certified sets. | Explain when the system should not recommend a route. |
| Reproducible science | Claims need inspectable artifacts and maintainable code. | Use tests, docs checks, theorem maps, manifests, and provenance. | Make the route decision a publishable evidence object. |

The central synthesis is that none of the literatures alone is enough for the stated thesis objective. Shortest-path work gives routes but not evidence-aware decisions. Multiobjective work gives tradeoffs but not necessarily audited preference state. Robust routing gives uncertainty models but not necessarily local proof artifacts. VOI gives metareasoning but not route-specific certification. Selective classification gives abstention but not freight-route semantics. Reproducibility work gives artifact discipline but not the route-decision algorithm.

This repository's contribution is the integration. It turns those separate ideas into a system that can produce a recommendation, a certified set, a non-certification state, a VOI action, or an abstention with local evidence. That is a defensible applied-systems thesis claim because it is specific, inspectable, and bounded.

#### AS15.10 Contribution Positioning For The Final Paper

The final paper or thesis should describe the contribution in three levels.

First, the conceptual contribution is an evidence-aware freight-route decision contract. A route output is not enough. The system must state the candidate context, cost/evidence assumptions, uncertainty support, preference state, certification status, and abstention reason when applicable.

Second, the systems contribution is a working architecture that composes route evidence, candidate diversification, physical/economic modelling, uncertainty worlds, certification, VOI, preference updates, and artifacts. This is the main applied engineering result.

Third, the evaluation contribution is a set of local checks and artifacts that show the system behaving under success, ambiguity, insufficiency, and failure conditions. The thesis should value negative results here because they demonstrate that the system does not always force a route recommendation.

The thesis should avoid saying "we solve routing." A better claim is: "We design and evaluate an auditable route-decision layer for freight routing that uses routing engines as evidence sources and exposes when a route recommendation is certified, non-certified, or refused." That sentence is ambitious enough to matter and narrow enough to defend.

### AS16. Publishable-Thesis Narrative Skeleton

This section turns the master evidence base into a thesis or paper outline. It is written as a reusable structure: each chapter or section has a purpose, the evidence it should draw from, the claims it can safely make, and the claim boundaries it must preserve. The final thesis can be shorter and more polished than this report, but it should keep the same discipline.

#### AS16.1 Title And Abstract

Working title:

> Auditable Freight-Route Decision Support With Candidate Diversification, Uncertainty Certification, Value Of Information, Preference State, And Typed Abstention

The abstract should make four points:

- The problem is not merely finding a shortest route; it is making a defensible freight-route recommendation under multiple objectives, uncertainty, incomplete preferences, and imperfect evidence.
- Existing route engines and logistics products are operationally valuable, but their usual public surfaces do not provide local proof objects for recommendation, non-certification, and abstention.
- The system composes route evidence, candidate diversification, physical/economic modelling, uncertainty worlds, certification, VOI actions, preference-state updates, and provenance artifacts.
- The evaluation demonstrates recommendation, certified-set, non-certification, and abstention behavior through local artifacts, tests, docs checks, and claim matrices.

The abstract should not claim better map coverage, live traffic, fleet optimization, enterprise integration, or production reliability than commercial systems.

#### AS16.2 Chapter 1: Problem And Motivation

Purpose:

- Establish why freight route decisions are high-stakes enough to need explanation.
- Distinguish route computation from route decision support.
- Introduce the central failure mode: a system can produce a plausible route without exposing why it should be trusted.

Core argument:

- Freight routing involves time, monetary cost, emissions, physical feasibility, reliability, risk, and user preferences.
- Evidence can be incomplete, stale, conflicting, or too expensive to improve.
- A responsible route-decision system should sometimes recommend, sometimes return a certified set, sometimes request more information, and sometimes abstain.

Repository evidence:

- Route response and certification sections.
- DCCS, REFC, VOI, preference-state, and artifact-provenance descriptions.
- Negative-result sections showing non-certification and refusal are expected outcomes.

Safe claims:

- The repository demonstrates an auditable route-decision framing.
- The system exposes reasons for recommendation and non-recommendation.
- The project is a research prototype, not a commercial TMS or fleet optimizer.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not imply that route-decision transparency alone solves all logistics planning.
- Do not imply that the local artifact stack has the data breadth of commercial mapping platforms.

#### AS16.3 Chapter 2: Related Work

Purpose:

- Place the work against path algorithms, route engines, commercial route optimization, decision theory, uncertainty, selective abstention, and reproducible scientific software.
- Show that the project is not isolated from existing research or products.
- Define the precise gap: auditable, evidence-aware, abstaining, reproducible route-decision support.

Suggested structure:

- Shortest-path foundations: Dijkstra and A*.
- Alternative generation: Yen and Eppstein.
- Scalable road routing: contraction hierarchies, customizable route planning, OSRM.
- Multiobjective and constrained routing: Martins, Hassin, and the multiobjective survey literature.
- Robust routing: Yu and Yang, Dokka and Goerigk, and robust/distributionally robust surveys.
- Decision analysis and VOI: Howard, Russell and Wefald, Keeney and Raiffa, Boutilier and coauthors.
- Abstention: Chow, Geifman and El-Yaniv, SelectiveNet.
- Reproducibility: FAIR and scientific-computing best practices.
- Existing systems: OSRM, openrouteservice, GraphHopper, Google Routes, Google Route Optimization, ArcGIS Network Analyst/VRP, HERE Tour Planning, Trimble PC*Miler, PTV, Descartes, ORTEC, Transporeon.

Repository evidence:

- AS13, AS14, and AS15.
- Theorem map and claim matrix, meaning the proof-maturity ledger and claim-status register that prevent related-work claims from being upgraded beyond current evidence.
- Route-engine baseline and artifact sections.

Safe claims:

- Route computation and route optimization are mature fields.
- Many systems provide strong operational routing capabilities.
- The gap is not route calculation but visible certification and refusal evidence.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not characterize vendors as weak overall.
- Do not claim novelty in shortest-path theory.
- Do not claim a full robust optimization breakthrough.

#### AS16.4 Chapter 3: System Requirements And Design Principles

Purpose:

- Derive requirements from the problem and literature.
- Define what the system must expose to be thesis-grade.

Candidate requirements:

- R1: Generate or collect more than one plausible route candidate.
- R2: Model physical and economic freight attributes rather than only distance and duration.
- R3: Evaluate candidate behavior across uncertainty worlds or scenario evidence.
- R4: Track preference state and preference insufficiency.
- R5: Certify route recommendations only under explicit support and threshold conditions.
- R6: Return certified sets or typed abstentions when evidence is insufficient.
- R7: Use VOI to decide whether additional search, evidence, or preference information is worth acquiring.
- R8: Emit replayable or inspectable artifacts that support the route-decision claim.
- R9: Preserve negative results and limitations.

Repository evidence:

- Backend architecture sections.
- Certification model sections.
- VOI pipeline spec, the thesis-facing DCCS/REFC/VOI-AD2R contract for modes, candidate lifecycle, module interfaces, artifacts, budgets, determinism, and uncertified semantics.
- Frontend evidence panel sections.
- Docs checks and artifact inventories.

Safe claims:

- The system operationalizes these requirements in a concrete prototype.
- The design makes evidence support and decision limits visible.

Claim boundaries:

- The system requirements are research requirements, not complete enterprise product requirements.
- Scalability, uptime, fleet assignment, and live data coverage remain outside the central contribution.

#### AS16.5 Chapter 4: Algorithmic Pipeline

Purpose:

- Explain the end-to-end route-decision flow in a way that a reviewer can inspect.
- Keep the pipeline modular so each stage has an evidence role.

Pipeline narrative:

1. Ingest a freight route request with origin, destination, vehicle or shipment assumptions, user preferences, and scenario controls.
2. Query route evidence sources or route engines to obtain baseline and alternative candidates.
3. Diversify and maintain a candidate frontier so the decision is not locked to the first route.
4. Compute physical and economic attributes, including time, cost, emissions, constraints, and risk-related quantities where available.
5. Evaluate route candidates across uncertainty worlds or evidence scenarios.
6. Build a certification state from route frontier outputs, support summaries, manifests, and preference context.
7. Determine whether the result is a certified singleton, certified set, non-certification, VOI action, or typed abstention.
8. Emit route response artifacts, manifests, summaries, theorem/claim links, and UI evidence surfaces.

Repository evidence:

- DCCS descriptions for candidate diversification and unresolved frontier mass.
- REFC descriptions for certification and witness state.
- VOI traces and action scoring.
- Preference-state update sections.
- Artifact provenance and report-generation sections.
- AX95, which names the combined method as Evidence-Bounded Route-Decision Certification (EB-RDC), gives the algorithm box, states formal inputs/outputs, and records the proof-sketch lemmas.

Safe claims:

- The system demonstrates a coherent pipeline from route evidence to auditable decision output.
- Each stage has a documented role in the final route-decision claim.
- EB-RDC is a route-decision certification algorithm over bounded evidence and preference assumptions, not a new shortest-path algorithm.

Claim boundaries:

- The pipeline is not proof that any external route engine is globally correct.
- The pipeline's certification is conditional on inputs, assumptions, evidence sources, and thresholds.

#### AS16.6 Chapter 5: Implementation

Purpose:

- Show that the design is not merely conceptual.
- Describe the implemented backend, frontend, data/artifact surfaces, and verification hooks.

Implementation topics:

- Backend API surfaces for route requests, certification payloads, strictness, and artifacts.
- Certification models and compatibility layers.
- Route candidate and evidence summaries.
- VOI controller outputs.
- Preference-state updates and compatible route sets.
- Frontend panels for route certification, baselines, alternatives, and artifact links.
- Documentation and theorem-map integration.

Repository evidence:

- Backend API docs and tests.
- Frontend certification panel descriptions.
- Theorem map, theorem package, claim matrix, and negative results: respectively the proof-maturity ledger, partial-proof statement package, implementation claim register, and conservative record of unsupported or failed claims.
- Docs consistency checks.

Safe claims:

- The implementation exposes route-decision evidence through code, tests, docs, and user-facing surfaces.
- The architecture is sufficient to evaluate the thesis claim in a local research setting.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not claim production hardening equivalent to a vendor platform.
- Do not claim complete operational logistics coverage.

#### AS16.7 Chapter 6: Evaluation Design

Purpose:

- Explain how the thesis evaluates a decision-support architecture, not just path length or travel time.
- Include both positive and negative evidence.

Evaluation questions:

- Does the system generate and preserve meaningful route alternatives?
- Does the certification state distinguish certified recommendations from uncertain or unsupported decisions?
- Does the world manifest preserve distinct unique and effective support counts?
- Does VOI select sensible additional actions or stop conditions?
- Does preference ambiguity lead to queries, certified sets, or abstention rather than arbitrary decisions?
- Are artifacts sufficiently traceable for a reader to inspect the claim?
- Do docs, tests, and claim matrices remain consistent?

Evaluation evidence:

- Targeted backend tests for certification-state and world-fidelity behavior.
- Docs checks and diff hygiene checks.
- Route artifact bundles and sample manifests that identify the concrete files, endpoints, manifest shapes, focused-VOI outputs, and retrieval flow used to replay evaluation evidence.
- Negative-result examples.
- Frontend evidence surfaces showing how the decision is exposed to an operator.

Safe claims:

- The evaluation demonstrates the intended decision semantics on the repository's scenarios and tests.
- The system makes both success and insufficiency visible.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not treat test passing as proof of real-world routing superiority.
- Do not generalize beyond the scenarios, evidence sources, and assumptions evaluated.

#### AS16.8 Chapter 7: Results

Purpose:

- Present what the system can now do, with emphasis on route-decision behavior rather than only engineering volume.

Expected result categories:

- Certified singleton: one route is supported strongly enough under the current evidence and preferences.
- Certified set: more than one route remains acceptable or indistinguishable under the decision conditions.
- Non-certification: the system has candidates but cannot justify a route decision under the required support.
- VOI action: the system recommends more search, more evidence, or more preference information before deciding.
- Typed abstention: the system refuses to decide and names the reason.
- Artifact replay: the system emits enough local evidence for a reader to inspect the outcome.

Repository evidence:

- Certification summaries.
- VOI outputs.
- Preference and world-fidelity summaries.
- Artifact manifests and docs report sections.

Safe claims:

- The project demonstrates a richer route-decision outcome space than a route-only API response.
- The result set includes both affirmative and refusal outcomes.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not frame abstention as a weakness when it is the correct decision under insufficient evidence.
- Do not imply that every abstention is desirable; some may reveal missing data, weak modelling, or engineering gaps.

#### AS16.9 Chapter 8: Limitations And Threats To Validity

Purpose:

- Make the thesis more credible by naming exactly where the system is limited.

Key limitations:

- Map and routing evidence depend on route engines, data vintages, and available local infrastructure.
- Live traffic and proprietary freight data are not equivalent to commercial provider data.
- Uncertainty worlds are constructed models, not exhaustive representations of the real world.
- Preference state can represent and query tradeoffs, but it does not fully solve human preference learning.
- Certification is conditional on candidate coverage, thresholds, evidence support, and model assumptions.
- The prototype does not replace fleet-scale route optimization, transport management, dispatch, procurement, telematics, or enterprise integrations.
- Local reproducibility is stronger than black-box inspection, but external services may not be perfectly replayable over time.

Repository evidence:

- Negative results, meaning the conservative evidence companion that records unsupported claims, current gate shortfalls, and publication-safe limits.
- Claim-boundary tables.
- Source policy and strictness sections.
- Docs checks and artifact inventories.

Safe claims:

- The project is transparent about its own evidence limits.
- Limitations are part of the decision contract, not hidden caveats.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not soften limitations so much that the thesis sounds like a product brochure.
- Do not let limitations erase the narrow contribution: auditable, abstaining route-decision support remains valuable.

#### AS16.10 Chapter 9: Discussion And Implications

Purpose:

- Interpret what the system means for route-decision support and applied AI/optimization practice.

Discussion points:

- Routing systems should distinguish route computation from route-decision justification.
- Route alternatives are evidence, not just convenience.
- Refusal can be a responsible decision outcome.
- Preference and evidence insufficiency should be visible to users.
- Reproducibility artifacts can make applied decision-support systems more credible.
- Commercial systems may remain operationally stronger while research prototypes remain more inspectable.

Repository evidence:

- AS14 comparison with vendor and open-source systems.
- AS15 academic synthesis.
- Theorem map and claim matrix, meaning the proof-maturity ledger and claim-status register used to keep discussion claims evidence-bounded.

Safe claims:

- The repository offers a template for evidence-aware route-decision research.
- The design is transferable as an architectural pattern, even if the exact freight data and interfaces change.

Claim boundaries:

- Do not claim the architecture is the only way to implement auditable route decisions.
- Do not claim transfer without revalidation in new domains.

#### AS16.11 Chapter 10: Conclusion

Purpose:

- Close with the narrow but meaningful contribution.

Conclusion shape:

- Restate the problem: shortest-route output is insufficient for defensible freight route decisions under uncertainty and multiple objectives.
- Summarize the design: route evidence sources plus candidate diversification, physical/economic modelling, uncertainty worlds, certification, VOI, preference state, typed abstention, and provenance.
- Summarize the evaluation: local tests, artifacts, docs checks, and negative results show the decision contract in action.
- State the contribution: an auditable, evidence-aware, abstaining route-decision research artifact.
- State the boundary: not a replacement for commercial routing or TMS platforms, but a stronger public thesis artifact for explaining why a route is recommended, not certified, or refused.

Final safe thesis claim:

> This thesis designs and evaluates an auditable freight-route decision system that uses route engines as evidence sources and adds candidate diversification, uncertainty-aware certification, value-of-information control, preference-state updates, typed abstention, and artifact provenance, enabling route recommendations and refusals to be inspected as reproducible decision claims.

That claim is ambitious enough to support a publishable applied thesis. It also remains bounded: it does not require the project to beat commercial providers on map coverage, traffic data, fleet optimization, integrations, or production reliability.

## Appendix AT: Thesis-Ready Prose Answers For The Paper

This appendix is written as paper-ready prose rather than as a planning checklist. It gives direct answers to the questions a thesis examiner or reviewer is likely to ask: what was built, what problem it solves, why the problem is hard, what existing systems leave open, how the design works, how it was evaluated, what succeeded, what failed, and how the limitations should be stated without weakening the contribution. The intended use is simple: these paragraphs can be lifted, condensed, or adapted into the introduction, related-work synthesis, system-design chapter, evaluation chapter, and conclusion of a final thesis or publishable applied-systems paper.

### AT1. The Project Built An Auditable Freight-Route Decision System

The project built an auditable freight-route decision system, not merely a route display, route API wrapper, or shortest-path demonstration. Its central object is a route decision that can be explained through evidence. A route recommendation is treated as a claim that must be supported by route alternatives, physical and economic modelling, uncertainty support, preference state, certification status, and reproducible artifacts. The system therefore asks a stronger question than "which path did the router return?" It asks whether the available evidence justifies recommending a route, returning a set of acceptable routes, collecting more information, or refusing to decide.

The system is built around the idea that route engines are evidence sources, not the whole contribution. OSRM-style, openrouteservice-style, GraphHopper-style, commercial, or internal route engines can compute paths, distances, durations, and geometries. Those outputs are valuable, but they are not enough to prove a freight decision. The project uses route outputs as part of an evidential chain and then adds candidate diversification, cost modelling, uncertainty worlds, certification, value-of-information control, preference-state management, typed abstention, and artifact provenance. That layered framing is what makes the system a thesis contribution rather than another route-engine comparison.

Several backend modules embody this decision framing. `backend/app/decision_critical.py` captures decision-critical quantities and the conditions under which route differences matter. `backend/app/evidence_certification.py` and `backend/app/certification_models.py` give the system a vocabulary for route evidence, witnesses, world support, and certification state. `backend/app/voi_controller.py` makes additional search and evidence collection accountable rather than automatic. `backend/app/preference_state.py` and `backend/app/preference_update.py` represent user ambiguity as state that can be narrowed or contradicted. `backend/app/abstention.py` makes refusal an explicit output rather than an unhandled exception.

The project also built an artifact discipline around the decision system. `backend/app/run_store.py` and the documentation surfaces describe how route runs, manifests, policy hashes, and provenance can be preserved. `docs/api-cookbook.md` explains the request and response surface a reviewer can exercise. `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md` and `docs/negative_results.md` show that the project is not relying on a single happy-path demonstration. The output is intended to be inspectable by a thesis reader who wants to know why the system recommended, withheld, or rejected a route decision.

The most important result is that the system changes the route recommendation from a black-box answer into a conditional evidence object. The system can say that one route is certified under the current candidate frontier and world manifest. It can say that a set of routes remains certified because the available evidence does not distinguish them enough. It can say that additional evidence has enough decision value to justify further computation. It can also say that it should not decide because support, preference clarity, budget, or modelling assumptions are insufficient. That richer outcome space is the core project achievement.

### AT2. The Addressed Problem Is Decision Justification, Not Shortest-Path Search

The addressed problem is decision justification. The project does not claim to invent a better Dijkstra algorithm, a faster contraction hierarchy, or a more complete global road network. Those are important routing problems, but they are not the research gap this repository addresses. The gap is that a route engine can return a plausible route while leaving the decision maker unable to inspect why that route should be trusted, which alternatives were considered, what uncertainty supports the result, which preferences were assumed, and why the system did or did not have enough evidence to certify the recommendation.

This distinction matters because shortest-path correctness is conditional on the graph, weights, and objective. A route that is shortest under one scalar cost can be dominated or fragile once the decision includes freight cost, emissions, disruption risk, route restrictions, reliability, or user preference. In real freight contexts, the path computation is only one step in a larger decision. The project therefore treats shortest-path engines as providers of route evidence and concentrates its research claim on the layer that turns evidence into an auditable recommendation or abstention.

`backend/app/decision_critical.py` is central to this claim because it focuses attention on whether route differences are decision-critical rather than merely numerically different. A small change in duration may be irrelevant if the monetary or emissions tradeoff is large. A route that wins nominally may be fragile if a small perturbation flips the decision. A candidate may look inferior under a proxy rank but become important when preferences, uncertainty, or support thresholds are considered. Decision justification requires these distinctions to be visible.

This is also why ranking proxies directly is not enough. A proxy rank can order candidates according to a simplified score, but it cannot certify that the ranking is robust, that the candidate set is sufficiently explored, or that the user's preferences make the top item uniquely acceptable. The system therefore uses candidate envelopes, unresolved mass, pairwise gaps, flip radius, decision regions, certified sets, and abstention states. These objects make the decision boundary visible instead of pretending that a single score is the same as a defensible recommendation.

The paper-ready claim should be phrased accordingly: this project addresses the problem of auditable route-decision justification under bounded evidence. It does not solve every problem in routing. It does not replace commercial map data or logistics optimization. It demonstrates how a freight route decision can be supported, qualified, or refused through explicit evidence and replayable artifacts.

### AT3. The Problem Is Hard Because Search, Evidence, Preferences, And Evaluation All Fail Differently

The problem is hard because the route-decision pipeline can fail in several different ways, and those failures should not be collapsed into one generic error. Search can fail by not exploring enough alternatives. Evidence can fail by being stale, inconsistent, incomplete, or unsupported across worlds. Preferences can fail by being under-specified, contradictory, or too broad to distinguish candidate routes. Evaluation can fail by measuring only runtime success while ignoring whether the recommendation was actually justified. A research-grade route decision system must separate these failure modes so that each one leads to the correct response.

Search failure is subtle because a router can always return something plausible. A single best path under one cost model may hide a nearby alternative that becomes better under a different traffic, emissions, price, or preference assumption. Candidate diversification and DCCS address this by refusing to treat the first route as the full decision space. The candidate envelope and unresolved mass expose what remains unknown about the frontier. That is better than ranking proxies directly because it lets the system say whether the search space itself is sufficiently covered before certifying a route.

Evidence failure is different from search failure. A route can be well explored but poorly supported. The system may have many candidates yet lack reliable world evidence, source agreement, freshness, or model support. This is where `backend/app/evidence_certification.py` and `backend/app/certification_models.py` matter. They let the system represent certification as a conditional claim over a particular manifest, support basis, and candidate set. They also preserve distinctions such as `unique_world_count` and `effective_world_count`, which matter because many nominal worlds do not necessarily produce equally strong independent support. A thesis certificate that confuses unique worlds with effective evidential support would overstate the evidence.

Preference failure is also distinct. A route can be searchable and evidence-supported while still not be uniquely recommended because the user's tradeoffs are not known. `backend/app/preference_state.py` and `backend/app/preference_update.py` make that ambiguity explicit. Preference updates must shrink or clarify the compatible decision space; otherwise they are not useful evidence. If a preference question does not reduce ambiguity, reveal a contradiction, or distinguish certified alternatives, the system should not pretend that the user's decision state has improved.

Evaluation failure is the final challenge. A system that always returns a route may look successful under ordinary API tests, but it may be unsafe as decision support because it cannot show when it should refuse. This project evaluates the decision contract, not just runtime success. `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`, `docs/api-cookbook.md`, and `docs/negative_results.md` support that evaluation stance by documenting checks, reproducible surfaces, and negative cases. The thesis should argue that success includes correct non-decision, not just a rendered route.

### AT4. Existing Routing And Logistics Systems Leave A Research Gap Around Certification And Refusal

Existing routing and logistics systems are strong at many things this project does not try to surpass. Open-source route engines can compute road routes efficiently. Commercial mapping providers can offer global coverage, live traffic, geocoding, service guarantees, and rich developer ecosystems. Logistics optimization vendors can solve fleet-scale assignment, scheduling, dispatch, visibility, procurement, and telematics problems. The thesis should acknowledge those strengths directly because the project's contribution is not operational superiority over those systems.

The research gap is narrower and more defensible. Many existing systems expose route outputs, optimization plans, status objects, warnings, or operational reports, but they do not usually expose a local proof object explaining why a route recommendation is certified, why it is not certified, and when the system should refuse to decide. A route API can return alternatives, but alternatives alone are not a certificate. A fleet optimizer can return a plan, but a plan alone does not show candidate-frontier unresolved mass, world-support effectiveness, preference ambiguity, or VOI reasoning. A logistics platform can be operationally powerful while still being unsuitable as a thesis-grade evidence artifact.

This project positions route engines as evidence sources in exactly that gap. Their outputs are useful, but the thesis contribution begins when those outputs are wrapped in decision evidence. `backend/app/evidence_certification.py` and `backend/app/certification_models.py` make certification conditional and inspectable. `backend/app/abstention.py` makes refusal explicit. `backend/app/run_store.py` preserves artifacts and provenance. These surfaces are designed for a reader inspecting the claim, not only for a dispatcher seeking an operational answer.

The system is therefore stronger than existing products only for a bounded research objective: auditable, evidence-aware, abstaining, reproducible route-decision support. It should not claim better map coverage, better live traffic, better routing speed, better commercial reliability, better fleet optimization, or better enterprise integration. It should claim that the local repository exposes route-decision evidence in a way that most black-box or product-oriented systems do not. That claim is both ambitious and fair.

The final paper can state the gap as follows. Route computation and route optimization are mature, but route-decision certification remains underexposed in practical systems. A thesis examiner cannot easily inspect the candidate frontier, support-conditioned world evidence, preference ambiguity, VOI actions, typed abstention reasons, policy hashes, manifests, and provenance for most commercial outputs. This project fills that research gap by making those objects first-class parts of the route decision.

### AT5. The Core Design Is A Layered Evidence-To-Decision Pipeline

The core design is a layered evidence-to-decision pipeline. The route engine layer generates or collects route candidates. The diversification layer prevents the first route from becoming the entire decision space. The modelling layer computes freight-relevant quantities such as time, cost, emissions, and scenario-sensitive attributes. The uncertainty layer evaluates candidates across worlds or evidence conditions. The certification layer converts those evaluations into conditional claims. The VOI layer decides whether more computation or evidence is worth the cost. The preference layer records user tradeoffs and ambiguity. The abstention layer names conditions under which the system should not recommend a route. The artifact layer makes the whole process inspectable.

This design is valuable because it assigns each layer a clear epistemic role. Route engines provide path evidence. DCCS provides candidate-space evidence. REFC provides certification evidence. VOI provides metareasoning evidence. Preference state provides decision-maker evidence. Typed abstention provides non-certification semantics and remedies. Run storage and provenance provide reproducibility evidence. A route recommendation is therefore not a single opaque object; it is the endpoint of a chain that can be audited.

The backend modules reinforce this architecture. `backend/app/decision_critical.py` helps identify when route differences matter for a decision. `backend/app/evidence_certification.py` and `backend/app/certification_models.py` define how route evidence becomes certification state. `backend/app/voi_controller.py` controls whether the system should continue gathering evidence. `backend/app/preference_state.py` and `backend/app/preference_update.py` encode preference evolution. `backend/app/abstention.py` records why a non-decision is the correct output. `backend/app/run_store.py` preserves the artifacts needed to inspect a run after the fact.

The pipeline is intentionally conditional. It does not declare that a route is the best route in the real world. It declares that a route is certified under the current candidate set, evidence sources, world manifest, support assumptions, thresholds, preferences, and policy. That conditional language is a strength because it prevents the thesis from overclaiming. It is more defensible to expose the boundary of a claim than to pretend that local evidence establishes global truth.

The design also gives the frontend and documentation a real evidence role. A user-facing route panel should not merely draw a line on a map. It should surface alternatives, certification status, support summaries, explanations, artifacts, and abstention reasons. `docs/api-cookbook.md` helps reviewers exercise the API surface, while `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md` explains the checks that keep the evidence contract stable. This makes the repository a coherent applied system rather than a collection of disconnected algorithms.

### AT6. Candidate Diversification And DCCS Prevent A Premature Single-Route Answer

Candidate diversification matters because a premature single-route answer can look confident while being poorly justified. If the system only ranks the candidates it happened to receive, it may confuse local proxy dominance with decision certainty. DCCS addresses this by treating candidate generation as an evidential problem. The system must understand what candidates have been explored, what envelope they occupy, how much unresolved mass remains, and whether the frontier is rich enough to support a recommendation.

DCCS candidate envelopes are better than ranking proxies directly because they preserve information about the candidate space. A proxy rank compresses each route into a scalar or simplified ordering. That can be useful for sorting, but it hides whether unexplored candidates could still alter the decision. A candidate envelope records the range and structure of plausible alternatives. Unresolved mass captures the remaining search uncertainty. Together, these ideas let the system distinguish "this route currently ranks first" from "the candidate frontier is sufficiently resolved to certify this route."

This distinction is essential for a thesis about decision justification. A single route can be top-ranked under current evidence while still being fragile because the frontier is incomplete. Another route can be second-ranked but close enough to matter under small preference or scenario changes. DCCS makes those possibilities visible. It gives the certification layer a more honest input than a bare list sorted by duration or generalized cost.

`backend/app/decision_critical.py` connects directly to this logic by focusing on differences that change decisions. Candidate diversification is not about producing alternatives for decoration. It is about identifying whether route comparisons are stable enough to support a decision. Pairwise gaps, flip radius, and decision regions only become meaningful when the system has a serious candidate set to compare. Without DCCS, those fragility measures would be applied to an impoverished frontier.

The final paper should present DCCS as a guardrail against false certainty. It does not guarantee that every possible route has been explored, and it should not be described that way. Its contribution is to expose candidate-space incompleteness and make unresolved search mass part of the decision record. That is substantially stronger than assuming the best available proxy-ranked route is automatically the route the system should recommend.

### AT7. REFC Turns Route Alternatives Into Conditional Certification Claims

REFC turns route alternatives into conditional certification claims. Its role is to decide whether the available route evidence supports a singleton recommendation, a certified set, a non-certification state, or a refusal path. This is a different task from route scoring. Route scoring estimates how candidates compare. Certification asks whether the comparison is strong enough, supported enough, and preference-compatible enough to justify a decision claim.

The certification must be described as conditional, not as real-world truth. A REFC certificate is valid relative to the candidate frontier, evidence sources, world manifest, policy thresholds, support assumptions, and preference state used by the system. It does not prove that the selected route is objectively best in every possible real-world condition. This conditional framing is not a weakness. It is the only honest way to state a route-decision claim when the evidence is finite, modelled, and dependent on external sources.

`backend/app/evidence_certification.py` and `backend/app/certification_models.py` provide the language for this conditional claim. They represent witnesses, world-fidelity summaries, certified sets, and route-support status in a way that can be inspected. The distinction between `unique_world_count` and `effective_world_count` is especially important. Unique world count says how many distinct worlds or scenarios are present. Effective world count says how much independent or usable support remains after the system accounts for redundancy, weighting, support quality, or manifest semantics. If those counts collapse into one value, the certificate can exaggerate support by treating nominal variety as evidential strength.

REFC also makes fragility visible through pairwise gap, flip radius, decision region, and certified set states. A pairwise gap shows how much separates two candidates under the current decision metric. A flip radius indicates how little perturbation may be needed before the decision changes. A decision region describes where a route remains valid under preference or scenario variation. A certified set acknowledges that more than one route can remain defensible. These objects are important because a recommendation is not only about which route wins; it is also about how stable that win is.

The thesis should present REFC as the bridge between computation and claim discipline. It accepts route alternatives and uncertainty summaries, then returns a status that can be defended. Sometimes that status is a certified recommendation. Sometimes it is a certified set. Sometimes it is non-certification. The system's credibility comes from preserving all of those outcomes instead of always forcing a single answer.

### AT8. VOI Makes Additional Computation And Evidence Collection Accountable

VOI makes additional computation and evidence collection accountable. In a route-decision system, there is always more the system could do. It could search for more candidates, query another evidence source, refine an uncertainty world, ask a preference question, or wait for better data. The question is not whether more information might be interesting. The question is whether it has enough expected decision value to justify its cost. `backend/app/voi_controller.py` and `docs/voi-pipeline-spec.md` make that question part of the system rather than a manual afterthought.

This matters because unbounded information gathering is not a practical decision procedure. A system that always asks for more evidence may never decide. A system that never asks for more evidence may decide too early. VOI provides the middle ground. It asks whether the next action is likely to change the recommendation, reduce fragility, resolve a certified set, clarify a preference ambiguity, or turn an abstention into a supported decision. If not, stopping can be the rational action.

The phrase "VOI stops or acts based on decision value, not curiosity" is important for the thesis. Curiosity would collect evidence because it is available or interesting. Decision value collects evidence because it is expected to change the route decision or the confidence of the decision in a meaningful way. This aligns the system with bounded rationality: computation and evidence have cost, so they must be justified by their effect on the decision.

VOI also interacts with abstention. If a needed evidence action has high value but cannot be performed within budget, the correct output may be a budget-related or evidence-related abstention. If a preference question has high value, the system should ask it instead of guessing. If more candidate search has low value because the decision region is already stable, the system can stop and certify. These outcomes make the decision process inspectable.

The final paper should treat VOI as one of the system's main originality points. It is not merely an optimization speedup. It is a governance layer over computation and evidence. It explains why the system spent effort, why it stopped, and why it refused when necessary. That accountability is a major reason the project is stronger as a thesis artifact than a route-only response.

### AT9. Preference State Turns User Ambiguity Into Auditable Decision State

Preference state turns user ambiguity into auditable decision state. Freight route decisions depend on tradeoffs: time against cost, emissions against reliability, tolls against distance, risk against predictability, and sometimes organizational constraints against driver or customer preferences. If those preferences are hidden inside a fixed weight vector, the system may appear objective while actually relying on assumptions the user never endorsed. `backend/app/preference_state.py` and `backend/app/preference_update.py` address this by making preference information explicit, updateable, and inspectable.

Preference updates must shrink or clarify the compatible decision space. A useful update can rule out routes that violate a stated preference, reduce a set of compatible utility weights, distinguish two otherwise tied candidates, or reveal that the user's preferences conflict. An update that merely records more text without changing the decision state is not sufficient for certification. The thesis should emphasize that preference elicitation is not a user-interface flourish; it is evidence about the decision boundary.

This is where certified sets become important. If the current preference state cannot distinguish two or more routes, the system should not invent precision. It can return a certified set, request more preference information, or abstain due to preference ambiguity. That behavior is more honest than selecting the first route after an arbitrary tie-break. It also gives a reviewer a clear way to inspect how user ambiguity affected the outcome.

Preference state also protects the system from overfitting to one assumed decision maker. Different freight operators may value time, cost, emissions, reliability, and route restrictions differently. The repository's design does not pretend those tradeoffs are universal. Instead, it records the preference assumptions under which a recommendation is valid. If those assumptions change, the certificate can change too.

The final paper should present preference state as part of the evidence chain. It is not enough to say that the system supports preferences. The stronger claim is that the system can show when preferences certify a route, when they leave multiple routes acceptable, when they require more elicitation, and when they contradict the decision. That is a thesis-ready contribution because it converts human ambiguity into auditable state rather than hiding it.

### AT10. Typed Abstention Makes Non-Decision A Responsible Output

Typed abstention makes non-decision a responsible output. In many systems, not returning a route is treated as failure. In this project, refusal can be the correct answer when the evidence does not support a recommendation. `backend/app/abstention.py` gives the system explicit categories for those cases, so a non-decision can be explained rather than disguised as an error or forced into a weak recommendation.

This distinction is central to the contribution. A route-decision system that always recommends a route can be dangerous or misleading when support is insufficient. It may recommend based on incomplete candidate search, weak world evidence, unclear preferences, budget limits, source-policy violations, or fragile decision boundaries. Typed abstention allows the system to state which condition failed and what kind of evidence would be needed to proceed.

Typed abstention is not failure because the system is fulfilling its decision contract. The contract is not "always output a route." The contract is "recommend a route only when the evidence supports doing so, and otherwise explain why not." Under that contract, an abstention due to insufficient support is a successful detection of a decision boundary. An abstention due to preference ambiguity is a successful refusal to guess. An abstention due to budget limits is a successful acknowledgement that more valuable evidence cannot be obtained within the allowed resources.

Abstention also improves evaluation. A test or case study should not only check whether a route was returned. It should check whether the right type of route decision was returned. If the evidence is intentionally incomplete, the correct output may be abstention. If two routes remain compatible, the correct output may be a certified set. If a route is fragile, the correct output may be a VOI action. This richer evaluation language is supported by `docs/negative_results.md` and `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`.

The final paper should be unapologetic about abstention. It should not describe refusal as a missing feature. It should describe typed abstention as the mechanism that prevents the system from overstating its evidence. This is one of the clearest ways the project differs from ordinary route-output systems.

### AT11. Artifacts And Provenance Make The Thesis Reproducible Rather Than Anecdotal

Artifacts and provenance make the thesis reproducible rather than anecdotal. A screenshot can show that a route appeared on a map, but it cannot prove which candidates were considered, which policy was active, which world manifest supported the result, which preference state applied, or why the system abstained. Exploratory notebooks and informal notes can be useful during development, but they are weaker as thesis evidence when they are not tied to stable APIs, manifests, policy hashes, tests, and run artifacts. This project therefore treats artifacts as part of the decision claim.

`backend/app/run_store.py` is important because it gives route runs and decision evidence a durable surface. A run can preserve request parameters, outputs, summaries, and provenance in a form that can be inspected later. Policy hashes make it possible to identify which decision policy governed a result. Manifests describe the worlds, evidence sources, and assumptions that shaped certification. Provenance links the recommendation or abstention to the actual evidence path rather than to a narrative written after the fact.

This artifact discipline is stronger than screenshots and informal exploratory files because it supports audit. A reviewer can compare an API response from `docs/api-cookbook.md` with the documented claim. A maintainer can run documentation checks against `docs/quality-gates-and-benchmarks.md`. A thesis examiner can inspect `docs/negative_results.md` to see that the system records failures and limits rather than only successful demos. The artifacts turn the project into a reproducible evidence base.
