### AV13. Evaluation Measurements

The evaluation should be stated carefully. The current evidence supports the existence and inspectability of the selective decision contract. It does not support universal deployment claims or blanket superiority over mature routing products. The strongest local evidence surfaces include strict preflight checks, graph coverage evidence, named thesis evaluation lanes, checked artifacts, run manifests, cohort summaries, support summaries, baseline comparison surfaces, hot-rerun evidence, and negative-result documentation.

The graph evidence is concrete: `16,782,614` nodes, `17,271,476` edges, graph size about `4123.27 MB`, worst fixture nearest-node gap `2545.053 m`, UK bounding box `lat 49.75..61.1`, `lon -8.75..2.25`, and `coverage_passed=true`. Those values should be cited as local graph-readiness evidence, not as a proof that every UK freight movement is covered perfectly.

The checked thesis-lane campaign `backend/out/thesis_campaigns/dominance_cluster5_cardiff_bath_corr12p5_r2` contains 20 evaluation rows, 4 summary rows, strict live readiness pass rate `1.0`, evaluation rerun success rate `0.8`, backend ready wait `161.38 ms`, route-graph warmup elapsed `10000.0 ms`, and variant runtimes `V0=9176.741 ms`, `A=5315.91825 ms`, `B=5787.824 ms`, and `C=2794.579 ms`. This is descriptive local evidence for that campaign. It is not a universal benchmark closure.

The checked full-suite verdict in `out/headline_exports/current_checked/full_suite_curated_latest_20260411/publishability_verdict.json` remains conservative while being applied-evidence green: `publishable_on_current_evidence=true`, `adoption_claim_supported=true`, `hot_rerun_all_green=true`, `sample_size_failure_count=0`, `fairness_failure_count=0`, and `publishability_blockers=[]`. This is exactly the kind of nuance a publishable thesis needs. The system has strong evidence surfaces, but deployment and theorem-grade claims remain explicitly outside the checked verdict surface.

The evaluation code also protects against overclaiming. It downgrades claims when confidence intervals cross zero, effects have mixed sign, agreement is insufficient, effects are flat, or Holm-adjusted significance does not hold:

```python
if ci_crosses_zero:
    claim_direction = "inconclusive"
if mixed_sign or insufficient_agreement or flat_effect:
    claim_scope = "narrowed"
if holm_adjusted_non_significant:
    claim_direction = "inconclusive"
```

The exact names differ across the evaluation functions, but the design point is stable: the evaluator narrows claims when the statistics do not justify the headline. That makes the negative-result discipline part of the research contribution. A weaker thesis would delete or ignore limitations. This repository keeps claim boundaries visible.

### AV14. Successful Mechanisms And Evidence Strengths

The strongest result is evidence exposure. The project makes route candidates, certificates, fragility, value of refresh, preference ambiguity, action traces, support summaries, abstention classes, manifests, and provenance visible as first-class data. That is why someone reading this report can understand the project at nearly the same level as someone reading the codebase and other markdown files.

DCCS worked as an auditable bridge between route generation and expensive refinement. It does not merely select top proxy routes; it records why a route is decision-critical or not. REFC worked as a bounded certification layer because it converts evidence-world variation into a visible certificate and fragility map. VOI worked as a controller because it expresses why the next action is or is not worth taking. Preference state worked because it records uncertainty reduction rather than pretending default weights are final preferences. Typed abstention worked because it prevents unsupported singleton claims.

The frontend evidence panels also worked conceptually. They move the project from a backend-only research prototype to an inspectable decision tool. A reviewer can see certification basis, support state, preference traces, artifact-backed audit surfaces, V0/A/B/C proof tiles, OSRM/ORS comparison navigation, and run-inspector links.

### AV15. Remaining Failures And Limitations

The checked evidence summarised in this report, especially the `2026-04-14` full-suite companion and the maintained negative-result ledgers, does not justify claiming universal superiority over OSRM or ORS. It does not justify unconditional validity outside the supported UK-style scope. It does not justify unconditional deployability under all live-source conditions. It does not prove theorem-backed closure for the whole REFC/DCCS/VOI package. It does not give a blanket green status for every `G11.*` and `P14.*` gate. It does not prove complete reviewer-package materialisation, seed robustness for every claim, or commercial readiness as a TMS product.

The system is also asset-dependent. It relies on graph coverage, route-engine availability, evidence snapshots, support assumptions, thresholds, and preference state. The strict preflight can fail if ORS or live evidence is unavailable. Backend-only operation should start from `backend/` with `uv run uvicorn app.main:app ...`; the docs warn against the repo-root `uv run --project backend uvicorn ...` form for this layout. The frontend route-compute fallback sequence is stream Pareto, JSON Pareto, then single-route fallback, with default degrade policy `12 -> 6 -> 3`; strict HTTP 4xx business failures are terminal. Those operational details belong in the thesis because they define the actual system envelope.

The proof maturity is also mixed. DCCS fields are auditable workflow and diagnostic fields, not theorem-level guarantees. REFC is bounded stress-world certification, not a universal proof of real-world optimality. VOI uses forecasted action value, not omniscient value of information. Preference elicitation records and reduces ambiguity, but it does not learn a complete human utility function. These limits do not invalidate the project; they make the contribution precise.

### AV16. Advantages Over Simpler Alternatives

A pure route-engine wrapper would have been simpler, but it would have inherited the main weakness of route APIs: the returned route would look authoritative even when evidence was stale, preferences were ambiguous, or search was incomplete. It would also give the thesis little to defend beyond integration. This project is more suitable for thesis evidence because it can explain the state of the decision.

A pure custom-graph router would have provided more algorithmic control, but it would have shifted the thesis toward rebuilding infrastructure that OSRM, openrouteservice, GraphHopper, and academic speedup methods already address well. This project is more defensible as an applied-research system because it spends complexity where the research gap is: selective certification, value-of-information control, preference ambiguity, typed abstention, and reproducible evidence.

A scalar multiobjective score would have been easier to present, but it would have hidden the fact that time, money, CO2, support, evidence freshness, and preference ambiguity are not all the same kind of uncertainty. This project is more inspectable because it separates objective tradeoff from evidence support and preference support.

A full commercial-style VRP optimiser would have been impressive but mis-scoped. HERE, PTV, ArcGIS, GraphHopper, Descartes, ORTEC, Transporeon, and Google already show that fleet optimisation and logistics planning are mature product categories. This project is more appropriate for a publishable applied thesis because it narrows the problem to auditable selective route recommendation and then exposes the evidence chain in source code and artifacts.

A no-abstention design would have produced more "answers", but weaker science. The best decision under missing evidence is sometimes not to decide. Typed abstention makes the system more honest and more useful: the operator learns which blocker must be resolved, and the reviewer can see that the route was not overclaimed.

### AV17. Literature Review Paragraphs For The Thesis

Classical shortest-path research gives the computational foundation for routing but does not by itself solve freight-route decision justification. Dijkstra's 1959 algorithm established the standard nonnegative shortest-path baseline [Dijkstra 1959](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390). A* added heuristic search for minimum-cost paths [Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael 1968](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136). Yen and Eppstein provide foundations for alternative-path enumeration [Yen 1971](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.17.11.712), [Eppstein 1998](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539795290477). Road-network speedup research, including contraction hierarchies and customizable route planning, shows how large road networks can be queried efficiently [Geisberger et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-68552-4_24), [Delling et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.2014.0579). WhatIf Freight Router builds on that tradition but targets a different layer: it asks when a route recommendation is evidentially justified, not only when a shortest path can be computed.

Multiobjective shortest-path research is directly relevant because freight routes involve competing objectives. Martins' multiobjective shortest-path work and later algorithms such as the improved multiobjective shortest-path algorithm by Maristany de las Casas, Sedeño-Noda, and Borndörfer show that efficient-path sets can be treated algorithmically [Maristany de las Casas et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cor.2021.105424). This repository does not claim to invent multiobjective shortest paths. Its contribution is to connect multiobjective route evidence to certification, preference state, value-of-information control, and typed abstention.

Robust routing research is relevant because freight costs are unstable. Robust shortest-path work studies routes under interval or scenario uncertainty, and later exact methods show how difficult robust shortest-path variants can become [Yu and Yang 1998](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0305-0548(97)00085-3), [Montemanni and Gambardella 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0305-0548(03)00114-X). WhatIf Freight Router uses this motivation but chooses a bounded empirical certification route: it samples evidence worlds, records winner fractions, and exposes fragility rather than claiming a universal robust optimum.

Decision-analysis literature justifies the system's action policy. Howard's information value theory motivates asking whether more information is worth collecting [Howard 1966](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074). Multi-attribute utility theory motivates explicit tradeoff modelling [Keeney and Raiffa 1993](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139174084). Preference elicitation work motivates asking targeted questions only when they reduce regret or ambiguity [Wang and Boutilier 2003](https://research.google/pubs/incremental-utility-elicitation-with-the-minimax-regret-decision-criterion/). The repository operationalises these ideas through VOI actions, preference shrinkage traces, and certified-only preference constraints.

Selective-decision literature justifies abstention. Chow's reject-option work shows that refusing a decision can be part of the optimal error/reject tradeoff [Chow 1970](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406). In this project, abstention is adapted to route recommendation: the system can refuse a singleton when search, evidence, preference, budget, support, or model assumptions block certification. This is a stronger scientific posture than always returning a route.

Reproducibility literature justifies the artifact-first evaluation design. FAIR principles emphasise findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable research objects, including workflows and tools [Wilkinson et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18). Reproducible research and scientific-computing best practices motivate manifests, scripts, versioned artifacts, explicit checks, and negative-result reporting [Peng 2011](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1213847), [Wilson et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001745). This repository follows that direction by exposing manifests, checked bundles, route artifacts, reviewer exports, `paper_artifact_index.json`, and docs consistency checks.

### AV18. Problem Solved: Auditable Selective Freight Decisions

The project solved the problem of turning freight-route evidence into an auditable selective decision. It did not merely compute paths. It built a pipeline that can decide, certify a set, ask for more information, or abstain with a typed reason. This solves a real gap between routing engines and thesis-grade decision justification. Existing tools can be excellent route providers or optimisers, but the thesis must show why a recommendation is justified under the exact evidence available in the repository. WhatIf Freight Router creates that evidence chain.

### AV19. Difficulty: Interacting Search, Evidence, Preference, And Risk Uncertainty

It is hard because the route recommendation depends on interacting uncertainties. Search incompleteness can leave hidden challengers. Evidence freshness can change cost. Tolls, terrain, fuel, carbon, weather, and stochastic regimes can affect route dominance in different directions. Preferences can make a route unacceptable even if it is cheap. Tail risk can make average-cost winners fragile. A thesis-grade system must separate these causes because each one has a different remedy. More route search does not fix stale fuel evidence. A preference query does not fix an unsupported world model. Evidence refresh does not prove search completeness. This project is hard because it keeps those failure modes separate and visible.

### AV20. Alternative Solution Space And The Remaining Gap

The alternatives are route-engine wrappers, custom graph routers, scalar multiobjective ranking, full VRP/TMS products, and commercial route APIs. OSRM, openrouteservice, and GraphHopper are strong routing and spatial APIs. Google Routes, HERE Tour Planning, ArcGIS Network Analyst, Trimble PC*Miler, PTV, Descartes, ORTEC, and Transporeon show mature commercial planning surfaces. Academic shortest-path, robust-routing, multiobjective-routing, VOI, preference-elicitation, and reject-option work provide theory. The reason this project is needed is that none of those alternatives, as publicly exposed, gives this repository's exact combination of source-readable evidence ledgers, sampled-world certification, value-of-refresh traces, typed abstention, preference shrinkage, docs checks, and reproducible local thesis artifacts.

### AV21. Designed System: A Layered Selective Freight Decision Engine

The designed system is a bounded UK-focused selective freight-route decision engine. It combines route candidate generation, DCCS decision-critical selection, REFC evidence certification, VOI action control, preference-state updates, typed abstention, signed run artifacts, a `DecisionPackage` API contract, frontend proof panels, docs consistency checks, and explicit negative-result gates. The design is not a monolith. Each layer answers a different question: DCCS asks which candidate is worth refining; REFC asks whether the winner is stable under evidence worlds; VOI asks whether more action is worth its cost; preference state asks whether the user's tradeoffs are sufficiently known; abstention asks why the system cannot certify; the run store asks whether the evidence can be replayed and inspected.

### AV22. Design Justification: Separated Failure Modes And Evidence-Cost Control

The design is justified because the failure modes are separable. Search, evidence, preference, budget, and model-support failures require different actions. A single route score cannot express all of them. The layered design is also justified by the literature: routing algorithms supply candidate paths; multiobjective and robust routing motivate multidimensional and uncertain costs; VOI theory motivates bounded action selection; preference elicitation motivates targeted queries; reject-option theory motivates abstention; reproducibility principles motivate manifests and artifacts. The design is more suitable for thesis evidence than simpler alternatives because it exposes the decision boundary instead of hiding it.

### AV23. Evaluation Method: Preflight, Variant Runs, Artifacts, And Negative Gates

It was evaluated through a combination of runtime preflight, graph coverage evidence, thesis variants, route artifacts, evaluator lanes, checked full-suite surfaces, docs consistency checks, and negative-result diagnostics. The evaluation includes local evidence for strict preflight readiness, graph size and coverage, thesis campaign outputs, variant runtimes, run manifests, artifact inventories, baseline comparisons, hot rerun status, fairness/sample-size counts, publishability blockers, and checked full-suite verdict fields. It also includes a docs checker, `python scripts/check_docs.py`, which verifies links, related-doc coverage, local paths, endpoint parity, notebook references, and theorem-claim consistency.

### AV24. Findings, Failures, And Limitations

What worked is the evidence contract. The project can show how a route decision was produced, why it was certified or not, which evidence families were involved, what action was considered next, what preference ambiguity remained, and which artifacts support the claim. What remains incomplete is deployment-grade certification and theorem maturity for the whole system. The limitations are UK scope, dependency on route engines and evidence assets, bounded empirical certification rather than universal proof, incomplete theorem maturity for the whole system, and no claim of commercial TMS readiness. These limits should be stated openly because they make the thesis credible.

### AV25. Thesis Use Of This Appendix

This appendix is the master evidence base for turning code and artifacts into chapters. The introduction material is concentrated in AV1, AV18, and AV19. The literature-review material is concentrated in AV3, AV4, and AV17. The design-chapter evidence is concentrated in AV5 through AV12. The evaluation material is concentrated in AV13 and AV23. The discussion and limitations material is concentrated in AV14, AV15, and AV24. The claim boundary is defined by AV16 and the safe comparative statements throughout this appendix.

The most defensible final thesis claim is: WhatIf Freight Router demonstrates that freight-route recommendations can be represented as conditional, auditable evidence objects rather than opaque route outputs. Within a bounded UK-focused prototype, the system shows how route engines can be used as evidence sources and augmented with candidate diversification, selective certification, value-of-information control, preference-state updates, typed abstention, and artifact provenance. Its strongest result is not unconditional route superiority, but a reproducible architecture for deciding, qualifying, or refusing freight-route recommendations with explicit evidence.

## Appendix AW: Extended Literature Review, Existing-Solution Comparison, And Algorithmic Deviations

This appendix is a thesis-ready literature and positioning ledger. It is intentionally more detailed than a normal README section because the thesis report is the master evidence base. A reader should not need to read every source file before understanding why the project exists, which academic ideas it uses, where it deviates from the academic norm, and why those deviations are justified for a freight-route evidence system.

For readability, this appendix uses two project acronyms repeatedly: DCCS means Decision-Critical Candidate Search, the route-candidate triage layer that decides which alternatives are worth refining; REFC means Route-Evidence Frontier Certification, the strict-frontier certification layer that decides whether the evidence supports a singleton, a certified set, further action, or typed abstention.

The claim boundary matters. WhatIf Freight Router is not a faster replacement for OSRM, openrouteservice, GraphHopper, Google Routes, HERE, ArcGIS Network Analyst, PTV xTour, Trimble PC*Miler, ORTEC, Descartes, or Transporeon. Those products and engines solve large parts of operational routing, mapping, fleet planning, and transport management. The thesis contribution is narrower and more research-facing: route outputs are treated as evidence objects that may be challenged, stress-tested, refreshed, preference-qualified, or refused. The project is better for this thesis objective because it exposes why a recommendation is or is not justified; it is not claiming universal superiority as a route engine, fleet optimiser, traffic predictor, or emissions regulator.

### AW1. The Core Problem In Literature Terms

The project sits at the intersection of five research traditions. The first is shortest-path and route-search theory, beginning with Dijkstra's nonnegative shortest-path algorithm [Dijkstra 1959](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390), heuristic search with A* [Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael 1968](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136), alternative-path enumeration [Yen 1971](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.17.11.712), and efficient k-shortest-path enumeration [Eppstein 1998](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539795290477). The second is road-network engineering, including contraction hierarchies [Geisberger et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-68552-4_24), customizable route planning [Delling et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.2014.0579), and deployed routing engines such as OSRM [Luxen and Vetter 2011](https://doi.org/10.1145/2093973.2094062), [Project OSRM 2026, OSRM v26.4.0 API docs](https://project-osrm.org/docs/v26.4.0/), openrouteservice [openrouteservice API documentation](https://giscience.github.io/openrouteservice/api-reference/endpoints/), and GraphHopper [GraphHopper API documentation](https://docs.graphhopper.com/openapi). The third is multiobjective, robust, and stochastic decision-making, where a route is not only a distance-minimising path but a compromise between cost, time, emissions, tail risk, evidence confidence, and preference support. The fourth is decision analysis, value of information, preference elicitation, and metareasoning [Howard 1966](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074), [Russell and Wefald 1991](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(91)90015-C), [Frazier, Powell, and Dayanik 2009](https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.1080.0314), [Settles 2009](https://burrsettles.com/pub/settles.activelearning_20090109.pdf). The fifth is selective decision-making and reproducible research, where refusing a decision can be rational [Chow 1970](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406), [Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/7073-selective-classification-for-deep-neural-networks), and where the evidence chain should be findable, inspectable, and replayable [Wilkinson et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18), [Peng 2011](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1213847), [Wilson et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001745).

The unresolved gap is that these traditions usually optimise different objects. A route engine optimises a path. A VRP system optimises a plan. A robust optimiser optimises an uncertain mathematical instance. A preference-elicitation method optimises what question to ask. A selective classifier decides whether to predict. A reproducibility framework records evidence. This project combines those objects into one local thesis system: it asks whether a freight route recommendation is certified enough to show, what evidence would most improve certification, which preferences remain unresolved, and which typed reason explains refusal.

### AW2. Standard Shortest-Path Mathematics And The Project Deviation

The academic shortest-path baseline is normally written as a scalar path problem. Given a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), origin \(s\), and destination \(t\), the goal is:

```text
p* = argmin_{p in P(s,t)} sum_{e in p} c_e
```

This is the mathematical object solved by Dijkstra-style and A*-style methods when the edge weights are known and the decision objective is scalar. It is also the object approximated or accelerated by many road-network methods after preprocessing. That object is necessary but insufficient for the thesis. A freight recommendation is not justified merely because it is shortest under one cost vector. It may be invalidated by unrefined candidates, stale tolls, weak traffic evidence, preference ambiguity, or a route whose average cost is good but tail risk is unacceptable.

The project therefore changes the decision object from "find one shortest path" to "produce a conditional decision package". In thesis notation:

```text
K_raw = candidate_routes(G, s, t, mechanisms, budgets)
K_refined = DCCS(K_raw, evidence_state, preference_state, certification_state)
C = certify(K_refined, sampled_worlds, preferences, thresholds)
decision = singleton(C) or certified_set(C) or typed_abstention(C)
```

That is the central algorithmic deviation. The project does still use shortest-path logic, but it wraps it in a decision-critical evidence layer. This is why a reader should not evaluate the project as if its novelty were "Dijkstra but slightly changed". The meaningful change is that a route is not the final result; a route plus its certificate, alternatives, stress worlds, unresolved ambiguity, action ledger, and artifact provenance is the final result.

The implementation preserves the shortest-path baseline in code rather than pretending the project invented graph search. The k-shortest module uses a Dijkstra/A* hybrid with budgets and path-state constraints, so it can act as a bounded candidate generator inside the larger decision system:

```python
def _dijkstra_shortest_path(
    *,
    adjacency: dict[str, tuple[tuple[str, float], ...]],
    start: str,
    goal: str,
    banned_nodes: set[str] | None = None,
    banned_edges: set[tuple[str, str]] | None = None,
    max_hops: int = 220,
    explored_counter: list[int] | None = None,
    max_state_budget: int | None = None,
    max_repeat_per_node: int = 1,
    max_cost_limit: float | None = None,
    transition_state_fn: TransitionStateFn | None = None,
    heuristic_fn: HeuristicFn | None = None,
    deadline_monotonic_s: float | None = None,
) -> PathResult:
    ...
```

The important thesis point is not that this is a new shortest-path algorithm. The important point is that candidate generation is bounded and instrumented so later stages can say whether search was sufficient. In the canonical scalar shortest-path formulation, the path is the optimisation output. This project treats the path result as a claim that can be challenged.

### AW3. A*, Yen, Eppstein, And Why Candidate Enumeration Was Not Enough

A* improves point-to-point search by using a heuristic \(h(v)\) to guide expansion:

```text
f(v) = g(v) + h(v)
```

Yen-style k-shortest paths and Eppstein-style enumeration then generalise single-path search into ranked alternatives. Those methods are relevant because a freight decision needs alternatives. However, the academic k-shortest objective is still usually rank-oriented: return the first \(k\) loopless paths under a scalar edge cost. That does not answer whether the returned set contains the alternatives that matter for certification. Two paths can be adjacent in a k-shortest list but almost identical in road overlap, fuel exposure, evidence weakness, or preference implications. Conversely, a slightly longer route can matter because it uses a different corridor, avoids a weak evidence segment, or changes the emissions-risk tradeoff.

The project therefore changes alternative enumeration into Decision-Critical Candidate Search (DCCS) triage. It uses route alternatives as raw material, then asks which candidates are worth refining for the decision. The DCCS configuration shows this explicitly:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DCCSConfig:
    mode: str = "bootstrap"
    pipeline_variant: str = "dccs"
    search_budget: int = 3
    bootstrap_seed_size: int = 2
    refinement_cost_floor: float = 1.0
    near_duplicate_threshold: float = 0.82
    objective_gap_weight: float = 1.0
    mechanism_gap_weight: float = 0.45
    overlap_penalty_weight: float = 1.25
    stretch_penalty_weight: float = 0.5
    cost_weight: float = 1.0
```

The `near_duplicate_threshold = 0.82` is a thesis-specific engineering prior, not a universal graph-theory constant and not a proven optimum. It encodes the repository's stance that UK road alternatives often share unavoidable trunk-road segments, so the system should avoid filling the candidate set with same-corridor variants without deleting every high-overlap route. The thesis should treat this as a tunable design choice whose sensitivity should be evaluated when making performance claims.

The DCCS score also deviates from a k-shortest ranking because it divides predicted decision benefit by a penalty/cost term. The simplified excerpt below follows the actual score shape in `backend/app/decision_critical.py`, where gains include objective closeness, mechanism diversity, flip probability, time preservation, criticality, proxy/audit/preference value, possible/necessary-best changes, search completeness, and hidden-challenger risk:

```python
gain = (
    (config.objective_gap_weight * record.objective_gap)
    + (config.mechanism_gap_weight * record.mechanism_gap * support_gate)
    + (config.challenger_gain_weight * record.flip_probability * support_gate)
    + (0.25 * (1.0 - record.overlap))
    + (config.challenger_time_preservation_weight * record.time_preservation_bonus * time_bonus_scale)
    + (config.challenger_candidate_criticality_weight * criticality_score)
    + (config.challenger_expected_proxy_value_weight * record.expected_proxy_value)
    + (config.challenger_expected_audit_value_weight * record.expected_audit_value)
    + (config.challenger_preference_sensitivity_weight * record.preference_query_sensitivity)
    + (config.challenger_possible_best_change_weight * record.changes_possible_best_probability)
    + (config.challenger_necessary_best_change_weight * record.changes_necessary_best_probability)
    + (config.challenger_search_completeness_weight * record.search_completeness_contribution)
    + (config.challenger_hidden_challenger_weight * record.hidden_challenger_risk)
)
penalty = (
    (config.overlap_penalty_weight * record.overlap)
    + (config.stretch_penalty_weight * max(0.0, record.stretch - 1.0))
    + (config.cost_weight * record.predicted_refine_cost)
)
score = gain / max(1e-9, penalty)
```

This is closer to bounded metareasoning than to pure route enumeration. The academic norm asks "which path is next in the sorted order?" The project asks "which candidate is most likely to change or strengthen the final certified decision per unit of effort?" That is the correct question for a thesis evidence system because compute and evidence collection are part of the method.

Publication citation bridge: DCCS can also be connected to algorithm-selection literature without claiming a new shortest-path primitive. Rice formalised the algorithm-selection problem as choosing a method conditional on instance features and performance criteria [Rice 1976](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2458(08)60520-3), and Kotthoff surveys feature-based algorithm selection for combinatorial search [Kotthoff 2014](https://doi.org/10.1609/AIMAG.V35I3.2460). The repo adaptation is narrower: it selects which route candidate or evidence action is worth the next refinement step, so the paper should call it decision-critical computational triage rather than a general algorithm-selection theorem.

### AW4. Road-Network Speedups And Why The Project Delegates Route Engines

Contraction hierarchies, customizable route planning, and modern routing engines show that large road-network queries can be made fast through preprocessing, hierarchy, and careful graph engineering. OSRM is a deployed example of high-performance OpenStreetMap routing [Luxen and Vetter 2011](https://doi.org/10.1145/2093973.2094062), [Project OSRM 2026, OSRM v26.4.0 API docs](https://project-osrm.org/docs/v26.4.0/). The public openrouteservice API ecosystem includes directions, isochrones, matrices, POIs, and optimization; this repository uses ORS as a directions/reference-route source [openrouteservice API documentation](https://giscience.github.io/openrouteservice/api-reference/endpoints/). GraphHopper exposes routing, matrices, route optimisation, geocoding, map matching, and route-optimization APIs [GraphHopper API documentation](https://docs.graphhopper.com/openapi).

The project does not compete with these engines at the preprocessing layer. That is a deliberate design decision. Rebuilding contraction hierarchies or a production-grade routing engine would produce a large infrastructure project but would weaken the thesis contribution: the hard research question here is not whether a graph can be searched, but whether a route recommendation can be audited, challenged, refreshed, preference-qualified, and refused. The project uses route engines and local graph assets as evidence providers, then adds the evidence-control layer that route engines normally do not expose.

That design fixes a common weakness in route-engine-only systems for thesis purposes. A route API can return a plausible path, but it usually does not expose a local, source-readable certificate explaining hidden-challenger risk, evidence freshness, preference ambiguity, VOI action ranking, or typed abstention. WhatIf Freight Router adds those objects in the local codebase and artifacts. It is better aligned with a publishable applied thesis because the contribution is inspectable rather than hidden behind a product API.

### AW5. Multiobjective Shortest Paths, Pareto Sets, And Why Scalarisation Is Not Enough

Freight routing is naturally multiobjective. A route may be fast, cheap, low-emission, low-risk, operationally supported, or preference-compatible, but these objectives can conflict. Multiobjective shortest-path research studies efficient paths under vector costs:

```text
c(p) = (duration(p), cost(p), emissions(p), risk(p), ...)
p_i dominates p_j iff c_m(p_i) <= c_m(p_j) for every objective m
and c_m(p_i) < c_m(p_j) for at least one objective.
```

The repository uses this Pareto idea for route candidates through tuple-vector dominance with tolerance:

```python
def dominates(a: tuple[float, ...], b: tuple[float, ...], *, tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    if len(a) != len(b):
        raise ValueError("dimension mismatch")
    le_all = True
    lt_any = False
    for ai, bi in zip(a, b, strict=True):
        if ai > bi + tol:
            le_all = False
            break
        if ai < bi - tol:
            lt_any = True
    return le_all and lt_any
```

However, the project intentionally does not stop at Pareto filtering. A pure Pareto set can become too large and can still be under-explained. A scalar weighted sum is easier to display:

```text
U(p; w) = w_time time(p) + w_cost cost(p) + w_co2 co2(p) + w_risk risk(p)
```

but it collapses evidence confidence, preference ambiguity, and model support into one number. That is dangerous in a thesis because it can make a route appear objectively best when it is merely best under one unchallenged weight vector. WhatIf Freight Router therefore separates vector-objective dominance from certification and preference support. The route can be Pareto-efficient and still uncertified. That is not a failure; it is the key difference between route ranking and route justification.

### AW6. Robust Optimisation, Stochastic Routing, And Bounded Certification

Robust shortest-path and stochastic routing research ask how routing should behave when costs are uncertain. Robust optimisation often seeks a route that performs well under all costs in an uncertainty set, or minimises worst-case regret. Stochastic programming often optimises expectation, probability of constraint satisfaction, or sampled scenarios. This project borrows the motivation but avoids overclaiming a theorem-complete robust optimum.

The project's certification object is bounded and empirical:

```text
Omega_hat = {sampled evidence worlds available to this run}
winner_fraction(r) = count_{omega in Omega_hat}[r wins in omega] / |Omega_hat|
certificate = f(winner_fraction, pairwise gaps, frontier mass, support state, thresholds)
```

This is closer to sample-average evidence certification than to universal robust optimisation. The distinction is essential. The project can show that a recommendation is stable under the recorded stress worlds and support assumptions. It cannot prove that the recommendation is globally optimal under every possible traffic, toll, fuel, carbon, weather, and incident regime. That limitation is a strength for thesis credibility because the system records the boundary rather than hiding it.

The confidence-sequence code makes this bounded nature explicit. It uses a conservative anytime Hoeffding-style interval with a summable error schedule:

```python
def anytime_hoeffding_interval(
    *,
    success_count: int,
    sample_count: int,
    delta: float,
) -> ConfidenceInterval:
    delta_n = delta / (sample_count * (sample_count + 1))
    radius = math.sqrt(math.log(2.0 / delta_n) / (2.0 * sample_count))
    center = success_count / sample_count
    return ConfidenceInterval(
        lower=max(0.0, center - radius),
        upper=min(1.0, center + radius),
        center=center,
        radius=radius,
    )
```

The academic connection is to confidence sequences and optional-stopping-safe inference [Howard et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1214/20-AOS1991). The project's implementation is deliberately conservative and transparent: it is not a conformal predictor [Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer 2005](https://doi.org/10.1007/b106715), not a full empirical-Bernstein procedure [Maurer and Pontil 2009](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.3740), and not a distribution-free guarantee over future road states. It is a documented certificate over the sampled evidence universe used by the run.

### AW7. CVaR, Tail Risk, And The Project's Freight-Specific Risk Objective

Risk-sensitive routing often needs more than expected cost. Conditional value at risk (CVaR) is a standard tail-risk measure formalised in optimisation by Rockafellar and Uryasev [Rockafellar and Uryasev 2000](https://doi.org/10.21314/JOR.2000.038). For losses \(L\), the population version is:

```text
CVaR_alpha(L) = E[L | L >= VaR_alpha(L)]
```

The project implements an empirical version in `risk_model.py` by integrating the empirical quantile tail. It then uses route-specific normalisation so duration, money, emissions, and risk are comparable without pretending they are the same physical quantity:

```python
def normalized_objective_components(
    *,
    duration_s: float,
    monetary_cost: float,
    emissions_kg: float,
    distance_km: float | None,
    vehicle_type: str | None = None,
    vehicle_bucket: str | None = None,
    corridor_bucket: str | None = None,
    day_kind: str | None = None,
    local_time_slot: str | None = None,
) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    dist = max(1.0, float(distance_km or 0.0))
    refs = load_risk_normalization_reference(
        vehicle_type=vehicle_type,
        vehicle_bucket=vehicle_bucket,
        corridor_bucket=corridor_bucket,
        day_kind=day_kind,
        local_time_slot=local_time_slot,
    )
    return (
        max(0.0, float(duration_s)) / max(dist * refs.duration_s_per_km, 1e-9),
        max(0.0, float(monetary_cost)) / max(dist * refs.monetary_gbp_per_km, 1e-9),
        max(0.0, float(emissions_kg)) / max(dist * refs.emissions_kg_per_km, 1e-9),
    )
```

The deviation from the academic norm is that CVaR is not used as a standalone optimiser. It is used as part of a decision package that also contains evidence support, preference support, and abstention. That is justified because a freight operator does not only need "the route with best CVaR"; they need to know whether the tail-risk claim is supported by evidence and whether unresolved preferences can overturn the recommendation.

### AW8. Eco-Routing, Pollution Routing, And Freight Emissions Standards

Green freight and eco-routing literature shows that the shortest or fastest route is often not the lowest-emission route. The Pollution-Routing Problem connects speed, load, fuel, and emissions to routing decisions [Bektas and Laporte 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trb.2011.02.004). Green road-freight surveys describe how freight routing, vehicle choice, speed, consolidation, and emissions interact [Demir, Bektas, and Laporte 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2013.12.033). Eco-routing work also shows that fuel and emission outcomes depend on speed profiles, road grade, congestion, and vehicle characteristics [Ericsson, Larsson, and Brundell-Freij 2006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2006.10.001), [Ahn and Rakha 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trd.2013.09.006), [Boriboonsomsin and Barth 2009](https://doi.org/10.3141/2139-03).

The project's freight-emissions layer is designed around that literature but keeps the thesis claim bounded. It does not claim to be HBEFA [HBEFA methodology](https://www.hbefa.net/en/methodology), COPERT [COPERT methodology](https://copert.emisia.com/copert/methodology/), MOVES [USEPA 2024, MOVES5](https://www.epa.gov/moves/latest-version-motor-vehicle-emission-simulator-moves), or a regulatory-grade emissions model. It uses a local fuel/energy model and terrain physics as a transparent evidence approximation. The real implementation reflects this by deriving speed from segment duration, converting route grade into the calibration surface unit, clamping inputs to the available calibration axes, deriving load factor from the vehicle profile, applying regional fuel-price context, and interpolating calibrated fuel or energy surfaces:

```python
def segment_energy_and_emissions(
    *,
    vehicle: VehicleProfile,
    emissions_context: EmissionsContext,
    distance_km: float,
    duration_s: float,
    grade: float,
    fuel_price_multiplier: float,
    departure_time_utc: datetime | None = None,
    route_centroid_lat: float | None = None,
    route_centroid_lon: float | None = None,
) -> SegmentEnergyResult:
    speed_kmh = (distance_km / (duration_s / 3600.0)) if duration_s > 0 else 0.0
    grade_pct = float(grade) * 100.0
    consumption_surface = load_fuel_consumption_surface()
    snapshot = load_fuel_price_snapshot(as_of_utc=departure_time_utc)
    klass = _vehicle_class(vehicle, emissions_context)
    load_factor = _derived_load_factor(vehicle, klass=klass)
    load_factor = _clamp(
        load_factor,
        consumption_surface.axes.load_factor[0],
        consumption_surface.axes.load_factor[-1],
    )
    speed_value = _clamp(speed_kmh, consumption_surface.axes.speed_kmh[0], consumption_surface.axes.speed_kmh[-1])
    grade_value = _clamp(grade_pct, consumption_surface.axes.grade_pct[0], consumption_surface.axes.grade_pct[-1])
    temp_value = _clamp(
        float(emissions_context.ambient_temp_c),
        consumption_surface.axes.ambient_temp_c[0],
        consumption_surface.axes.ambient_temp_c[-1],
    )
    region_mult = _regional_multiplier(snapshot.regional_multipliers, lat=route_centroid_lat, lon=route_centroid_lon)
```

The terrain physics layer uses physical force terms as a transparent route modifier. The excerpt below is from the actual duration-multiplier logic rather than a regulatory emissions simulator:

```python
G_MPS2 = 9.80665
AIR_DENSITY_KG_M3 = 1.225

rolling_force = params.mass_kg * G_MPS2 * params.c_rr
aero_force = 0.5 * AIR_DENSITY_KG_M3 * params.drag_area_m2 * (v_ms ** 2)
grade_force = params.mass_kg * G_MPS2 * grade
baseline_force = max(250.0, rolling_force + aero_force)
raw_force = rolling_force + aero_force + max(grade_force, -0.85 * baseline_force)
uplift = raw_force / baseline_force
if grade < 0.0:
    downhill_recovery = min(abs(grade) * params.regen_efficiency, 0.32)
    uplift = max(0.72, uplift + downhill_recovery)
```

This is better suited to thesis evidence than a black-box emissions API because the assumptions can be inspected. It is informed by carbon-accounting and policy contexts such as ISO 14083 [ISO 14083](https://www.iso.org/standard/78864.html), UK greenhouse-gas conversion factors [DESNZ conversion factors 2025](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/greenhouse-gas-reporting-conversion-factors-2025), and UK carbon valuation guidance [UK carbon valuation guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/valuing-greenhouse-gas-emissions-in-policy-appraisal/valuation-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-for-policy-appraisal-and-evaluation), while not claiming formal ISO 14083 compliance, GLEC-style chain accounting, or regulatory model certification.

### AW9. Value Of Information, Metareasoning, And The VOI-AD2R Deviation

Classical value of information asks how much expected utility would improve if information were observed before choosing an action [Howard 1966](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074). Metareasoning asks whether computation itself is worth doing [Russell and Wefald 1991](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(91)90015-C). Knowledge-gradient policies ask which measurement has the highest expected value for future decisions [Frazier, Powell, and Dayanik 2009](https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.1080.0314). Active-learning surveys explain analogous query-selection principles for labels and models [Settles 2009](https://burrsettles.com/pub/settles.activelearning_20090109.pdf).

The project adapts these ideas to route certification. It does not compute exact global VOI over all future worlds. Instead, it uses a deterministic myopic value-per-cost controller over the action families the backend can actually take: refine search, refresh evidence, resample worlds, query preferences, or stop. The scoring equation is explicit:

```python
q_score = (
    (cfg.lambda_certificate * predicted_winner_lcb_gain(scored_action))
    + (cfg.lambda_margin * predicted_gap_lcb_gain(scored_action))
    + (cfg.lambda_frontier * predicted_boundary_contraction(scored_action))
    + (cfg.lambda_radius_or_flip_budget * predicted_radius_or_flip_budget_gain(scored_action))
    + (cfg.lambda_unresolved_mass * predicted_unresolved_mass_reduction(scored_action))
    + (cfg.lambda_preference_ambiguity * predicted_preference_ambiguity_reduction(scored_action))
) / (cost + cfg.epsilon)
```

The default weights encode the thesis judgement about what matters most:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class VOIConfig:
    certificate_threshold: float = 0.67
    stop_threshold: float = 0.02
    search_budget: int = 3
    evidence_budget: int = 2
    max_iterations: int = 8
    top_k_refine: int = 2
    resample_increment: int = 25
    lambda_certificate: float = 0.60
    lambda_margin: float = 0.25
    lambda_frontier: float = 0.15
    lambda_radius_or_flip_budget: float = 0.02
    lambda_unresolved_mass: float = 0.02
    lambda_preference_ambiguity: float = 0.02
```

The higher certificate and margin weights are justified because the thesis outcome is a certified route decision, not generic model improvement. Frontier contraction matters because hidden challengers can invalidate the winner. Lower preference and unresolved-mass weights do not mean they are unimportant; they mean they are secondary unless they are predicted to affect certification. This is a meaningful deviation from standard active learning, which often optimises label uncertainty or expected model change. Here the target is decision certification under bounded budget.

### AW10. Preference Elicitation And Necessary/Possible Winner Logic

Preference elicitation literature studies how to ask questions that reduce uncertainty over a user's utility function. In route recommendation, this matters because a route that is fastest may not be preferred when emissions, tolls, support confidence, or tail risk matter. Multi-attribute utility theory provides the general foundation [Keeney and Raiffa 1993](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139174084). Incremental utility elicitation and minimax-regret decision criteria motivate asking targeted questions only when they can affect the decision [Wang and Boutilier 2003](https://research.google/pubs/incremental-utility-elicitation-with-the-minimax-regret-decision-criterion/).

The project adapts this to a necessary/possible route-winner view. The equations below are the conceptual decision-analysis target; the implementation records compatible-set summaries, probabilities, route-id sets, shrinkage traces, and invariants rather than claiming a complete symbolic proof over every possible continuous weight vector:

```text
W = compatible preference weights after observed constraints
necessary_best(r) = for all w in W, r is best under w
possible_best(r) = exists w in W such that r is best under w
```

That is stronger for route evidence than asking a generic survey question because every preference query is tied to whether the certified decision can change. The implementation stores preference state and uses it in DCCS and VOI rather than treating preferences as a one-off UI setting. The thesis should phrase this as implemented necessary/possible-winner evidence summaries, not as a theorem that exhaustively enumerates an arbitrary continuous preference space. That fixes a common weakness in simple weighted-route planners: the chosen weights look precise even when the user has not actually supplied enough information to justify them.

### AW11. Selective Decision, Reject Options, And Typed Abstention

Selective decision literature argues that a system can improve reliability by abstaining when confidence is insufficient. Chow's reject-option classifier formalises the error/reject tradeoff [Chow 1970](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406). Selective classification later developed neural and distributional variants [Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/7073-selective-classification-for-deep-neural-networks). Route recommendation needs a more diagnostic form of abstention because the failure cause determines the remedy.

The project therefore uses typed abstention rather than a single "low confidence" flag:

```python
TYPED_ABSTENTION_REASONS = {
    "uncertified_due_to_search": "Expand route search or refine challengers.",
    "uncertified_due_to_evidence": "Refresh stale or proxy evidence.",
    "uncertified_due_to_preference": "Ask a preference question.",
    "uncertified_due_to_out_of_support_world_model": "Do not extrapolate beyond support.",
    "uncertified_due_to_budget": "Increase or reallocate budget.",
    "uncertified_due_to_model_assumption": "Review model assumptions before deciding.",
}
```

This is not just UI polish. It is an algorithmic contract. A hidden-challenger failure should not be repaired by asking the user a preference question. A stale fuel-price failure should not be repaired by expanding k-shortest search. A preference ambiguity failure should not be repaired by pretending evidence is stale. Typed abstention fixes this by mapping failure mode to next action.

### AW12. Existing Open-Source Routing Engines

OSRM is a high-performance routing engine built around OSM data and preprocessing for fast shortest-path queries [Luxen and Vetter 2011](https://doi.org/10.1145/2093973.2094062), [Project OSRM 2026, OSRM v26.4.0 API docs](https://project-osrm.org/docs/v26.4.0/). It is excellent infrastructure for generating routes, but it is not designed as a thesis evidence-certification system. It can tell a client about routes, durations, alternatives, and annotations, but it does not expose this repository's DCCS candidate-criticality ledger, sampled evidence-world certificate, VOI action score, preference shrinkage trace, or typed abstention reason.

openrouteservice exposes broad routing and geospatial services, including directions, isochrones, matrices, POIs, and optimization in its public API ecosystem [openrouteservice API documentation](https://giscience.github.io/openrouteservice/api-reference/endpoints/). This repository uses ORS as an external directions/reference-route provider, but its public API contract is still service-oriented rather than thesis-evidence-oriented. WhatIf Freight Router is more useful for the thesis because the evidence states and failure modes are local code and local artifacts.

GraphHopper exposes route planning, matrices, route optimisation, map matching, geocoding, route-optimization APIs, and vehicle/profile options [GraphHopper API documentation](https://docs.graphhopper.com/openapi). The thesis project does not need to outperform GraphHopper as a routing platform. It instead adds a research wrapper that asks whether the returned or locally generated alternatives are decision-certified under the evidence available to the project.

The common issue across these engines is not poor routing. It is that their public-facing objective is route service delivery, while the thesis objective is inspectable decision justification. The project fixes that gap by making the route result conditional on certification and by preserving the chain of evidence.

### AW13. Existing Commercial Routing And Logistics Platforms

Commercial systems such as Google Routes [Google Routes API documentation](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/routes), Google Route Optimization [Google Route Optimization documentation](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/route-optimization/overview), HERE Tour Planning [HERE Tour Planning documentation](https://docs.here.com/tour-planning/docs/introduction-tour-planning), the ArcGIS Vehicle Routing Problem layer [ArcGIS Network Analyst VRP documentation](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/network-analyst/make-vehicle-routing-problem-analysis-layer.htm), and PTV xTour [PTV xTour API documentation](https://api.cloud.ptvgroup.com/manual/Content/API-Documentation/xtour/API_Documentation.html) solve mature operational problems. Collectively, these systems can route vehicles, sequence jobs, satisfy operational constraints, optimise fleets, and expose enterprise APIs.

The project should not claim to be operationally broader than those systems. Its advantage is research inspectability. Their public APIs and documentation generally do not expose this repository's local proof objects, source-readable candidate ledgers, and replayable decision artifacts. WhatIf Freight Router is better for this thesis because the codebase contains the evidence model, abstention categories, action scores, docs checks, artifact manifests, and negative-result ledgers. A commercial product may be more complete for deployment; this project is more complete as an auditable local research artifact.

This distinction is the right one to defend in the thesis. The project does not need to show that it beats Google or HERE on global routing quality. It needs to show that a route recommendation can be made more scientifically accountable. The codebase does that by recording why it decided, why it did not decide, and what further action would matter.

### AW14. Vehicle Routing Problem Literature And Why This Is Not A Full VRP Thesis

The Vehicle Routing Problem begins with fleet-level planning rather than single route certification. The classic VRP asks how a fleet should serve many customers under capacity and cost constraints, with foundational work by Dantzig and Ramser's truck-dispatching formulation [Dantzig and Ramser 1959](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.6.1.80) and later savings heuristics by Clarke and Wright [Clarke and Wright 1964](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.12.4.568). Modern VRP surveys and handbooks cover capacity, time windows, pickup and delivery, stochastic variants, green VRP, and rich operational constraints. Laporte's fifty-year survey gives the historical and methodological context for why VRP variants are a mature field rather than a missing feature list [Laporte 2009](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1090.0301). Braysy and Gendreau's VRPTW survey papers explain why time-window variants usually need specialised construction and metaheuristic search [Braysy and Gendreau 2005a](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1030.0056), [Braysy and Gendreau 2005b](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1030.0057). Those are important references because freight systems often become VRP systems.

Freight planning is also broader than VRP. Service-network design models carrier service selection, schedules, terminal operations, consolidation, and routing at a tactical network level [Crainic 2000](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0377-2217(99)00233-7). Intermodal freight research covers rail-road and multimodal planning opportunities that a road-only route-decision prototype does not solve [Macharis and Bontekoning 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0377-2217(03)00161-9). That comparison helps the paper avoid a weak overclaim. The repo is not a freight-network-design solver, not an intermodal planning suite, and not a VRPTW metaheuristic. Its stronger and more defensible contribution is the route-level evidence contract that can sit below, beside, or inside those larger planning systems.

This repository deliberately narrows the target. A full VRP thesis would optimise many vehicles, jobs, depots, shifts, and time windows. WhatIf Freight Router instead asks a route-level evidence question: given a route recommendation and alternatives, is the recommendation certified under evidence and preference uncertainty? That is narrower, but not weaker for the thesis. It avoids hiding the novel contribution inside fleet scheduling complexity. It also makes the evidence chain inspectable enough to audit.

The relationship can be stated as:

```text
VRP: choose a fleet plan over many jobs and vehicles.
WhatIf Freight Router: certify or refuse a route recommendation under evidence, risk, and preference uncertainty.
```

This narrower scope is a strength because it makes the contribution measurable and source-readable.

### AW15. Algorithmic Deviations Summary

The table below summarises the main places where the project changes the academic norm.

| Area | Academic or product norm | Project adaptation | Why the adaptation is justified |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shortest path | Return \(p^* = argmin_p \sum c_e\). | Treat paths as evidence candidates inside a certification pipeline. | The thesis needs justified recommendations, not only paths. |
| A* and k-shortest | Use heuristic or ranked enumeration to find paths efficiently. | Use bounded generation plus DCCS to refine decision-critical challengers. | The most decision-relevant challenger is not always the next scalar-shortest path. |
| Pareto filtering | Return nondominated routes under vector objectives. | Combine Pareto evidence with certification, preference state, and typed abstention. | A nondominated route can still be uncertified. |
| Scalar utility | Rank routes by one weighted score. | Keep weights, evidence support, risk, and preference ambiguity separate. | Collapsing all uncertainty into one score hides failure causes. |
| Robust routing | Optimise worst-case or regret over uncertainty sets. | Certify over bounded sampled evidence worlds and record support limits. | The code can audit the worlds it used without overclaiming universal robustness. |
| CVaR | Optimise a tail-risk objective. | Use empirical tail risk as one component of route evidence. | Tail risk matters, but certification also needs evidence and preference support. |
| VOI | Compute expected value of information or computation. | Use deterministic myopic value-per-cost action scores. | Exact global VOI is mis-scoped; bounded action choice is implementable and inspectable. |
| Preference elicitation | Ask questions to learn utility. | Ask only when preference ambiguity can affect route certification. | Query burden is tied to decision value. |
| Selective classification | Abstain under low confidence. | Abstain with typed route-specific failure reasons. | Each route failure mode has a different remedy. |
| Reproducibility | Publish data/code or notebooks. | Maintain checked docs, manifests, run artifacts, negative results, and a theorem map. | Thesis claims must remain traceable after code changes. |

### AW16. Why The Project Addresses Gaps Relative To The Thesis Evidence Contract

The project addresses a gap relative to this thesis evidence contract. OSRM, openrouteservice, and GraphHopper can return good routes, but public route-engine documentation generally does not expose this repository's exact local proof objects, sampled evidence certificates, VOI traces, preference-state traces, typed abstention reasons, theorem maps, and replayable artifact bundles.

The project addresses a commercial-product evidence gap by making the reasoning inspectable. Google, HERE, ArcGIS, PTV, and similar tools are valuable because they operationalise routing at scale. Public commercial-product documentation generally does not expose this repository's exact local proof objects, sampled evidence certificates, VOI traces, preference-state traces, typed abstention reasons, theorem maps, and replayable artifact bundles. This repository is therefore more appropriate for academic evidence because the calculations are visible.

The project fixes a scalar-ranking gap by preserving the distinction between objective quality and evidential support. A route can have low travel time and still fail certification. A route can be low emission and still rely on weak proxy evidence. A route can be cheap and still be preference-ambiguous. The code preserves these distinctions rather than flattening them.

The project fixes a robust-optimisation communication gap by making the uncertainty boundary explicit. Instead of saying "robust" and implying universal protection, the project records sampled worlds, confidence intervals, stress states, and abstention reasons. That is more honest and easier to defend.

The project fixes a preference-elicitation gap by tying questions to certification. It does not ask preferences for their own sake. It asks when the answer can shrink the possible-winner set or change the action decision.

The project fixes a reproducibility gap by making docs checks and artifact indexes part of the system. The thesis can point to the exact route evidence, API response, generated artifacts, negative gates, and consistency checks that support a claim.
