The repo therefore implements narrower, explicit veto and guard concepts instead of a full hidden outranking relation:

```python
# backend/app/preference_queries.py
PreferenceQueryType = Literal["pairwise", "threshold", "ratio", "veto", "time_guard"]
```

This is a stronger thesis design because every hard preference condition appears as a typed constraint with a trace, not as a number buried inside a concordance matrix. The final-paper claim can be:

```text
Unlike classical AHP/TOPSIS/VIKOR deployments that mainly return a final ranking,
and unlike outranking methods that require a separate threshold model,
WhatIf Freight Router treats ranking as one layer in a certification-oriented
decision-aiding pipeline.
```

Useful transport-specific MCDA citations include MAMCA for multi-actor transport decisions [Macharis et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2012.08.008), range-based MAMCA under uncertainty [Macharis et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2017.06.036), and recent MCDA work in urban freight and logistics [Alvarez Gallo and Maheut 2023](https://doi.org/10.3390/math11194089). The repo is better aligned with a publishable freight-decision problem because it preserves why a recommendation was made, why it might not be certifiable, and what information would improve the decision.

### AX44. Imprecise Preferences, Robust Ordinal Regression, And Compatible-Set Traces

The preference subsystem is linked to robust ordinal regression and imprecise-preference MCDA, not only to minimax regret. UTA learns additive utility functions from ordinal comparisons using linear programming [Jacquet-Lagreze and Siskos 1982](https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-2217(82)90155-2). Robust ordinal regression generalises this idea by considering the set of all value functions compatible with the decision maker's preference information, rather than selecting one fitted utility model too early [Greco, Mousseau, and Slowinski 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2007.08.013). That literature is directly relevant because the codebase records compatible-set summaries, possible-best routes, necessary-best routes, and shrinkage traces.

```python
# backend/app/preference_state.py
class CompatibleSetSummary(BaseModel):
    route_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    compatible_set_size: int = Field(default=0, ge=0)
    compatible_set_volume_proxy: float = Field(default=1.0, ge=0.0)
    necessary_best_prob: float = Field(default=0.0, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    possible_best_prob: float = Field(default=1.0, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    necessary_best_route_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    possible_best_route_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
```

The important paper claim is that the implementation uses an engineering approximation of this robust-preference idea. It does not solve the full continuous robust ordinal regression problem. Instead, it preserves the same scientific discipline: do not collapse incomplete preferences into a single utility vector unless the evidence justifies doing so. Each accepted answer can only shrink the recorded compatible evidence when before/after summaries are supplied:

```python
# backend/app/preference_update.py
if after_size_int > before_size_int:
    raise ValueError("valid preference updates cannot increase compatible set size")
if after_volume_value > before_volume_value + 1e-12:
    raise ValueError("valid preference updates cannot increase compatible-set volume")
```

The paper-level equation is:

```text
C_{t+1} approx C_t intersect constraint(answer_t)
|C_{t+1}| <= |C_t|
volume(C_{t+1}) <= volume(C_t)
```

Necessary and possible winner language is linked to computational social choice. Konczak and Lang define possible and necessary winners under incomplete preferences [Konczak and Lang 2005](https://www.eecs.harvard.edu/cs286r/courses/fall11/papers/KL05.pdf), while Xia and Conitzer characterise the complexity of possible/necessary winner problems for common voting rules [Xia and Conitzer 2011](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.3186). Pini and coauthors connect incompleteness, incomparability, and elicitation in preference aggregation [Pini et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2010.11.009). The repo borrows the distinction, not the exact voting-rule theorem. "Necessary-best" means necessary under the inspected compatible preference evidence; "possible-best" means still possible under stored summaries. That caveat is publishable because it prevents overclaiming.

### AX45. Trace-Based Explainability, Recourse, And Why A Final Rank Is Not Enough

The explainability claim is explicit. The system is not explainable because it prints a natural-language sentence after ranking. It is explainable because the decision is decomposed into auditable objects: objective normalisation, scalar score terms, Pareto filtering, candidate criticality, compatible preference state, decision boundary, root-cause tags, and operational remediation evidence. This aligns with Miller's argument that explanations are contrastive, selective, and socially situated [Miller 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2018.07.007), Ribeiro et al.'s emphasis on local explanations for trust [Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin 2016](https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939778), and Guidotti et al.'s survey of explanation methods for opaque decision systems [Guidotti et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1145/3236009).

The code's strongest explainability evidence is intrinsic trace design, not model-agnostic post-hoc explanation. The preference query trace exposes query history, shrinkage trace, compatible-set summary, invariants, contradiction record, irrelevance flag, and provenance:

```python
# backend/app/preference_runtime.py
return {
    "schema_version": "preference-query-trace-v1",
    "selected_route_id": effective_selected_route_id,
    "terminal_type": preference_state.terminal_type,
    "query_count": int(summary.get("query_count", 0) or 0),
    "query_history": _serialize_records(preference_state.query_history),
    "shrinkage_trace": shrinkage_trace,
    "compatible_set_summary": summary.get("compatible_set_summary", {}),
    "derived_invariants": summary.get("derived_invariants", {}),
    "contradiction_record": summary.get("contradiction_record", {}),
    "preference_irrelevance_proven": bool(summary.get("preference_irrelevance_proven", False)),
}
```

The decision-region and abstention layers are operational remediation evidence. Counterfactual explanation and algorithmic recourse literature argues that useful explanations can identify what would need to change [Wachter, Mittelstadt, and Russell 2017](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3063289), [Ustun, Spangher, and Liu 2019](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287566). In this repo, the remedy is operational rather than personal: refine search, refresh evidence, ask a preference query, expand the world model, increase budget, or abstain with a typed reason. This is not individual algorithmic recourse in the credit or lending sense; it is system-level next-action evidence for freight decision support.

### AX46. Road-Network Speed-Up Algorithms Are Infrastructure Baselines, Not Novelty

Single-criterion point-to-point road routing has mature, very fast techniques under specified metrics because preprocessing and algorithm engineering are well developed. Contraction Hierarchies are a standard road-network speed-up family [Geisberger et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-68552-4_24), with exact road-network CH results [Geisberger et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1110.0401). Customizable Route Planning supports metric customization after preprocessing [Delling et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.2014.0579). ALT landmarks are a goal-directed shortest-path speed-up [Goldberg and Harrelson 2005](https://doi.org/10.1145/1070432.1070455), and Arc-Flags are another preprocessing-based route-planning approach [Hilger et al.](https://doi.org/10.1090/dimacs/074/03). Bast et al. give the wider algorithm-engineering survey [Bast et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-49487-6_2). This wording is deliberately narrower than "routing is solved": multiobjective, uncertain, preference-limited freight decision support remains open.

Customizable Contraction Hierarchies should be named explicitly as a speed-up comparator family, not as implemented thesis novelty. The relevant boundary is: CH and CCH accelerate road-network routing through preprocessing/customization; this repo instead uses OSRM MLD plus transparent bounded graph search, with turn penalties and scenario transforms recorded as auditable engineering logic rather than as a CCH implementation. Cite CH [Geisberger et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-68552-4_24), exact road-network CH [Geisberger et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1110.0401), CRP/MLD-style customization [Delling et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.2014.0579), CCH [Dibbelt, Strasser, and Wagner 2016](https://doi.org/10.1145/2886843), and turn-cost complications for CCH [Buchhold et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.4230/OASIcs.ATMOS.2020.9).

The report states directly: this project does not claim a faster shortest-path engine. It uses OSRM/MLD as the fast routing substrate and puts the contribution above it: auditable candidate evidence, certification, abstention, and replayable decision state. The local OSRM script shows this infrastructure choice:

```sh
osrm-partition "$OSRM_BASE"
osrm-customize "$OSRM_BASE"
exec osrm-routed --algorithm mld "$OSRM_BASE"
```

The local graph search is intentionally transparent rather than landmark-preprocessed. Compared with ALT or Arc-Flags, the route graph heuristic uses a simple Haversine/min-cost lower bound:

```python
distance_m = _haversine_m(lat, lon, goal_lat, goal_lon)
h_speed = distance_m / max_speed_mps
h_cost_density = distance_m * min_cost_per_meter if min_cost_per_meter > 0.0 else 0.0
return max(0.0, h_speed, h_cost_density)
```

That is weaker for query speed than industrial preprocessing, but better for thesis auditability because the heuristic is explainable from route geometry and cost density. The production-speed problem is delegated to OSRM; the research contribution is in route-decision evidence.

### AX47. Constrained, Time-Dependent, And Alternative-Route Literature Explain Why Freight Routing Is Hard

Problem hardness is framed through constrained shortest paths, not only shortest paths. Freight routing becomes hard because side constraints and operational states are added to graph traversal. The constrained/resource-constrained shortest path lineage includes Joksch [Joksch 1966](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-247X(66)90020-5), Handler and Zang [Handler and Zang 1980](https://doi.org/10.1002/net.3230100403), Irnich and Desaulniers' SPPRC survey chapter [Irnich and Desaulniers 2005](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-25486-2_2), and recent constrained shortest-path-at-scale work [Vera et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2021.2166).

The route graph includes stateful operational logic such as geometric U-turn filtering and proxy turn penalties alongside edge-cost shortest-path machinery. The code rejects U-turn-like transitions and assigns hard-turn penalties:

```python
if delta >= 165.0:
    return None
if delta >= 120.0:
    turn_class = "hard_turn"
    turn_penalty = 22.0
```

This is not a guarantee that all legal turn restrictions are encoded. Alternative-route quality is explained through overlap, stretch, and local optimality. Abraham and coauthors define good alternatives as meaningfully different, low-stretch, and locally reasonable [Abraham et al. 2010a](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-13193-6_3), [Abraham et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1145/2444016.2444019). Route-choice literature warns that overlapping alternatives are correlated, not independent choices [Bovy 2009](https://doi.org/10.1080/01441640802078673), [Frejinger and Bierlaire 2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trb.2006.06.003), [Bovy, Bekhor, and Prato 2008](https://doi.org/10.3141/2076-15). The project improves on naive `k` alternatives by measuring overlap, stretch, and criticality before spending refinement/certification budget.

Time-dependent and stochastic routing are limitations and motivation, not fully solved here. Time-dependent shortest-path work starts early [Cooke and Halsey 1966](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-247X(66)90009-6), and later work formalizes FIFO/non-FIFO and dynamic travel-time assumptions [Orda and Rom 1990](https://doi.org/10.1145/79147.214078). Stochastic time-dependent fastest paths add another layer of complexity [Hall 1986](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.20.3.182), [Miller-Hooks and Mahmassani 2000](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.34.2.198.12304). The repo does not claim full adaptive time-dependent optimal routing. It evaluates scenario-transformed static candidates and records uncertainty/certification state.

### AX48. Truck And Hazardous-Materials Constraints Are Honest Boundaries

Truck routing has legal and safety constraints that are not fully captured by a passenger-car route engine. Hazardous-material routing shows how risk, exposure, and time-varying networks change the objective [Erkut and Verter 2000](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-3894(99)00084-9), [Miller-Hooks and Mahmassani 1998](https://doi.org/10.3141/1645-18), and risk-equity hazmat optimization remains an active transportation problem [Liu, Gan, Wu, and Sun 2024](https://doi.org/10.1177/03611981231223186). Legal truck routing can also involve height, weight, axle, bridge, tunnel, permit, and hazmat restrictions.

This repository models toll, turn, road-class, evidence, fuel, carbon, and uncertainty pressure, but it does not claim complete statutory truck routing. Some code surfaces are proxy penalties, not legal guarantees:

```text
toll_propensity_penalty
direction_legality_proxy
road_class_mix
turn_penalty
```

That boundary strengthens the paper rather than weakening it. The system can still be publishable as a freight-route decision evidence architecture, but it states that full legal truck restriction compliance is a future integration requirement or external-engine responsibility, not a proven property of the current repo.

### AX49. Stochastic Uncertainty Is Correlated, Bounded, And Replayable, Not Distributional Truth

The uncertainty model is positioned as calibrated stochastic stress summarisation, not a claim that real traffic, fuel, weather, and emissions uncertainty are fully captured by a parametric distribution. The code uses deterministic replay seeds, correlated shocks, regime tables, bounded multiplicative factors, and empirical quantile mappings. This is closer to auditable simulation plus scenario analysis than to an unconstrained probabilistic oracle. Copula literature motivates the importance of dependence modelling [Nelsen 2006](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28678-0), but the implemented claim is narrower: the repo uses regime-level correlation matrices and Cholesky-correlated shocks, not a fitted copula model. Variance reduction can be linked to antithetic variates in Monte Carlo simulation [Hammersley and Morton 1956](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100031455).

The report highlights the bounded implementation shape:

```python
sample_count = max(8, min(requested_samples, 600))
sigma_clamped = _bounded(requested_sigma, low=0.0, high=0.6)
seed = _stable_seed(
    route_signature=route_signature,
    departure_slot=_departure_slot(departure_time_utc),
    user_seed=0 if user_seed is None else int(user_seed),
)
l_factor = _cholesky_cached(regime.corr)
```

and the variance-reduction design:

```python
z = _correlated_standard_normals(rng, l_factor=l_factor)
_append_from_shocks(z)
antithetic = (-z[0], -z[1], -z[2], -z[3], -z[4])
_append_from_shocks(antithetic)
```

The safe claim is not "the distribution is true". The safe claim is that stochastic route pressure is replayable, bounded, correlated, and documented enough to support empirical route-decision stress testing.

### AX50. Conformal Prediction Is An Important Comparator But Not A Repo Claim

This report makes a clear negative claim: this system does not claim conformal validity. Conformal prediction gives finite-sample predictive coverage under exchangeability, as in Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer [Vovk et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-06649-8), Lei et al. [Lei et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2017.1307116), and the tutorial by Angelopoulos and Bates [Angelopoulos and Bates 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511). Weighted conformal prediction handles covariate shift only under additional weighting assumptions [Tibshirani et al. 2019](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/8522-conformal-prediction-under-covariate-shift).

This project has changing route worlds, live evidence, cached/proxy data, and explicit stress cases, so exchangeability is not the right guarantee. The stronger and more honest claim is that the code returns certified singleton, certified set, or typed abstention under its inspected evidence-world model. That is a different guarantee family, and this report keeps the boundary visible.

### AX51. Design-Science Framing, Research Questions, Ablations, And Threats To Validity

This section records an earlier four-question draft framing that helped organise the evidence base before the final RQ table was consolidated in AX89. In that draft, RQ1 asked whether a freight-routing system can move beyond a single shortest-path answer and produce auditable decision outcomes: a certified singleton, certified set, or typed abstention. RQ2 asked whether decision-critical candidate search, route-evidence refresh, and value-of-information refinement provide better evidence discipline than a monolithic OSRM/ORS shortest-path comparison. RQ3 asked whether the system remains reproducible under live-data, model-asset, route-graph, and stochastic-world dependencies. RQ4 asked where the current method fails and which claims must remain conditional. The paper should use AX89 as the final consolidated RQ set; this older paragraph is retained as provenance for how the evidence questions developed.

This is a design-science contribution in the sense of Hevner et al. [Hevner et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.2307/25148625) and Wieringa [Wieringa 2014](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-43839-8): the contribution is an implemented artifact plus evidence about its behaviour. The contribution taxonomy separates artifact, method, evaluation, and governance:

```text
artifact contribution:
  dccs_refc live route-decision pipeline

method contribution:
  DCCS + REFC + VOI + certified sets + typed abstention

evaluation contribution:
  lane-based evaluation rather than one aggregate leaderboard

governance contribution:
  claim matrix + theorem map + provenance + negative results
```

The evaluation methodology is controlled, lane-based, and evidence-bounded. The system compares `V0=legacy`, `A=dccs`, `B=dccs_refc`, and `C=voi`, so each ablation adds one design layer instead of mixing all changes at once. This follows empirical software-engineering guidance that evaluation design should expose the factor under test rather than only report a final system score [Wohlin et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-29044-2). Negative results are part of the contribution because they prevent publication bias and false-positive storytelling [Ioannidis 2005](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124), [Fanelli 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-011-0494-7).

Threats to validity distinguish internal, construct, external, and conclusion validity. Internal validity is threatened by live-source volatility, cache reuse, stochastic-world sampling, and local route-engine availability; these are mitigated by strict preflight, signed manifests, fixed seeds, and explicit provenance rather than by pretending the system is deterministic. Construct validity is threatened if weighted margins, hypervolume, confidence certificates, and proxy-audit calibration are treated as the real operational objective; the report describes them as reviewable proxies for freight-routing decision quality. External validity is limited by UK assets, UK traffic/fuel/toll/carbon assumptions, and the explicit route-graph subset. Conclusion validity is limited by lane sample-size requirements, method-specific claim boundaries, and deployment-scope assumptions, which is why the suite uses BCa bootstrap intervals, Holm correction, and explicit claim narrowing machinery. Demsar's guidance on comparing classifiers across datasets is relevant to the comparative-statistics caution [Demsar 2006](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v7/demsar06a.html).

The reproducibility section states that the project targets artifact review, not just rerunnable scripts. The one-command capsule, strict preflight, model-asset manifest, fixed seeds, route-graph identity, and thesis artifact provenance align with FAIR data principles [Wilkinson et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18), W3C PROV-DM [W3C PROV-DM](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/), ACM artifact badging [ACM artifact review and badging](https://www.acm.org/publications/policies/artifact-review-and-badging-current), and computational reproducibility guidance [Sandve et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285).

The data-provenance section identifies each external dependency as a scoped source, not as ground truth. OSM-derived routing cites OpenStreetMap attribution and licensing [OpenStreetMap copyright](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright/en) and VGI quality literature [Haklay 2010](https://doi.org/10.1068/b35097). DfT road traffic counts, GOV.UK conversion factors, and Open-Meteo are input sources with scope and freshness boundaries [DfT road traffic counts](https://www.data.gov.uk/dataset/208c0e7b-353f-4e2d-8b7a-1a7118467acc/gb-road-traffic-counts), [GOV.UK conversion factors](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/government-conversion-factors-for-company-reporting), [Open-Meteo docs](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs).

The ethics and safety section frames the system as decision support, not automated dispatch authority. The responsible-deployment contribution is that unsupported or insufficiently evidenced cases terminate as typed abstentions with recommended next actions instead of producing overconfident route recommendations. This aligns with NIST AI RMF risk-management framing [NIST AI RMF 1.0](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), algorithmic-accountability arguments [Diakopoulos 2015](https://doi.org/10.1080/21670811.2014.976411), and warnings that explanation alone does not solve accountability [Selbst and Barocas 2018](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3126971).

### AX52. Decision-Critical Candidate Search Is Metareasoning, Not A K-Shortest Wrapper

The paper needs to say plainly that DCCS is a control policy over scarce evidence work. A normal `k`-shortest-path layer asks for more paths; DCCS asks which route candidates deserve refinement because they could change the decision. That distinction is the bridge to value-of-information and metareasoning: Howard's value-of-information theory says information matters when it can change a decision [Howard 1966](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074), and Russell and Wefald's metareasoning account treats computation itself as an action with expected value and cost [Russell and Wefald 1991](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(91)90015-C). The implementation adapts that idea to freight routing by making route refinement compete against budget, overlap, challenger pressure, support mass, preference relevance, and predicted refinement cost.

The routing literature supplies the lower layer: Yen-style candidate enumeration is a source of alternative paths [Yen 1971](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.17.11.712), and alternative-route research explains why overlap, stretch, and local reasonableness matter [Abraham et al. 2010a](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-13193-6_3), [Abraham et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1145/2444016.2444019). WhatIf Freight Router changes the question from "how many alternatives did the engine return?" to "which alternatives are decision-critical enough to justify spending the next refinement slot?" That is why the code exposes a candidate-criticality ledger rather than only a sorted path list:

```python
# backend/app/candidate_criticality.py
support_mass = candidate_envelope.support_mass if candidate_envelope is not None else 0.0
action_cost = max(0.0, _as_float(predicted_refine_cost))
denominator = max(1.0, action_cost)
criticality_score = (
    winner_lcb_lift
    + pairwise_gap_lcb_lift
    + flip_radius_lift
    + unresolved_winner_mass
    + preference_relevance
    + search_deficiency_risk
) / denominator
```

The tuned route-pipeline variables are also part of the method. `ROUTE_PIPELINE_SEARCH_BUDGET=6` gives the live route path enough room for an initial frontier, a challenger, and rescue/diversity work without letting a single request become an open-ended search job. `ROUTE_PIPELINE_EVIDENCE_BUDGET=3` keeps evidence refresh bounded. `ROUTE_PIPELINE_CERT_WORLD_COUNT=64` gives a moderate sampled-world basis for route certificates, while the hard setting bounds it between 10 and 500 so experiments can scale without silently becoming unbounded. `ROUTE_PIPELINE_CERTIFICATE_THRESHOLD=0.70` is an operational certification threshold, not a theorem that 70 percent is universally optimal. The code makes these assumptions explicit and bounded:

```python
# backend/app/settings.py
route_pipeline_search_budget: int = Field(default=6, ge=1, le=128)
route_pipeline_evidence_budget: int = Field(default=3, ge=0, le=64)
route_pipeline_cert_world_count: int = Field(default=64, ge=10, le=500)
route_pipeline_certificate_threshold: float = Field(default=0.70, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
route_pipeline_tau_stop: float = Field(default=0.03, ge=0.0)
route_pipeline_search_completeness_threshold: float = Field(default=0.84, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
```

The DCCS-specific knobs then encode the paper's candidate-search design. `ROUTE_DCCS_BOOTSTRAP_COUNT=3` preserves a small initial evidence set before VOI/refinement starts. `ROUTE_DCCS_OVERLAP_THRESHOLD=0.82` makes near-duplicate pressure explicit. The p-flip weights favour objective gap (`2.1`) first, then overlap (`1.4`), mechanism gap (`1.2`), and detour/stretch (`0.9`), with a negative bias (`-0.15`) so candidates need positive evidence pressure rather than being refined automatically. These are not hidden magic numbers; they are bounded, named, inspectable, and therefore defensible as tuned engineering defaults:

```python
# backend/app/settings.py and backend/app/main.py
route_dccs_overlap_threshold: float = Field(default=0.82, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
route_dccs_bootstrap_count: int = Field(default=3, ge=1, le=32)
route_dccs_pflip_bias: float = Field(default=-0.15)
route_dccs_pflip_gap_weight: float = Field(default=2.1, ge=0.0)
route_dccs_pflip_mechanism_weight: float = Field(default=1.2, ge=0.0)
route_dccs_pflip_overlap_weight: float = Field(default=1.4, ge=0.0)
route_dccs_pflip_detour_weight: float = Field(default=0.9, ge=0.0)

DCCSConfig(
    search_budget=max(0, int(search_budget)),
    bootstrap_seed_size=max(1, int(settings.route_dccs_bootstrap_count)),
    near_duplicate_threshold=float(settings.route_dccs_overlap_threshold),
    flip_bias=float(settings.route_dccs_pflip_bias),
    flip_objective_weight=float(settings.route_dccs_pflip_gap_weight),
    flip_mechanism_weight=float(settings.route_dccs_pflip_mechanism_weight),
    flip_overlap_weight=float(settings.route_dccs_pflip_overlap_weight),
    flip_stretch_weight=float(settings.route_dccs_pflip_detour_weight),
)
```

This is better aligned with the thesis evidence objective than `first_n`, `random_n`, or corridor-uniform refinement because those alternatives spend effort without asking whether the candidate can change the selected route, certified set, or abstention reason. It is not better because it is theoretically optimal for every graph; it is better for this thesis because it makes the computation budget part of the auditable decision object.

### AX53. Certification Semantics, Selective Refusal, And Why The Terminal Object Matters

The terminal object is one of the most important publishable ideas in the codebase. A conventional routing API returns a route or an error. This project returns a decision state: certified singleton, certified set, or typed abstention. The distinction connects to selective classification and reject-option work: Chow formalised the error/reject tradeoff [Chow 1970](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1970.1054406), El-Yaniv and Wiener formalised risk-coverage tradeoffs [El-Yaniv and Wiener 2010](https://jmlr.org/papers/v11/el-yaniv10a.html), and later selective prediction work shows that refusing unsupported predictions is a legitimate design action rather than a failure mode [Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08500), [SelectiveNet 2019](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/geifman19a.html).

The route-specific adaptation is that rejection is not an undifferentiated "no answer". The code classifies why a route could not be certified and attaches a remedy:

```python
# backend/app/abstention.py
TypedAbstentionReason = Literal[
    "typed_abstention_recommended",
    "uncertified_due_to_search",
    "uncertified_due_to_evidence",
    "uncertified_due_to_preference",
    "uncertified_due_to_out_of_support_world_model",
    "uncertified_due_to_budget",
    "uncertified_due_to_model_assumption",
]

return {
    "uncertified_due_to_search": "expand_search",
    "uncertified_due_to_evidence": "refresh_evidence",
    "uncertified_due_to_preference": "ask_preference",
    "uncertified_due_to_out_of_support_world_model": "expand_world_model",
    "uncertified_due_to_budget": "increase_budget",
    "uncertified_due_to_model_assumption": "review_model_assumptions",
}[self.reason_code]
```

The certified-set object then distinguishes a singleton recommendation from a safe set of remaining candidates. This matters because a paper reviewer may ask what happens when the top route is not uniquely justified. The answer is in the code: `CertifiedSetState.safe` is true only when certification and support both hold, and singleton certification depends on a decision-region certificate, a winner threshold, and challengers being excluded or unresolved in a visible way.

```python
# backend/app/certified_set.py
certified = bool(
    support_flag
    and decision_certified
    and winner_score >= threshold_value
    and excluded
)
exclusion_basis = [
    "confidence_state_threshold",
    "decision_region_certified" if decision_certified else "decision_region_not_certified",
    "winner_threshold_met" if winner_score >= threshold_value else "winner_threshold_not_met",
]
if not support_flag:
    exclusion_basis.append("support_flag_false")
```

This is also where the report must keep robust-optimization and conformal-prediction boundaries visible. Robust shortest-path and distributionally robust optimization are relevant comparators [Aissi et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2008.09.012), [Delage and Ye 2010](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.1090.0741), [Wiesemann, Kuhn, and Sim 2014](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2014.1314), [Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn 2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10107-017-1172-1), but this implementation does not claim global distributional robustness. Conformal prediction is relevant because it gives finite-sample coverage under exchangeability [Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-06649-8), [Angelopoulos and Bates 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511), but this repo does not claim exchangeability-based conformal validity. Its defensible claim is narrower and stronger for the artifact: each terminal decision carries its inspected evidence, support state, abstention cause, and route-specific remedy.

### AX54. Multi-Fidelity Evidence And Proxy-Audit Limits Are Part Of The Contribution

The codebase has to use mixed evidence: live sources, route-engine results, cached artifacts, proxy predictions, and audited slices. The paper does not hide that. Multi-fidelity and model-calibration literature explains why combining lower- and higher-fidelity evidence is useful but dangerous if uncertainty and bias are not visible; Kennedy and O'Hagan's calibration work is the standard reference point for model discrepancy thinking [Kennedy and O'Hagan 2001](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00294), while later uncertainty-quantification work warns that calibration assumptions can be fragile [Tuo and Wu 2016](https://doi.org/10.1137/151005841). Model-card and dataset-documentation practice supplies the documentation standard [Mitchell et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287596), [Gebru et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1145/3458723).

The repo's improvement is not that proxy data is magically true. It is that proxy, audit, support, positivity, correction, leakage safety, and recommendation state are explicit. Causal-inference sources justify the caution: propensity scores depend on treatment/assignment assumptions [Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/70.1.41), and doubly robust estimators only protect conclusions under their modelling assumptions [Bang and Robins 2005](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00377.x). The implementation preserves those assumptions instead of treating proxy correction as an automatic validity machine:

```python
# backend/app/support_model.py
class MultiFidelitySummary:
    proxy_world_count: int = 0
    audit_world_count: int = 0
    proxy_bias_model_version: str = ""
    audit_propensity_version: str = ""
    proxy_correction_active: bool = False
    multi_fidelity_certificate_basis: str = "proxy_only"
    correction_training_leakage_safe: bool = False
    propensity_training_leakage_safe: bool = False
    leakage_safe_training: bool = False
    correction_path_estimator: str = "proxy_only"
    proxy_only_fraction: float = 1.0
```

The positivity diagnostic is equally important. If audit coverage is weak or propensities are small, the code recommends collecting more audit evidence or widening support instead of certifying through a thin proxy layer:

```python
# backend/app/support_model.py
positivity_ok = (
    audited_count > 0
    and coverage_ratio >= _clamp01(min_audit_coverage_ratio)
    and minimum_propensity >= _clamp01(min_propensity)
)
if audited_count <= 0:
    recommendation = "collect_initial_audits"
elif coverage_ratio < _clamp01(min_audit_coverage_ratio):
    recommendation = "increase_audit_coverage"
elif weak_overlap_detected:
    recommendation = "widen_support_before_proxy_certification"
else:
    recommendation = "ready_for_support_aware_correction"
```

This is a publishable design point because many applied routing systems expose a result and perhaps a confidence number, but not the support conditions under which that number can be trusted. The repo is better for a thesis evidence base because it can say why a proxy-supported decision is in support, weakly supported, proxy-only, partially audited, or not certifiable.

### AX55. Emissions And Carbon Are Route-Decision Evidence, Not A Regulatory Inventory

The paper can now make a strong but bounded emissions claim. The Pollution-Routing Problem shows that fuel and emissions belong inside routing decisions [Bektas and Laporte 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trb.2011.02.004). Green road-freight surveys show that speed, load, vehicle type, grade, and operating context materially affect energy and emissions [Demir, Bektas, and Laporte 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2013.12.033), [Koç, Bektas, and Laporte 2026](https://doi.org/10.1080/01605682.2024.2446655). Eco-routing work shows that the green route may differ from the fastest route because grade and speed change fuel use [Boriboonsomsin and Barth 2009](https://doi.org/10.3141/2139-03), [Boriboonsomsin et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1109/TITS.2012.2204051). Heavy-duty emissions modelling literature makes the same point for truck-like vehicles [Barth et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.3141/1880-02).

The repo improves on a cosmetic `kgCO2 = distance * factor` label by making emissions part of segment cost, uncertainty, scope adjustment, carbon price, and route selection. The code explicitly records fuel factors and then interpolates consumption over load, speed, grade, and temperature:

```python
# backend/app/fuel_energy_model.py
FUEL_EMISSIONS_KG_PER_L = {
    "diesel": 2.68,
    "petrol": 2.31,
    "lng": 1.51,
}

liters_per_100km = _interp_grid4d(
    fuel_grid,
    load_axis=consumption_surface.axes.load_factor,
    speed_axis=consumption_surface.axes.speed_kmh,
    grade_axis=consumption_surface.axes.grade_pct,
    temp_axis=consumption_surface.axes.ambient_temp_c,
    load_factor=load_factor,
    speed_kmh=speed_value,
    grade_pct=grade_value,
    ambient_temp_c=temp_value,
)
emissions_factor = FUEL_EMISSIONS_KG_PER_L.get(fuel_type, FUEL_EMISSIONS_KG_PER_L["diesel"])
emissions_kg = liters * emissions_factor
```

The standards boundary is just as important as the code. ISO 14083 is the correct external standard reference for quantifying and reporting transport-chain greenhouse gas emissions [ISO 14083:2023](https://www.iso.org/standard/78864.html). HBEFA, COPERT, EPA MOVES5, DESNZ/GOV.UK conversion factors, and GLEC are proper comparators for official factors or accounting frameworks [HBEFA methodology](https://www.hbefa.net/en/methodology), [COPERT methodology](https://copert.emisia.com/copert/methodology/), [USEPA 2024, MOVES5](https://www.epa.gov/moves/latest-version-motor-vehicle-emission-simulator-moves), [GOV.UK conversion factors](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/government-conversion-factors-for-company-reporting), [Smart Freight Centre 2025, GLEC Framework v3.2](https://smart-freight-centre-media.s3.amazonaws.com/documents/GLEC_FRAMEWORK_v3.2_21_10_25_1.pdf). The paper's claim is therefore not "this replaces ISO, MOVES, HBEFA, COPERT, or GLEC." The claim is that route-level emissions evidence is integrated into a transparent decision pipeline, with the assumptions visible enough for critique.

### AX56. What The Published Paper Can Claim As Its Central Contribution

The problem addressed is not ordinary route calculation. The addressed problem is auditable freight-route decision support under competing objectives, incomplete preferences, uncertain evidence, and bounded computation. The system takes fast routing engines and local graph logic as infrastructure, then builds a decision layer that records candidate provenance, objective tradeoffs, route evidence, sampled worlds, preference state, certificate status, and typed abstention. That is the bridge from a codebase to a publishable applied paper: the artifact demonstrates how route recommendation can become an evidence object rather than a one-line API answer.

The problem is hard because each individual subproblem has a mature literature and none of them alone solves the applied workflow. Fast road routing is addressed by CH, MLD, CRP, ALT, Arc-Flags, and OSRM-like engines. Multiobjective routing is addressed by Pareto, scalarisation, MCDA, and compromise ranking. Uncertainty is addressed by robust optimization, stochastic shortest paths, confidence sequences, CVaR, scenario analysis, and conformal prediction under separate assumptions. Preference ambiguity is addressed by utility elicitation and robust ordinal regression. Explainability is addressed by XAI and recourse literature. The codebase's contribution is to join these concerns in one inspectable route-decision contract, while keeping each guarantee scoped to what the code and artifacts actually support.

The main alternatives are clear. Commercial systems such as Google Routes, HERE, ArcGIS VRP, PTV xTour, Trimble PC*Miler, Descartes, ORTEC, and Transporeon are stronger operational products in their domains. Open systems such as OSRM, openrouteservice, and GraphHopper are strong routing substrates. Classical academic alternatives include VRP/VRPTW algorithms [Dantzig and Ramser 1959](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.6.1.80), [Solomon 1987](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.35.2.254), evolutionary multiobjective optimization such as NSGA-II [Deb et al. 2002](https://doi.org/10.1109/4235.996017), and robust/distributional shortest-path formulations. This repo is better for the stated research contribution because it does not hide the decision in an engine, a fleet optimiser, or an opaque evolutionary search. It makes the evidence state, abstention state, and claim boundary visible.

The design is justified because it is layered. Routing engines generate evidence; DCCS decides which candidates deserve scarce refinement; REFC evaluates route evidence over bounded worlds; VOI decides whether more search/evidence/preference work is worth its cost; MCDA/risk layers make time, money, emissions, and tail pressure comparable; support diagnostics stop proxy evidence from pretending to be audited truth; and provenance/signature layers make artifacts replayable. The architecture is better than a single monolithic optimiser for this project because thesis readers can inspect the moving parts and see where the recommendation came from.

The evaluation is evidence-bounded. It is not a vague claim that "the system is better". The evaluator separates `legacy`, `dccs`, `dccs_refc`, and `voi` lanes, records scoped metrics, preserves negative results, and keeps deployment limitations visible. That aligns with empirical software-engineering and artifact-review practice [Wohlin et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-29044-2), [ACM artifact review and badging](https://www.acm.org/publications/policies/artifact-review-and-badging-current), [FAIR principles](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18). The correct paper framing is that the project demonstrates a reproducible architecture and lane-specific evidence, not universal deployment readiness.

The limitations are explicit and strengthen the paper. The system does not prove UK-wide legal truck compliance, does not replace commercial fleet dispatch, does not replace regulatory emissions accounting, does not provide conformal coverage, does not prove global robust optimality, and does not make OSRM/ORS obsolete. It solves a more precise and more publishable problem: how to make freight-route recommendations conditional, reviewable, evidence-backed, and fail-closed when the evidence is not strong enough.

### AX57. Road-Routing Engines Are Substrates; The Contribution Is The Evidence Layer Above Them

A published paper must distinguish routing speed from decision evidence. The road-routing literature contains highly specialised point-to-point techniques: Dijkstra's algorithm gives the classical nonnegative shortest-path baseline [Dijkstra 1959](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390), A* adds an admissible lower-bound heuristic [Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael 1968](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136), contraction hierarchies accelerate road queries through node ordering and shortcuts [Geisberger et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-68552-4_24), customizable route planning separates metric-independent preprocessing from metric customization [Delling et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-20662-7_9), transit-node routing, hub labeling, reach, and highway-dimension work explain why road networks admit powerful speed-ups [Arz, Luxen, and Sanders 2013](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-38527-8_7), [Abraham et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-20662-7_20), [Goldberg, Kaplan, and Werneck 2006](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611972863.13), [Abraham et al. 2010b](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611973075.64). That literature is not a threat to the thesis claim; it defines the substrate boundary. WhatIf Freight Router does not claim to beat CH, CRP/MLD, transit-node routing, hub labels, OSRM, GraphHopper, or openrouteservice at raw shortest-path query latency. Its claim is that raw route computation is only the first evidence source in a freight decision contract.

The backend code reflects that substrate boundary because OSRM and ORS are explicit clients, not hidden competitors or replaced inventions:

```python
# backend/app/main.py
from .routing_ors import ORSClient, ORSError, ORSRoute, local_ors_runtime_manifest
from .routing_osrm import OSRMClient, OSRMError, extract_segment_annotations

app.state.osrm = OSRMClient(base_url=settings.osrm_base_url, profile=settings.osrm_profile)
app.state.ors = ORSClient(base_url=settings.ors_base_url, timeout_ms=settings.ors_directions_timeout_ms)
```

The implementation reflects that boundary. The local route graph has an optional A* lower-bound hook, but it is deliberately simple, inspectable, and bounded by settings rather than presented as a new road-routing accelerator:

```python
# backend/app/routing_graph.py
def _route_graph_heuristic_fn(graph: RouteGraph, *, goal_node_id: str):
    if not bool(settings.route_graph_a_star_heuristic_enabled):
        return None
    goal_coords = graph.nodes.get(goal_node_id)
    if goal_coords is None:
        return None
    max_speed_kph = float(settings.route_graph_heuristic_max_speed_kph)
    if not math.isfinite(max_speed_kph) or max_speed_kph <= 0.0:
        return None
    max_speed_mps = max(1.0, max_speed_kph / 3.6)
    min_cost_per_meter = max(0.0, float(getattr(graph, "min_cost_per_meter", 0.0)))
```

The better-than-alternative claim is therefore scoped. Commercial routers and engine libraries are better at industrial-grade routing coverage, preprocessed latency, and fleet integrations. This repo is better for a publishable decision-support artifact because it records what the route engine did, where it failed, how many states it explored, how many candidates were emitted, what budget was consumed, and why a path search returned no candidate. A black-box API normally hides those details behind a route response; this code promotes them into reportable evidence:

```python
# backend/app/routing_graph.py
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GraphCandidateDiagnostics:
    explored_states: int
    generated_paths: int
    emitted_paths: int
    candidate_budget: int
    effective_max_hops: int = 0
    effective_hops_floor: int = 0
    effective_state_budget_initial: int = 0
    effective_state_budget: int = 0
    no_path_reason: str = ""
    no_path_detail: str = ""
```

This is the correct paper framing: routing engines calculate candidate movement through a network; WhatIf Freight Router evaluates whether those candidates are enough to justify a route decision. That difference addresses a different layer from routing-engine papers and products: speed-up algorithms often optimise the path query but do not explain whether the resulting route recommendation is preference-stable, evidence-supported, carbon-scope-aware, or safe to certify.

### AX58. Choice-Set Generation Is A Research Problem, Not A UI Alternatives Toggle

Route-choice and alternative-route literature is essential because the paper cannot treat `alternatives=true` as a solved scientific method. Empirical shortest-path comparisons on road networks show that implementation details matter [Zhan and Noon 1998](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.32.1.65), and GIS routing work gives evidence for A* as an efficient road-network method under appropriate heuristics [Zeng and Church 2009](https://doi.org/10.1080/13658810801949850). Route-choice-set generation is harder than asking for `k` paths: Prato's review treats choice-set generation as a central modelling problem [Prato 2009](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1755-5345%2813%2970005-8), Bekhor, Ben-Akiva, and Ramming evaluate alternatives such as link elimination and labeling [Bekhor et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10479-006-0009-8), and limited-overlap K-shortest-path work formalises why candidates that share too much of the same corridor can be weak alternatives [Chondrogiannis et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00778-020-00604-x). Formal trajectory similarity measures such as the Frechet distance also show that route similarity is a nontrivial geometric concept [Alt and Godau 1995](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0218195995000064).

The repo adapts that literature into a pragmatic evidence policy. It uses corridor signatures and Jaccard-like node overlap as cheap deterministic screening signals. That is not a claim that node overlap is a full trajectory-similarity metric. It is a claim that the candidate generator records enough diversity evidence to avoid blindly refining duplicates:

```python
# backend/app/decision_critical.py
def _corridor_signature(path: tuple[str, ...]) -> str:
    if not path:
        return "empty"
    pivot = path[len(path) // 2]
    return _stable_hash([path[0], pivot, path[-1]])

def _overlap_ratio(path: tuple[str, ...], peer_paths: Sequence[tuple[str, ...]]) -> float:
    if not path or not peer_paths:
        return 0.0
    candidate = set(path)
    best = 0.0
    for peer in peer_paths:
        peer_set = set(peer)
        union = candidate | peer_set
        if union:
            best = max(best, len(candidate & peer_set) / len(union))
    return best
```

The baseline-selection policy makes that design visible. `first_n` and `random_n` are useful controls because they represent naive and stochastic alternatives. `uniform_corridor_n` is stronger because it samples across corridor signatures, but it is still only a baseline. DCCS is better for the thesis contribution because it moves beyond "diverse enough" and asks whether the candidate could alter the decision certificate:

```python
# backend/app/decision_critical.py
BASELINE_SELECTION_POLICIES = ("first_n", "random_n", "uniform_corridor_n", "corridor_uniform")

if policy_key == "uniform_corridor_n":
    corridor_to_ids: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for candidate in candidates:
        candidate_id = stable_candidate_id(candidate)
        path = _normalise_path(candidate.get("graph_path", candidate.get("path", candidate.get("node_ids"))))
        corridor_to_ids.setdefault(_corridor_signature(path), []).append(candidate_id)
```

This gives the published paper a clear answer to "why not just use OSRM alternatives, GraphHopper alternatives, or k-shortest paths?" Those methods produce route alternatives. The project turns alternatives into evidence-bearing candidates, records when diversity collapses, and allows the decision to abstain if the candidate set is too narrow to support the claim.

### AX59. Turn Costs, Scenario Transforms, And Via-Point Realisation Are Engineering Contributions With Explicit Limits

Plain shortest-path algorithms assume the cost of an arc can be evaluated independently. Road freight often violates that simplification: turn costs and restrictions are transition costs, not ordinary edge weights. Winter's turn-cost work explains this edge-edge structure [Winter 2002](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1020853410145), Vanhove and Fack compare shortest-path methods with turn restrictions [Vanhove and Fack 2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.orl.2012.06.001), and recent CCH work shows that turn costs complicate even modern preprocessing/customization pipelines [Buchhold et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.4230/OASIcs.ATMOS.2020.9). The repository implements a transition-state search hook so route generation can penalise or reject local movement patterns without pretending they are ordinary edge costs:

```python
# backend/app/k_shortest.py
if transition_state_fn is not None:
    prev_node = path[-2] if len(path) > 1 else None
    transition = transition_state_fn(prev_node, node, nxt)
    if transition is None:
        continue
    next_state_key, transition_penalty = transition
new_cost = cost + max(0.001, float(edge_cost)) + max(0.0, float(transition_penalty))
```

Yen-style spur generation remains visible too. Replacement-path and K-shortest-simple-path literature uses edge and node exclusion to expose alternatives, and this code follows that tradition while adding freight-specific diagnostics and transition logic:

```python
# backend/app/k_shortest.py
if tuple(p.nodes[: spur_idx + 1]) == root_path and len(p.nodes) > spur_idx + 1:
    banned_edges.add((p.nodes[spur_idx], p.nodes[spur_idx + 1]))

banned_nodes = set(root_path[:-1])
spur = _dijkstra_shortest_path(
    adjacency=adjacency,
    start=spur_node,
    goal=goal,
    banned_nodes=banned_nodes,
    banned_edges=banned_edges,
    transition_state_fn=transition_state_fn,
    heuristic_fn=heuristic_fn,
)
```

Scenario transforms are similarly bounded. Dynamic shortest-path research studies online graph updates and incremental repair, including Ramalingam and Reps's incremental shortest-path generalisation [Ramalingam and Reps 1996](https://doi.org/10.1006/jagm.1996.0046) and Demetrescu and Italiano's fully dynamic shortest-path work [Demetrescu and Italiano 2004](https://doi.org/10.1145/780542.780567). This repo does not claim either property. It instead evaluates scenario-transformed static candidate evidence and records the transform version. The transform coefficients are inspectable and clamped, so a reader can see how traffic, incidents, weather, hour bucket, road class, and duration multipliers affect segment duration:

```python
# backend/app/routing_graph.py
edge_time_scale = max(
    0.55,
    min(
        2.80,
        1.0
        + ((duration_multiplier - 1.0) * sensitivity * 0.36)
        + ((traffic_pressure - 1.0) * sensitivity * 0.24)
        + ((incident_pressure - 1.0) * sensitivity * 0.12)
        + ((weather_pressure - 1.0) * sensitivity * 0.08)
        + ((road_factor - 1.0) * sensitivity * 0.15),
    ),
)
base_segment_durations_s.append((seg_m / max(1.0, seg_speed_mps)) * edge_time_scale)
```

The limits are important. This is not full statutory UK truck legality, not full turn-restriction encoding, and not an online dynamic shortest-path algorithm. The design is still better for the paper's problem than a static route list because it captures the exact class of engineering uncertainty that applied freight decisions face: a candidate path must be generated, realised, stress-transformed, scored, and then either certified or rejected with a reason.

### AX60. SMAA, Robust Ordinal Thinking, And The Preference State Explain Why One Weight Vector Is Not Enough

A paper reviewer will ask why the system does not simply ask the user for weights and return a weighted sum. The answer belongs in MCDA and preference-uncertainty literature. Stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis (SMAA) was created for multicriteria decision problems with imprecise data and incomplete preferences [Lahdelma, Hokkanen, and Salminen 1998](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0377-2217%2897%2900163-X). SMAA-2 extends the idea to rank acceptability across all ranks [Lahdelma and Salminen 2001](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.49.3.444.11220), and Tervonen and Figueira survey the SMAA family as a practical decision-support approach under uncertainty [Tervonen and Figueira 2008](https://doi.org/10.1002/mcda.407). Robust ordinal regression makes a complementary point: decision conclusions should distinguish necessary conclusions from possible conclusions under compatible preference models [Greco, Mousseau, and Slowinski 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2007.08.013).

WhatIf Freight Router is not claiming to be a full SMAA implementation. It implements a route-specific evidence analogue: possible-best routes, necessary-best routes, compatible-set size, a volume proxy, support status, contradiction status, and invariants. This is better than a one-vector weighted-sum recommender because it preserves the uncertainty that remains after the current preference evidence:

```python
# backend/app/preference_state.py
class CompatibleSetSummary(BaseModel):
    route_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    compatible_set_size: int = Field(default=0, ge=0)
    compatible_set_volume_proxy: float = Field(default=1.0, ge=0.0)
    necessary_best_prob: float = Field(default=0.0, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    possible_best_prob: float = Field(default=1.0, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    necessary_best_route_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    possible_best_route_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    support_flag: bool = True
    support_reason: str | None = None
```

The invariant code is important because it shows that the project enforces relationships a thesis reader can reason about: necessary-best cannot exceed possible-best, necessary-best ids must be included in possible-best ids, compatible volume cannot become negative, and contradiction state is explicit:

```python
# backend/app/preference_update.py
def validate_preference_invariants(state: PreferenceState) -> dict[str, bool]:
    summary = state.compatible_set_summary
    return {
        "necessary_best_prob_le_possible_best_prob": summary.necessary_best_prob <= summary.possible_best_prob,
        "no_necessary_best_without_possible_best": set(summary.necessary_best_route_ids).issubset(
            set(summary.possible_best_route_ids)
        ),
        "compatible_set_volume_nonincreasing_after_query": volume_trace_nonincreasing(state),
        "preference_contradiction_free": not state.contradiction_record.contradiction_detected,
        "query_history_matches_trace_or_zero": len(state.shrinkage_trace) == 0
        or len(state.shrinkage_trace) <= len(state.query_history),
    }
```

The stronger published claim is not "the system knows the user's utility function." The stronger claim is that the system refuses to collapse missing preference information into fake precision. It is better than an ordinary weighted-sum dashboard because the route recommendation remains conditional on visible preference evidence, and when the evidence is insufficient the system can ask a typed query or abstain.

### AX61. Constructive Preference Elicitation, Rank Reversal, And Why Ranking Is Provisional

Constructive preference elicitation is another required external frame. Chajewska, Koller, and Parr argue that utility elicitation should be decision-directed rather than a separate demand for a complete utility model [Chajewska et al. 2000](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1579526). Conversational recommendation work shows how partial preference constraints can support recommendation without full utility identification [Viappiani and Boutilier 2009](https://doi.org/10.1145/1639714.1639732), and constructive preference literature argues that some preferences are formed through interaction rather than simply revealed [Pigozzi et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2017.00071). That literature maps directly onto the typed query design:

```python
# backend/app/preference_queries.py
PreferenceQueryType = Literal["pairwise", "threshold", "ratio", "veto", "time_guard"]
```

Each query type records a different kind of evidence. `pairwise` states a direct comparison, `threshold` states an acceptable bound, `ratio` states a tradeoff relation, `veto` states a hard exclusion, and `time_guard` states an operational time constraint. This is better than a generic slider because the system knows what kind of preference information changed the decision state. A slider changes a score; a typed query changes an evidence ledger.

Rank reversal literature then explains why the scalar rank remains provisional. Belton and Gear identified rank-reversal problems in AHP [Belton and Gear 1983](https://doi.org/10.1016/0305-0483%2883%2990047-6), and later work shows that rank reversal can occur in methods such as SAW and TOPSIS [Wang and Luo 2009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcm.2008.06.019), [Garcia-Cascales and Lamata 2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcm.2011.12.022). The repo therefore treats MCDA rankings as selection heuristics inside a larger certificate, not as final truth. This is where the design is stronger than a simple TOPSIS/VIKOR route selector: candidate-set sensitivity is not hidden.

The published paper can say that scalar score profiles are useful but insufficient. The final object is not "route with minimum scalar score"; it is a `DecisionPackage` carrying terminal type, selected route, certified set, abstention, certificate summary, preference state, and decision-region state:

```python
# backend/app/models.py
class DecisionPackage(BaseModel):
    terminal_type: Literal["certified_singleton", "certified_set", "typed_abstention"] = (
        "certified_singleton"
    )
    selected: "RouteOption | None" = None
    candidates: list["RouteOption"] = Field(default_factory=list)
    recommended_route: "RouteOption | None" = None
    certified_set: list["RouteOption"] = Field(default_factory=list)
    abstention: AbstentionRecord | None = None
    certificate_summary: dict[str, Any] | RouteCertificationSummary | None = None
    winner_confidence_state: WinnerConfidenceState | dict[str, Any] | None = None
    decision_region_state: DecisionRegionState | dict[str, Any] | None = None
    preference_state: PreferenceState = Field(default_factory=PreferenceState)
```

This addresses a rank-only MCDA dashboard gap. Many systems provide a ranked list without enough evidence about whether the rank is stable, whether the preference model is complete, or whether a near competitor could win under a plausible query. WhatIf Freight Router exposes those weaknesses as first-class state.

### AX62. Explanation, Recourse, And DSS Literature Make The System A Decision-Support Evidence Contract

The explanation claim needs to be stronger than "the UI explains the route." XAI literature distinguishes explanation generation from explanation usefulness and evaluation. Miller argues that human explanations are contrastive and social [Miller 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2018.07.007), Hoffman, Klein, and Mueller argue that XAI needs measurement criteria [Hoffman et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/1541931218621047), Abdul et al. map explainable and accountable systems across HCI and AI [Abdul et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174156), and Sokol and Flach propose explainability fact sheets as a structured way to assess explanation practice [Sokol and Flach 2020](https://doi.org/10.1145/3351095.3372870). Recourse literature adds another constraint: a counterfactual or remedy is only useful if it is feasible and actionable [Poyiadzi et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1145/3375627.3375850), [Karimi et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.04050).

The repo adapts that to freight decision support. It does not promise personal algorithmic recourse in the credit-scoring sense, and it does not produce magical counterfactuals such as "make a road shorter." It produces operational remediation evidence: expand search, refresh evidence, ask a preference query, widen the world model, increase a budget, or review a model assumption. The VOI controller makes those remedies finite by stopping when budgets are exhausted, when no feasible action exists, or when the best action is below the stop threshold:

```python
# backend/app/voi_controller.py
if state.remaining_search_budget <= 0 and state.remaining_evidence_budget <= 0:
    return _build_stop_certificate(
        state=state,
        config=cfg,
        fragility=fragility,
        current_certificate=current_certificate,
        stop_reason="budget_exhausted",
        best_rejected_action=best_rejected_action,
        certificate_value=certificate_value,
    )

actions = build_action_menu(state, dccs=dccs, fragility=fragility, config=cfg)
feasible_actions = [action for action in actions if action.kind != "stop"]
if not feasible_actions:
    return _build_stop_certificate(
        state=state,
        config=cfg,
        fragility=fragility,
        current_certificate=current_certificate,
        stop_reason=(
            "search_incomplete_no_action_worth_it"
            if state.search_completeness_score < cfg.search_completeness_threshold
            else "no_action_worth_it"
        ),
        best_rejected_action=best_rejected_action,
        certificate_value=certificate_value,
    )
top_action = feasible_actions[0]
if top_action.q_score < cfg.stop_threshold:
    best_rejected_action = top_action.as_dict()
    return _build_stop_certificate(
        state=state,
        config=cfg,
        fragility=fragility,
        current_certificate=current_certificate,
        stop_reason=(
            "search_incomplete_no_action_worth_it"
            if state.search_completeness_score < cfg.search_completeness_threshold
            else "no_action_worth_it"
        ),
        best_rejected_action=best_rejected_action,
        certificate_value=certificate_value,
    )
```

Classical decision-support-system literature gives this a discipline-level frame. DSS is not just optimisation; it is structured support for decisions involving data, models, and interaction [Keen 1987](https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-9236%2887%2990180-1), and Arnott and Pervan's DSS review stresses relevance, evaluation, and practical system contribution [Arnott and Pervan 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2007.09.003). WhatIf Freight Router is best described as a model-driven freight DSS with an evidence contract. That is a stronger and more defensible publication claim than "a green route app" because every recommendation is accompanied by terminal semantics, provenance, route evidence, preference evidence, support diagnostics, and a stop reason.

The comparison against commercial systems is therefore precise. Google Route Optimization, HERE Routing/Tour Planning, ArcGIS VRP, PTV xTour, Trimble routing reports, Descartes, ORTEC, and Transporeon are broader operational products. They are not displaced by this repo. This repo is better for a transparent academic contribution because its assumptions, code paths, evidence budgets, certificates, abstentions, and failure states are inspectable and can be cited directly.

### AX63. Tail Risk, CVaR, And Thesis-Specific Risk Penalties Are Explicitly Bounded

The risk model needs explicit academic framing because it is easy for a paper to overclaim risk optimality. CVaR, also called expected shortfall, is a coherent tail-risk measure in optimisation literature [Rockafellar and Uryasev 2000](https://doi.org/10.21314/JOR.2000.038), and coherent risk-measure theory gives the broader axiomatic background [Artzner et al. 1999](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9965.00068). The repository implements empirical CVaR over sampled values and then uses thesis-specific penalties on CVaR excess. It does not claim a full distributionally robust optimisation theorem.

The code is explicit about that boundary. The CVaR function integrates the empirical tail quantile function over `[alpha, 1]`, and the robust objective documents where it departs from textbook risk measures:

```python
# backend/app/risk_model.py
def cvar(values: Iterable[float], *, alpha: float = 0.95) -> float:
    ordered = sorted(float(v) for v in values)
    if not ordered:
        return 0.0
    n = len(ordered)
    if n == 1:
        return ordered[0]

    alpha_clamped = min(1.0, max(0.0, float(alpha)))
    if alpha_clamped >= 1.0:
        return ordered[-1]

    knots: list[float] = [alpha_clamped]
    for idx in range(n):
        p = idx / (n - 1)
        if alpha_clamped < p < 1.0:
            knots.append(p)
    knots.append(1.0)
```

```python
# backend/app/risk_model.py
def robust_objective(
    *,
    mean_value: float,
    cvar_value: float | None,
    risk_aversion: float,
    risk_family: str = "cvar_excess",
    risk_theta: float = 1.0,
) -> float:
    if cvar_value is None:
        return float(mean_value)
    tail_excess = max(0.0, float(cvar_value) - float(mean_value))
    risk = max(0.0, float(risk_aversion))
    family = str(risk_family or "cvar_excess").strip().lower()
    if family == "entropic":
        theta = max(1e-6, float(risk_theta))
        # This is a thesis-specific entropic-style tail penalty, not the
        # canonical entropic risk measure on the full loss distribution.
        penalty = math.log1p(risk * math.expm1(theta * tail_excess)) / theta
        return float(mean_value) + penalty
    if family == "downside_semivariance":
        scale = max(1.0, abs(float(mean_value)))
        # This is a thesis-specific quadratic penalty on CVaR excess, not the
        # textbook downside semivariance definition over centered tail losses.
        penalty = (tail_excess * tail_excess) / scale
        return float(mean_value) + (risk * penalty)
    return float(mean_value) + (risk * tail_excess)
```

This is better than a route score that mixes "risk" into a hidden coefficient because the paper can name the exact mathematical deviation. The implementation uses CVaR as tail evidence, then offers `cvar_excess`, `entropic`, and `downside_semivariance` families as bounded engineering penalties. That gives the thesis a publishable limitation as well as a contribution: the project is honest that these are decision-support penalties, not universal risk theorems.

### AX64. Publication-Grade Evaluation Requires Negative Results, Multiple-Comparison Caution, And Artifact Evidence

The final paper must be careful about evaluation language. Bootstrap methodology, multiple-comparison control, and empirical software-engineering evaluation practice are relevant because the repo compares lanes and metrics rather than proving a single theorem. Efron's bootstrap gives the general resampling background [Efron 1979](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176344552), Holm's procedure gives a standard way to control family-wise error under multiple hypotheses [Holm 1979](https://www.jstor.org/stable/4615733), and Demsar's warning about statistical comparisons across datasets explains why rank and significance summaries must be conservative [Demsar 2006](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v7/demsar06a.html). The paper also needs Ioannidis and Fanelli for negative-result caution because blocked claims and limitations are not embarrassing cleanup details; they are evidence that the claim boundary was enforced [Ioannidis 2005](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124), [Fanelli 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-011-0494-7).

Use Holm adjustment for pre-specified confirmatory claim families. For exploratory lane or metric screens, either report them as descriptive or separate them under false-discovery-rate control such as Benjamini-Hochberg [Benjamini and Hochberg 1995](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x). Shaffer's review is a useful broader anchor for multiple-hypothesis-testing choices and terminology [Shaffer 1995](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ps.46.020195.003021). This distinction prevents the paper from accidentally treating exploratory metric search as confirmatory evidence.

This repo is better for artifact review than an ordinary prototype because it has explicit verification surfaces: backend tests, docs consistency, endpoint parity, the Notebook reference ban, local path checks, and artifact manifests. The docs checker is useful precisely because it turns documentation consistency into a current gate rather than a narrative promise: the correct response to any docs inconsistency is to fix the source of inconsistency and keep the consistency suite active. That supports a publishable "fail closed" methodology across both runtime decisions and thesis documentation.

The paper's evaluation claim is therefore layered. It can claim that the codebase evaluates `legacy`, `dccs`, `dccs_refc`, and `voi` as incremental design lanes; that evidence is carried through manifests and docs checks; that negative and blocked cases remain visible; and that statistical language is bounded by sample size, seeds, live-source volatility, and UK asset scope. It cannot claim global superiority over every router, every MCDA method, or every emissions model. That restraint is a strength: it converts the thesis from a broad product claim into a reproducible applied-systems contribution.

### AX65. External Systems Landscape And The Exact Superiority Claim For The Paper

The paper needs a precise comparison against both academic algorithms and deployed route products. Open routing engines such as [OSRM](https://project-osrm.org/docs/v26.4.0/), [openrouteservice](https://openrouteservice.org/services/), and [GraphHopper](https://docs.graphhopper.com/openapi/routing) are strong route-computation substrates. Commercial systems such as [Google Route Optimization](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/route-optimization/overview), [HERE Routing](https://docs.here.com/routing/docs/routing-intro), [HERE Tour Planning](https://docs.here.com/tour-planning/docs/introduction-tour-planning), [ArcGIS Vehicle Routing Problem](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/3.6/help/analysis/networks/vehicle-routing-problem-analysis-layer.htm), [PTV xTour](https://api.cloud.ptvgroup.com/manual/Content/API-Documentation/xtour/API_Documentation.html), [Trimble Route Reports](https://developer.trimblemaps.com/restful-apis/routing/route-reports/overview/), [Descartes](https://www.descartes.com/solutions/routing-mobile-and-telematics/route-planning-and-optimization/operational-route-planning), [ORTEC](https://ortec.com/en/solutions/vehicle-routing), and [Transporeon](https://www.transporeon.com/en/platform/transport-execution-visibility-hub) are broader operational products. Academic VRP and green-routing work provides the mathematical ancestry: Dantzig and Ramser define the original truck-dispatching problem [Dantzig and Ramser 1959](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.6.1.80), Solomon gives classic VRPTW instances and heuristics [Solomon 1987](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.35.2.254), NSGA-II supplies a canonical multiobjective evolutionary baseline [Deb et al. 2002](https://doi.org/10.1109/4235.996017), and the Pollution-Routing Problem shows how fuel and emissions enter routing optimisation [Bektas and Laporte 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trb.2011.02.004).

The exact claim is that these alternatives are better at their own primary objectives, while this project is more appropriate for the paper's stated objective: building a transparent, route-level evidence contract for carbon-aware freight decisions under uncertainty and bounded computation. A commercial route product can return a high-quality route, ETAs, restrictions, fleet plans, and operational integrations. A mathematical PRP or VRP paper can prove or benchmark an optimisation formulation. WhatIf Freight Router instead joins routing, emissions, uncertainty, preference state, candidate criticality, VOI control, certification, abstention, provenance, and docs consistency in one inspectable artifact. That integration is the contribution.

The frontend baseline-comparison code is small but conceptually important because it shows how the system compares a smart route against a baseline without pretending distance is always the main outcome. ETA, monetary cost, CO2, and distance are kept as separate deltas before any summary score is derived:

```ts
// frontend/app/lib/baselineComparison.ts
const etaDeltaS = base.duration_s - smart.duration_s;
const costDelta = base.monetary_cost - smart.monetary_cost;
const co2Delta = base.emissions_kg - smart.emissions_kg;
const distanceDeltaKm = smart.distance_km - base.distance_km;

const etaPct = ratioPctLowerIsBetter(base.duration_s, smart.duration_s);
const costPct = ratioPctLowerIsBetter(base.monetary_cost, smart.monetary_cost);
const co2Pct = ratioPctLowerIsBetter(base.emissions_kg, smart.emissions_kg);
const distancePct = ratioPctDirect(base.distance_km, smart.distance_km);
```

The "Epic/Strong/Positive/Limited gain" score is therefore not the thesis theorem. It is a UI summary over deltas. The evidence object behind it remains the real contribution. This distinction matters in the published paper because reviewers will reject overclaiming a product score, but they can evaluate an evidence contract. The correct superiority statement is: the system is not universally better than OSRM, Google, HERE, ArcGIS, PTV, Trimble, Descartes, ORTEC, Transporeon, PRP, VRP, or NSGA-II. It is better as a transparent research artifact for explaining, auditing, and bounding a freight-route recommendation.

### AX66. Research Questions, Contribution Taxonomy, And Artifact Review Are Part Of The Scientific Claim

The consolidated AX89 RQ table absorbs two publication-level concerns: can a route recommender become publication-auditable by treating abstention, partial proof, and bounded evidence as first-class outputs rather than missing results; and can live freight-routing evaluation remain falsifiable when route graphs, weather, model manifests, evidence policies, and stochastic seeds all change the evidential world? AX89 is therefore the final numbering surface for those concerns. These questions place the project inside design-science research rather than ordinary product demonstration. Hevner et al.'s design-science framework requires a purposeful artifact, relevance, rigorous evaluation, and clear contribution [Hevner et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.2307/25148625), while Wieringa's design-science method stresses the cycle between problem investigation, treatment design, and treatment validation [Wieringa 2014](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-43839-8). The repo has exactly that shape: it designs an artifact, evaluates lanes, records negative evidence, and keeps claims tied to docs and artifacts.

The contribution taxonomy is therefore fivefold. First, the routing decision artifact turns route computation into a decision package. Second, the selective-certification method distinguishes singleton certification, certified sets, and typed abstention. Third, the evaluation lane system isolates `legacy`, `dccs`, `dccs_refc`, and `voi` rather than reporting a single mixed result. Fourth, the claim-governance layer separates theorem-backed, empirical, heuristic, and non-claim statements. Fifth, the artifact-review layer records provenance, policy hashes, and bundle identities so results are not detached from the environment that produced them.

The lane design is visible in code, which lets the paper cite evaluation methodology instead of describing it vaguely:

```python
# backend/scripts/run_thesis_evaluation.py
VARIANTS: tuple[str, ...] = ("V0", "A", "B", "C")
VARIANT_PIPELINE_MODE = {"V0": "legacy", "A": "dccs", "B": "dccs_refc", "C": "voi"}
STRICT_EVIDENCE_POLICY = "no_synthetic_no_proxy_no_fallback"

LANE_METADATA_DEFAULTS: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {
    "broad_cold_proof": {
        "why": "Broad matched-budget lane for headline route-quality, controller, and runtime evidence on a larger OD slice.",
        "headline_seed_repeat_required": True,
    },
    "focused_refc_proof": {
        "why": "Focused certification lane for REFC, selective-certification, fragility, and witness behavior on harder rows.",
        "headline_seed_repeat_required": True,
    },
    "focused_voi_proof": {
        "why": "Focused controller lane for VOI action quality, stop-vs-act behavior, and certificate lift on ambiguity-heavy rows.",
        "headline_seed_repeat_required": True,
    },
}
```

This is better than a leaderboard-style evaluation because each lane answers a different validity question. `V0` gives the legacy comparator. `A` tests whether DCCS improves candidate handling. `B` tests whether route evidence and certification change the decision state. `C` tests whether VOI improves the decision process under finite budgets. The strict evidence policy keeps the evaluation honest: the paper does not claim synthetic or proxy data as if it were live operational truth.

The docs checker is part of the scientific method because it prevents the thesis report, claim matrix, theorem map, API docs, and local paths from drifting apart.
